teile.einleitung: The head louse is a tiny insect that lives in people’s hair. Lice are a nuisance, but they have nothing to do with dirt. They can occur in all children and adults.
wichtigste: The head louse is a small insect without wings.
An adult louse is about 3 millimetres long.
It feeds on blood from the scalp.
Lice crawl across when heads touch.
Their eggs are called nits and stick firmly to the hairs.
Strong itching of the head can be a sign of lice.
Head lice also occur on clean hair.

abschnitte.text: The **head louse** is an insect without wings. An adult louse is about **3 millimetres** long, roughly as big as a sesame seed. It lives only in the hair on people’s heads. Several times a day it stings into the scalp and sucks a little **blood**. This is what it feeds on.

Head lice can neither fly nor jump. They **crawl** from one head to another when heads touch. This happens, for example, when playing, cuddling or when putting heads together. Lice have **nothing to do with dirt**. They also occur on clean hair and can happen to anyone.

The eggs of lice are called **nits**. The louse sticks them to the hairs close to the scalp. It is nice and warm there. After about a week, the young lice hatch. Nits cannot simply be shaken off, which distinguishes them from dandruff.

Louse bites **itch**. Anyone who often scratches their head should have their hair checked. With a **nit comb** you find lice and nits best, because it has very closely spaced teeth. Against lice there are also special treatments from the chemist’s. It is important to inform parents and the school so that the lice do not spread further.

gewusst: A head louse is about as big as a sesame seed.
Lice can neither jump nor fly, they only crawl.

teile.einleitung: In a dislocation, a joint jumps out of its normal position. In everyday language we say it is put out of joint. It hurts a lot and needs medical treatment.
wichtigste: Dislocation is the technical word for a joint being put out of place.
If a joint is only partly out of place, it is called a subluxation.
Putting it back is called reduction in medical language.
The joint capsule and ligaments are often injured too.
You should never put a joint back yourself, because nerves, vessels or bones can be injured.
In small children the head of the radius at the elbow easily slips out of place.

abschnitte.text: In a **joint** two bones meet. Normally they fit together exactly and are held by a **joint capsule** and **ligaments**. In a **dislocation** the bones jump out of position, usually through a fall or a blow. If the joint is only partly displaced, this is called a **subluxation**. The capsule and ligaments are often stretched or tear in the process.

The **shoulder** is especially often put out of joint, because it is very mobile. A dislocated shoulder can often be recognised by looking **angular** and having a **dip**. After the first dislocation it jumps out again more easily. The reason: the capsule and ligaments stay **stretched or torn** and hold the joint less well. Sometimes an operation is then needed.

In **small children**, the **head of the radius at the elbow** can easily slip out if they are pulled up sharply by the arm. The child then holds the arm still and does not want to use it. A doctor can usually put it back quickly. In a dislocation the **kneecap** almost always jumps **outwards**. This often happens during twisting movements in sport.

You should **never put a dislocated joint back yourself**. You can injure **nerves, vessels or bones** doing so. It is better to keep the joint still, cool it and get medical treatment quickly. There, an X-ray is usually taken first, to rule out a broken bone. Putting the joint back is called **reduction** in medical language. Afterwards the joint has to be rested for a while.

gewusst: The word “luxation” comes from the Latin “luxare”, which means to dislocate.
The shoulder is the joint that is put out of place most often in humans.

teile.einleitung: A smile is one of the first ways in which people show feelings. For it, many small muscles in the face work together. Almost everywhere in the world, a smile is understood as a friendly sign.
wichtigste: For smiling you need face muscles that pull the corners of the mouth upwards.
Many face muscles are attached directly to the skin.
All movements of the face are called facial expression.
A real, happy smile can often be recognised by little lines around the eyes.
Babies smile at people on purpose after about six weeks.
A smile usually shows joy and is understood almost everywhere.

abschnitte.text: For smiling you need your **face muscles**. They pull the **corners of the mouth upwards**, and the cheeks rise. Unlike most muscles in the body, many face muscles are attached **directly to the skin**. That is why the skin moves with them when they contract. Around the mouth lies the **ring muscle of the mouth**. With it you purse your lips, for example to whistle.

All movements of the face, for example smiling, frowning or marvelling, are called **facial expression**. With it we show others how we are, often without saying a word. A smile usually shows **joy**. But you can also smile out of politeness or embarrassment. A **real, happy smile** can often be recognised by small **lines around the eyes**, because the muscles around the eyes also work with it.

Even very small babies sometimes pull their mouth into a shape, for example in their sleep. They smile at people **on purpose** only **after about six weeks**, though. This smile is an important step: the baby makes contact. Parents are especially pleased about it and smile back.

**Almost everywhere** in the world, people understand a smile as a **friendly sign**. No common language is needed. That is why a smile also helps when travelling or with new classmates who do not yet speak German, French or Italian. Smiling is also catching: someone who is smiled at often smiles back.

gewusst: Even children who are blind from birth smile, although they have never seen it.
We recognise a smiling face even from a great distance.

teile.einleitung: A children’s hospital is a hospital only for children and young people. Specialists work there who know young patients especially well. Much is arranged so that children feel more comfortable.
wichtigste: A children’s hospital treats only children and young people.
In St Gallen there is the Eastern Switzerland Children’s Hospital.
Parents can often stay with their child, even overnight.
For children who have to stay a long time, there is a hospital school.
On many children’s wards there is a playroom.
Children can often take their cuddly toy with them.

abschnitte.text: A **children’s hospital** is a hospital that treats only **children and young people**. Paediatricians, paediatric surgeons and nursing staff work there who are specially trained for young patients. Devices and beds also come in the right size. In Switzerland there are several children’s hospitals, for example the Children’s Hospital Zurich, the University Children’s Hospital of both Basels and the **Eastern Switzerland Children’s Hospital** in **St Gallen**. Other hospitals have a children’s clinic of their own.

For a sick child it is important that their family is nearby. That is why **parents** in a children’s hospital can **often stay with their child**, even **overnight**. Sometimes there is a folding bed in the room for this, or a parents’ house nearby. Siblings can usually come to visit. Parents can help with many things and comfort their child.

Some children have to stay in hospital for a **long** time, for example after a serious illness or operation. So that they do not miss too much at school, large children’s hospitals have a **hospital school**. Teachers teach the children in small groups or right at the bedside. This way something of normal daily life is kept.

On many children’s wards there is a **playroom** with games, books and craft materials. There children can **take their minds off things** and meet other children. In some hospitals, **hospital clowns** also visit the children and make them laugh. Children can often take their **cuddly toy** or a favourite cushion with them. Familiar things help you feel more comfortable in a strange place.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the dream doctors of the Theodora Foundation have been visiting children in hospitals for many years.
Many children’s hospitals explain to children before an examination, using a doll or a teddy, what will happen.

teile.einleitung: In a bone marrow transplant, a sick person receives healthy blood stem cells. It is used mainly in severe blood diseases such as leukaemia. Today it is mostly called a stem cell transplant, because the cells often no longer come directly from the bone marrow at all.
wichtigste: For developing the bone marrow transplant, E. Donnall Thomas received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1990.
In an autologous transplant, the patient gets his own stem cells back.
In an allogeneic transplant, the cells come from another person.
For this, the HLA characteristics have to match as far as possible.
A sibling has a 25 per cent chance of having the same HLA characteristics.
Today blood stem cells are usually obtained from venous blood after giving G-CSF.
Cord blood is also a source of blood stem cells.

abschnitte.text: In the **bone marrow**, all blood cells arise from **blood stem cells**. In diseases such as **leukaemia**, a form of blood cancer, this blood formation no longer works properly. Often patients first receive strong chemotherapy, sometimes also radiation. After that they receive healthy stem cells through an infusion into a vein. The cells travel by themselves to the bone marrow and make new blood there.

In an **autologous** transplant, the patient gets his **own stem cells** back. They are collected and frozen before the treatment. In an **allogeneic** transplant, the cells come from **another person**. This donor has to match the recipient well. The breakthrough for the method was made by the US doctor **E. Donnall Thomas**, who received the **Nobel Prize** in Medicine for it in **1990**.

So that foreign cells are not rejected, certain tissue characteristics have to match. They are called **HLA characteristics** and sit on the surface of many cells. Everyone inherits them half from each parent. That is why a **sibling** has, with a probability of **25 per cent**, exactly the same HLA characteristics. If nobody in the family matches, you search in worldwide **donor registers**.

In the past, the bone marrow was taken under anaesthetic from the **pelvic bone**. Today blood stem cells are usually obtained from **venous blood**. For this, the donor is given a medicine called **G-CSF** for a few days. It lures the stem cells from the bone marrow into the blood. A machine then filters them out. A further source is **cord blood**, which can be obtained after the birth and stored.

A feared complication is **graft-versus-host disease**. In it, immune cells of the donor attack the recipient’s body, for example the skin, gut or liver. The same defensive power can also be useful, though. In the **graft-versus-leukaemia effect**, the donor cells fight cancer cells that are left over. Doctors try to promote the one and slow the other.

gewusst: “Graft” is the English word for transplant, “host” means the one who hosts, that is, the recipient.
Worldwide, many millions of people are registered as possible stem cell donors.

teile.einleitung: Laughing is one of the loveliest reactions of our body. We laugh at jokes, when playing and often simply because others are laughing.
wichtigste: When laughing you make noises, when smiling you do not.
When laughing loudly you can hardly speak any more.
After a good laugh the body often feels relaxed.
In the circus the clown makes people laugh.
In Swiss hospitals, the dream doctors of the Theodora Foundation visit sick children.
The spotted hyena and the laughing kookaburra make sounds that sound like laughing.

abschnitte.text: When **laughing**, we breathe out in bursts and make noises as we do so. That is the difference from **smiling**, in which only the face looks friendly. Many muscles in the face and belly work together. When laughing loudly, **speaking** is hardly possible any more. After a good laugh the body often feels **relaxed**.

To make others laugh, you tell a **joke**. In the circus the **clown** is in charge of this. With big shoes, a red nose and funny mishaps, he provides laughter. Laughing is catching: when others laugh, you often simply laugh along, even without knowing the reason.

In Switzerland, the **dream doctors** of the **Theodora Foundation** visit children in hospitals. They are artists dressed up as clowns. They play, do magic and make jokes. This way the children forget their worries and their illness for a moment. Laughing can help to ease fear and tension.

Some animals also make sounds that sound like laughing. The **spotted hyena** in Africa gives out giggling calls. In **Australia** lives a bird whose call sounds like loud laughter. It is called the **laughing kookaburra** and belongs to the kingfishers. In apes such as chimpanzees, it has been observed that when playing and being tickled they make panting sounds that are reminiscent of laughing.

gewusst: Tickling yourself hardly works, because the brain already knows your own movement in advance.
People laugh much more often when they are together with others than when they are alone.

teile.einleitung: Most people write with their right hand, but some write with their left. They are called left-handers. Being left-handed is completely normal and is usually something you are born with.
wichtigste: A left-hander mainly uses the left hand, for example for writing.
About 1 in 10 people is left-handed.
Left-handedness is usually inborn, you do not choose it.
Nowadays left-handed children are allowed to write with their left hand.
There are left-handed scissors and fountain pens for left-handers.
International Left-Handers Day is on 13 August.

abschnitte.text: Almost everyone has a **favourite hand** that is more skilful. In about 9 out of 10 people this is the right hand, and in about **1 in 10** it is the left. Someone who mainly writes with the left hand is a **left-hander**. People who use both hands equally well are called **ambidextrous**. This is rare.

Whether someone becomes left-handed is **not something you can choose**. It is usually **inborn** and has to do with the brain. In the past, left-handed children were often forced to write with their right hand. This was called **retraining**. Today we know that this can do harm. So the rule is: left-handed children should be **allowed to write with their left hand**.

Many things are made for right-handers, for example scissors, tin openers or rulers. A left-hander cuts badly with normal scissors because the blades are the wrong way round. That is why there are **left-handed scissors**. **Fountain pens for left-handers** also help, because when writing in ink the left hand drags over the fresh writing and easily **smudges** it. A suitable posture and a sheet of paper laid at an angle also help.

Every year on **13 August** it is **International Left-Handers Day**. On this day we are meant to remember that left-handers often come across things in everyday life that are built for right-handers. Many well-known sportswomen, artists and scientists are or were left-handed. In some sports, such as tennis or fencing, being left-handed can even be an advantage, because opponents are less used to it.

gewusst: Many animals also have a preferred paw or side.
Most people also have a favourite eye and a favourite foot.

teile.einleitung: Youth+Sport, J+S for short, is the federal government’s biggest sport promotion programme. It supports sports courses and camps for children and young people all over Switzerland. Many clubs and schools take part.
wichtigste: J+S stands for Jugend+Sport, Youth+Sport.
The Federal Office of Sport (FOSPO) is responsible.
The programme is meant for children and young people from about 5 to 20 years old.
Youth+Sport was founded in the 1970s.
Courses are led by J+S leaders who have done training for it.
Clubs receive financial contributions from the federal government for recognised J+S courses.

abschnitte.text: **Youth+Sport** wants as many children and young people as possible to do sport and enjoy movement. The programme is meant for young people **from about 5 to 20 years old**. For the younger ones there is **children’s sport**, and for the older ones **youth sport**. Many sports are offered, from football and swimming through skiing to orienteering and climbing. Sports camps in the holidays are also part of it.

Youth+Sport belongs to the **Federal Office of Sport**, **FOSPO** for short. It was founded in the **1970s** and replaced an older programme for young people. The cantons help with carrying it out. They have offices of their own that check courses and organise training. This way J+S works in all language regions of Switzerland.

Anyone who wants to lead a J+S course attends **training**. After that you are a **J+S leader** in a particular sport. In the courses you learn how to plan training, ensure safety and motivate children. Many young adults do this training alongside school, an apprenticeship or studies. Regular further training keeps the knowledge fresh.

If a club or a school runs a recognised J+S course or camp, it receives **financial contributions** from the federal government. The amount depends, among other things, on how many children take part and how long the course lasts. With the money, clubs can, for example, buy equipment or make camps cheaper. J+S also lends out sports equipment, such as tents or canoes.

In **Magglingen**, above Biel in the canton of Bern, lies the **Federal University for Sport**. Sports teachers and coaches are trained there, and FOSPO has its seat here too. In Ticino, in **Tenero** on Lake Maggiore, lies the federal government’s **national youth sports centre**. School classes, clubs and sports camps can train and stay overnight there.

gewusst: Every year, hundreds of thousands of children and young people take part in J+S courses and camps.
The Tenero youth sports centre even has a campsite right on the lake.

teile.einleitung: In strength training, you strengthen the muscles by making them work against a resistance. This can be your own body weight, a dumbbell or a machine. In sport, different kinds of strength are distinguished.
wichtigste: Maximum strength is the greatest force in a single effort.
Speed strength means developing a lot of force in a short time.
Strength endurance means repeating a force for a long time or often.
Several repetitions followed by a pause are called a set.
In isometric work you hold a position, for example in the plank.
The press-up trains with your own body weight.
Teenagers first learn exercises with little weight and clean technique.

abschnitte.text: **Maximum strength** is the greatest force that a muscle can produce in a single effort. It shows, for example, in the heaviest weight that you can lift exactly once. Weightlifters need a lot of maximum strength. It is also the basis for the other kinds of strength.

**Speed strength** is the ability to develop a lot of force in a very short time. A sprinter needs it at the start to push off explosively from the starting block. It is also important in the high jump, the long jump or the jump shot in handball.

**Strength endurance** means producing a force as often or as long as possible without tiring. You need it in rowing, in climbing or in many press-ups one after another. It is trained with lighter weight and many repetitions.

In training, you do an exercise several times in a row. A group of repetitions followed by a pause is called a **set**, for example 3 sets of 12 repetitions each. The **press-up** trains with your own body weight. For the dumbbell curl or the leg press you need weights or machines. In **isometric work** the muscle tenses without the joints moving, for example in the **plank** or the wall sit.

Teenagers should learn new strength exercises first with **little weight**. A wrong **technique** can overload joints and back. With light weight you learn the movement correctly first. After that you raise the load slowly. Warming up before training and enough recovery afterwards are also part of it.

gewusst: Many effective strength exercises need no equipment at all, only your own body.
In the plank the muscles work hard even though you do not move.

teile.einleitung: In an insect venom allergy, the body reacts very strongly to the venom of stinging insects. In Switzerland, bees and wasps are the main triggers. Such an allergy can be dangerous, but you can protect yourself well.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, bees and wasps most often cause an insect venom allergy.
A honeybee usually dies after it has stung a person.
A wasp has a smooth sting and can sting several times.
A hornet sting is hardly more dangerous than a wasp sting.
A sting in the mouth is dangerous even without an allergy, because the swelling can narrow the airways.
Wasps are especially common and pushy in late summer.

abschnitte.text: In an **insect venom allergy**, the immune system defends itself far too strongly against the venom of a sting. Normally the spot only swells a little and itches. In an allergy, the whole body can react, for example with a rash, difficulty breathing or dizziness. The most severe form is called **anaphylactic shock**. Then you must call the emergency number **144** at once. In Switzerland, **bees and wasps** are the main triggers.

The sting of a **honeybee** has small barbs. It stays stuck in the skin, and the bee usually **dies** afterwards. You should remove the sting quickly. The sting of a **wasp** is **smooth** and does not stay stuck, so it can sting **several times**. The old saying that a few **hornet stings** could kill a horse is **not true**: a hornet sting is hardly more dangerous than a wasp sting.

A **sting in the mouth or throat** is dangerous even without an allergy. The **swelling** can narrow the airways. As a first measure, it helps to **suck ice** or drink something cold, and you call for help at once. That is why outdoors you should not drink from open bottles or cans without looking inside. A straw or a glass with a lid helps.

In **late summer**, wasps are especially common and pushy, because their colonies are then at their biggest. They are attracted by sweet things and meat. Anyone who is allergic to bee venom should **not walk barefoot** across flowering meadows, because you could tread on a bee. Wildly swatting at the insects makes them more likely to attack. Staying calm is better.

People with an insect venom allergy often get an **emergency kit** from their doctor. It usually contains an **adrenaline auto-injector**, a syringe that you can give yourself in an emergency. There is also a treatment that slowly gets the body used to the venom. It is called **desensitisation** or hyposensitisation and protects very well against severe reactions.

gewusst: Among bees and wasps, only the females have a sting, the males cannot sting.
Hornets are rather shy and usually sting only when their nest is threatened.

teile.einleitung: The lung is the human organ of breathing. With every breath it takes oxygen from the air and gives carbon dioxide back out. Without the lungs we could survive only a few minutes.
wichtigste: When we breathe, the lungs take oxygen from the air.
Humans have two lungs, a right one and a left one.
The ribs protect the lungs from the outside.
In the alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out of the blood.
The most important breathing muscle is the diaphragm.
Smoking harms the lungs very badly.
At rest an adult breathes about 12 to 16 times a minute.

abschnitte.text: The **lungs** lie in the chest, well protected by the ribs. They consist of two **lobes**: the right has three sections, the left only two, because the heart needs room there. The lungs are soft and spongy and covered by a smooth skin, the pleura. Beneath the lungs lies the diaphragm, a plate of muscle that separates the chest from the belly.

Air gets through the nose or mouth into the throat and then into the **windpipe**. The windpipe divides into two main bronchi, one for each lung. These branch out ever more finely, like the branches of an upside-down tree. At the end of the smallest twigs sit hundreds of millions of tiny alveoli.

In the **alveoli** there is only a wafer-thin wall between the air and the blood. Oxygen passes from the air into the blood and is carried by the red blood cells to all the cells. At the same time the blood gives off carbon dioxide, a waste product of the cells. We breathe this out again.

When we breathe in, the **diaphragm** tightens and flattens, and muscles between the ribs lift the chest. The chest cavity becomes bigger, and the lungs draw in air like a bellows. When we breathe out, the diaphragm relaxes and the air flows out. At rest you breathe in about half a litre of air with each breath, and much more when doing sport.

**Smoking** harms the lungs very badly: tar and poisons clog the airways and destroy the alveoli. Smokers get lung cancer and a long-lasting cough much more often. Fine dust and exhaust fumes also put a strain on the lungs. Infections such as pneumonia, or diseases such as asthma, can make breathing difficult.

Endurance sport such as cycling, swimming or running trains the breathing muscles, heart and circulation. Fresh air and not smoking are the best things for the lungs. On high mountains in the Alps the air is thinner, so you get out of breath more quickly there. The **lung volume** of an adult is about 5 to 6 litres.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the two halves of the lungs.
Branching airways that lead from the windpipe into the lungs.
A plate of muscle beneath the lungs that helps with breathing.
A gas that is produced as waste in the cells and is breathed out.

gewusst: If you spread out all the alveoli of an adult, they would cover an area of about 100 square metres, roughly as much as a large flat.
The left lung is slightly smaller than the right, because the heart takes up some of its room.
In one day a person breathes over 10000 litres of air in and out.

teile.einleitung: In a local anaesthetic, only a small part of the body is made pain-free. You stay awake. Most children know it from the dentist.
wichtigste: Local anaesthesia means numbing one place only.
Only a small area is made pain-free, and you stay awake.
The drug blocks the nerves so that they do not pass on pain signals.
It is often used at the dentist or for small procedures.
After some time the effect wears off by itself.

abschnitte.text: In a **local anaesthetic**, only a small part of the body is made pain-free. You are awake and can talk. A **general anaesthetic**, in which you sleep deeply, is quite different. The local anaesthetic is well known from the **dentist**, for example before a hole is drilled. It is also often used when stitching a wound or for small operations.

Pain arises when **nerves** send a signal to the brain. The anaesthetic is injected or put on the skin as an ointment or spray. It **blocks the nerves** at that spot, so that they no longer pass on pain signals. The area then feels numb or furry. Sometimes you can still feel touch, but no pain.

After some time, usually one to a few hours, **the effect wears off** and the feeling returns. After an anaesthetic in the mouth you should wait until it has worn off before you eat. Otherwise you can easily bite your lip or cheek without noticing. A well-known drug for local anaesthesia is **lidocaine**.

gewusst: As early as the 19th century, a drug for numbing was used on the eye for the first time.

teile.einleitung: The sacrum is a large, triangular bone at the lower end of the spine. It joins the spine to the pelvis. In an adult it consists of five vertebrae fused together.
wichtigste: The sacrum consists of five fused vertebrae.
It has the shape of a triangle pointing downwards.
Directly above it lies the lumbar spine.
It joins the spine to the pelvis.
The joint to the ilium is called the sacroiliac joint.
The Latin name “os sacrum” means “sacred bone”.

abschnitte.text: The **sacrum** consists of **five sacral vertebrae**. In an adult they fuse into a single bone. That is why this part of the spine cannot move. The sacrum is broad at the top and tapers to a point at the bottom, like a **triangle**. It is also curved slightly backwards.

Directly above the sacrum lies the **lumbar spine**. Between the fifth lumbar vertebra and the sacrum there is another intervertebral disc. The sacrum is wedged in between the two hip bones. Through it the **weight of the upper body** passes to the **pelvis**. The upper edge that juts forwards is called the **promontory**. There the spine bends backwards.

On each side, a **sacroiliac joint** joins the sacrum to the **ilium**, a part of the hip bone. Strong **ligaments** hold this joint so firmly that it is almost immovable. This way the pelvis stays stable when we stand, walk or jump.

In the sacrum there are several openings, the **sacral foramina**. Through them **nerves** leave the spinal canal. These nerves supply, among other things, the **legs** and the **buttocks**. That is why problems in this area can also cause pain right down into the leg.
In Latin, the sacrum is called **os sacrum**. “Os” means bone and “sacrum” sacred, so together “sacred bone”. Where exactly this name comes from is not certain. There are various guesses about it.

gewusst: In a child, the sacral vertebrae are still separate and fuse only later.
The sacrum carries the whole weight of the upper body on to the pelvis.

teile.einleitung: The intensive care unit is a special ward in the hospital. There, very seriously ill or injured people are treated who have to be monitored all the time. A large team looks after them day and night.
wichtigste: Very seriously ill people go to the intensive care unit.
They are monitored round the clock.
Devices constantly measure heartbeat, blood pressure and oxygen in the blood.
If necessary, a machine helps with breathing.
More specialists work per patient than on an ordinary ward.

abschnitte.text: People whose lives are in danger go to the **intensive care unit**. They may be patients after a big operation, after a serious accident or with a dangerous illness. They have to be **monitored constantly**. For this, specially trained doctors and **nursing staff** work here. The field is called **intensive care medicine**.

Next to every bed there are **monitors**. They constantly show the **heartbeat**, the **blood pressure** and the **oxygen in the blood**. If a value becomes dangerous, the device sounds the alarm at once. If a person can no longer breathe enough on their own, a **ventilator** helps. Through **infusion pumps**, the patients receive exactly measured medicines and fluid.

In an intensive care unit, a nurse looks after only a few patients. This way they can react at once when something changes. The team works day and night, at weekends too. Visits from relatives are usually possible, but often subject to rules so that the patients have peace. As soon as someone is better, they are moved to an ordinary ward.

gewusst: On intensive care units the devices often beep, but not every sound means an emergency.
In Switzerland, intensive care units are recognised by a professional society according to fixed rules.

teile.einleitung: Ketone bodies are small molecules that the body makes as a replacement fuel. This happens mainly when little sugar is available, for example during fasting. They are made in the liver.
wichtigste: Ketone bodies are made in the liver from acetyl-CoA.
The liver makes ketone bodies but cannot use them itself.
Acetone is given off in the breath and smells fruity.
Little insulin and a lot of glucagon promote the making of ketone bodies.
In longer fasting, the brain covers a large part of its energy needs from ketone bodies.
In insulin deficiency, a dangerous diabetic ketoacidosis can arise.
With Kussmaul breathing, the body then tries to get rid of acid.

abschnitte.text: Normally the body uses mainly **sugar** (glucose) and **fat** as sources of energy. If sugar is missing for a longer time, for example during **fasting** or on a diet very low in carbohydrates, the body breaks down more fat. The **liver** turns part of the fatty acids into **ketone bodies**. The most important are **acetoacetate** and **beta-hydroxybutyrate**. A third ketone body, **acetone**, arises in small amounts on the side.

When fatty acids are broken down, a lot of **acetyl-CoA** arises in the liver. Normally it is burned in the **citric acid cycle**. For this it needs the substance **oxaloacetate**. In fasting, however, oxaloacetate is used up for **gluconeogenesis**, that is, the new making of sugar. That is why acetyl-CoA is increasingly converted into ketone bodies. This is controlled by hormones: **little insulin and a lot of glucagon** promote the making.

The liver makes ketone bodies but **cannot use them itself**, because it lacks an enzyme needed for that. It releases them into the blood. **Muscles**, the **heart** and above all the **brain** take them up. The brain can hardly use fatty acids. In **longer fasting**, though, it covers a large part of its energy needs from ketone bodies. This way the body has to break down less protein from the muscles to make sugar.

**Acetone** is volatile and is given off in the **breath**. It smells **fruity**, similar to nail varnish remover, which also contains acetone. In people who fast for a long time, or in a severe metabolic disorder, you can sometimes notice this smell in the breath. Doctors therefore watch for it.

In people with **type 1 diabetes**, insulin is missing. Without insulin, the liver makes ketone bodies unchecked. Because they are acidic, the blood becomes too acidic. This dangerous derailment is called **diabetic ketoacidosis**. The body tries to get rid of the acid by breathing deeply and fast. This breathing is called **Kussmaul breathing**, after the German doctor Adolf Kussmaul. Ketoacidosis is an emergency and has to be treated in hospital.

gewusst: The acetone in nail varnish remover is the same substance that the body makes in small amounts during fasting.
With test strips, you can measure ketone bodies in urine or blood.

teile.einleitung: Immunological memory makes sure that the body remembers disease-causing germs. If it meets the same germ a second time, it fights it off faster and more strongly. Vaccinations are based on this principle.
wichtigste: Memory cells make sure of a fast defence on second contact.
The second defence reaction, the secondary response, starts much faster.
In the secondary response, antibodies of the IgG class dominate.
In active immunisation, the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells.
Passive immunisation only passes on foreign antibodies and so does not protect for long.
Herd immunity also protects unvaccinated people indirectly.
Flu viruses change all the time, so a new vaccination is needed almost every year.

abschnitte.text: When a germ gets into the body for the first time, the immune system needs a few days to make suitable defence substances. This is called the **primary response**. In the process, **memory cells** also arise, which are special B cells and T cells. They often stay in the body for years. If the same germ comes back, they recognise it at once.

On the second contact, the **secondary response** takes place. It starts **much faster** and is much stronger than the first. Often the germ is fought off before you even become ill. In the primary response, the body first makes mainly antibodies of the IgM class. In the secondary response, **IgG dominates**, which fits the germ especially well.

In **active immunisation**, the usual vaccination, the body receives weakened or killed germs or parts of them. It then makes antibodies and memory cells **itself**, without becoming ill. In **passive immunisation**, you receive ready-made antibodies from outside. It works at once, but only **foreign antibodies** are passed on. The body breaks these down after a few weeks, and no memory cells arise.

When a large part of the population is immune, a germ can hardly spread any more. Then people who cannot be vaccinated are also protected indirectly, for example very small babies or sick people. This protection is called **herd immunity**. How many people have to be immune for it depends on how infectious a disease is.

Flu viruses **change their surface proteins all the time**. As a result, memory cells no longer recognise them well. That is why a **new flu vaccination** is needed almost every year. Sometimes, with a new flu variant, the immune system prefers to make antibodies against a variant it met earlier. This phenomenon is called **original antigenic sin**.

gewusst: Anyone who has had measles once is usually protected against it for life.
The first vaccination was developed by the English doctor Edward Jenner at the end of the 18th century, against smallpox.

teile.einleitung: In intermittent fasting, times for eating alternate with longer times without eating. There are different methods, for example 16:8 or 5:2. Experts are studying how well this form of eating works.
wichtigste: With 16:8, you fast for 16 hours and eat within a period of 8 hours.
With 5:2, you eat normally on 5 days and greatly reduced on 2 days.
In alternate-day fasting, you eat one day and fast one day in turn.
In the fasting phases, the insulin level falls clearly.
During fasting, cellular recycling, autophagy, increases.
Weight loss is similar to that with an equally strong calorie reduction.
People with diabetes who take medicines should fast only after talking to a doctor.

abschnitte.text: With the **16:8** method, you fast **16 hours** every day and eat only within a period of **8 hours**. An example: someone who eats their last meal at 7 pm may eat again the next day at **11 am**. A large part of the fasting time thus falls in the night. Water, unsweetened tea or black coffee are usually allowed during the fasting time.

With the **5:2** method, you eat normally on **5 days** of the week. On **2 days** you eat **greatly reduced**, that is, only very little. In **alternate-day fasting**, you alternate: one day eating, one day fasting. This form is stricter and harder for many people to keep up.

Without eating, the **insulin level** in the blood falls clearly. The body then draws on its energy reserves. With longer fasting, the **liver** makes more **ketone bodies** from fatty acids, which serve as carriers of energy. In addition, **autophagy** increases in the cells. This is a recycling process in which cells break down old components and reuse them.

Many people fast in order to lose weight. Studies have so far shown that the **weight loss** from intermittent fasting is **similar** to that with an **equally strong calorie reduction**. So it works mainly because you eat less overall. Some people find this method easier, though, than counting calories every day. Whether there are further benefits for health is still being researched.

Intermittent fasting is not suitable for everyone. **People with diabetes** who take medicines should try it only after **talking to a doctor**, because otherwise blood sugar can fall dangerously low. Fasting is also usually not recommended for children and teenagers who are growing. They regularly need enough energy and nutrients.

gewusst: For his research into autophagy, the Japanese researcher Yoshinori Ohsumi received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2016.
The body also fasts while sleeping at night, which is why breakfast is called “breakfast” in English, the breaking of the fast.

teile.einleitung: Carbon dioxide, CO2 for short, is a colourless gas that we breathe out with every breath. It arises in our body cells when they burn nutrients. Plants take it up again and build sugar from it.
wichtigste: Carbon dioxide arises in the body cells.
In the blood it is mostly carried as hydrogencarbonate.
We breathe it out through the lungs.
In the school experiment it is detected because limewater turns cloudy.
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air.
A CO2 traffic light in the classroom shows when the room should be aired.
Green plants build sugar from carbon dioxide.

abschnitte.titel: How it arises in the body
abschnitte.text: Our **body cells** need energy. They get it by breaking down nutrients such as sugar with the help of **oxygen**. This is called **cell respiration**. In the process, water and **carbon dioxide** arise. For the body, the gas is a waste product and has to go out again. The more we move, the more carbon dioxide arises, and the faster we breathe.

abschnitte.titel: The way out of the body
abschnitte.text: The carbon dioxide gets from the cells into the **blood**. There it is mostly carried as **hydrogencarbonate**, and a smaller part is dissolved or bound to the red blood cells. In the **lungs** it becomes a gas again and gets into the air sacs. When **breathing out**, it leaves the body. The carbon dioxide content in the blood, by the way, also controls how strongly we breathe.

Carbon dioxide is **colourless** and **odourless**. It is **heavier than air**, so it collects at the bottom in cellars or fermentation cellars. There it can become dangerous, because it displaces oxygen. In the **school experiment**, it is detected with **limewater**: if you blow breathed-out air into it, the clear limewater turns **cloudy**. The bubbles in mineral water are also made of carbon dioxide.

In a full room, many people breathe out carbon dioxide. The content in the air rises, and you become tired and unable to concentrate. As early as the 19th century, the researcher **Max von Pettenkofer** proposed a guideline value of **1000 ppm**, that is, 1000 parts per million. A **CO2 traffic light** measures the content and shows **when to air** the room. Many Swiss schools use such devices.

Green plants take carbon dioxide from the air. With the help of **sunlight** and water, **they build sugar from it** and give off oxygen. This process is called **photosynthesis**. Carbon dioxide is also a **greenhouse gas**. By burning coal, oil and natural gas, its share in the air has risen sharply, which is warming the climate.

gewusst: A person breathes out about a kilogram of carbon dioxide in a day.
Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide and is about minus 79 degrees cold.

teile.einleitung: Body height says how tall a person is from head to foot. Children grow for many years, until they are about 18 to 20 years old.
wichtigste: The body height of children is usually given in centimetres.
In the morning you are a tiny bit taller than in the evening.
Most people grow in height until about 18 to 20 years.
How tall a child becomes depends to a large extent on the parents.
Healthy food and enough sleep help with growing.
At 2.72 metres, Robert Wadlow was the tallest reliably measured person.

abschnitte.text: A child’s body height is usually measured in **centimetres**. You stand barefoot and straight against a wall and lay a book or a board flat on your head. You can calculate well with heights: if Lina is 120 cm and Tim 130 cm tall, then Tim is **10 cm** taller. If Mia was 115 cm tall and a year later 121 cm, she has grown **6 cm**.

In the **morning** you are a tiny bit taller than in the evening. This is due to the **intervertebral discs**, the soft cushions between the vertebrae. During the day they are squeezed together a little by standing and walking. At night, when you lie down, they recover. The difference is about one to two centimetres.

Children do not grow evenly. In the first year of life it goes very fast, later more slowly, and in teenagers there is often a **growth spurt**. Most people grow in height until about **18 to 20 years**. After that the **growth plates** in the bones are closed. How tall someone becomes depends to a large extent on the **parents**, that is, on the genes. Healthy food, exercise and enough **sleep** help the body to grow.

The tallest person whose height was reliably measured was the American **Robert Wadlow**. He grew to **2.72 metres**. His extraordinary height came from an illness in which the body made too much growth hormone. The tallest living man is considered (as of 2025) to be **Sultan Kösen** from **Turkey**. He is about 2.51 metres tall.

gewusst: Even as a child, Robert Wadlow was taller than most adults.
Astronauts grow a few centimetres taller in space, because the weight does not press on the spine.

teile.einleitung: A contact lens is a small, curved aid to sight that lies directly on the eye. For many people it replaces glasses. So that it does not harm the eye, it needs a lot of care and cleanliness.
wichtigste: A contact lens floats on the tear film above the cornea.
There are two main kinds: soft and rigid contact lenses.
The eye doctor Adolf Eugen Fick described one of the first glass contact lenses in Zurich in 1888.
Otto Wichterle developed the soft lens made of hydrogel around 1961.
Before inserting them, you always wash your hands thoroughly.
You never rinse contact lenses with tap water.
Ordinary contact lenses are not worn while sleeping.

abschnitte.text: The contact lens lies at the front of the eye, exactly over the **cornea**. The cornea is the transparent, curved layer in front of the pupil. Between the lens and the cornea lies a wafer-thin **tear film**. The lens floats on it and moves a little with it when you blink. Because the lens is so close to the eye, you see sharply even at the edge of the field of vision.

There are two main kinds of contact lenses. **Soft lenses** are made of a plastic that holds water and are flexible. They are a little bigger than the cornea and usually comfortable to wear at once. **Rigid lenses** are harder and smaller. You first have to get used to them, but they let a lot of oxygen through and last a long time.

abschnitte.titel: An invention with a link to Zurich
abschnitte.text: The eye doctor **Adolf Eugen Fick** worked in Zurich. In 1888 he described one of the first contact lenses made of glass and called it a “contact spectacle”. This glass lens was still large and uncomfortable. Around 1961, the Czech chemist **Otto Wichterle** developed the soft lens made of **hydrogel**. He even made the first pieces with a toy construction set.

abschnitte.titel: Cleanliness is the most important thing
abschnitte.text: Before inserting and removing them, you wash your **hands thoroughly**. This way no germs get on the lens. You never rinse contact lenses with tap water. In it, germs such as **acanthamoebae** can live, which can cause severe inflammation of the cornea. Lenses therefore belong only in the right **care solution** and in a clean container.

The cornea has no blood vessels and gets its oxygen mainly from the air. With the eyes closed, less oxygen arrives, and the lens slows it further. That is why you do not sleep in ordinary contact lenses, otherwise the risk of inflammation rises. An exception is **night lenses** (orthokeratology). These rigid lenses gently flatten the cornea at night, so that during the day you see sharply for a time without any aid.

gewusst: One of the first contact lenses in the world was described in Zurich.
Otto Wichterle built his first soft lenses with a toy construction set.

teile.einleitung: The head is the topmost part of our body. In it lies the brain, and on it sit important sense organs such as eyes, ears and nose. That is why the head is especially well protected.
wichtigste: In the head lies the brain, with which we think and learn.
The front part of the head with eyes, nose and mouth is called the face.
A person has two eyes and two ears.
The ears sit at the side of the head.
The temple lies between eye and ear.
On the head, most people grow hair.

abschnitte.text: In the head lies the **brain**. With it we think, learn and remember. It also controls the whole body. It is protected by the hard **skull**, a capsule of bone. At the **temple**, at the side between eye and ear, the skull is somewhat thinner. That is why you wear a helmet when cycling.

At the front of the head lie the eyes, nose and mouth. This part is called the **face**. A person has **two eyes**. With both eyes together you can judge well how far away something is. With the nose we smell, with the mouth we eat and speak. With the face we also show whether we are cheerful or sad.

The **ears** sit on the left and right of the head. This way we hear which direction a sound comes from. On top of the head, most people grow **hair**. It protects a little from sun and cold. Some people have less hair or a bald head, which is quite normal.

Animals also have a head with sense organs. The **owl** can turn its head especially far, up to three quarters of a full circle. It needs this because its big eyes can hardly move. This way it can still look in all directions.

In language the head comes up often. Someone who **buries their head in the sand** does not want to see a problem and hopes that it will go away by itself. Someone who **racks their brains**, literally “breaks their head”, thinks for a long time about a difficult question. The head, of course, does not break in the process.

gewusst: An owl can turn its head up to three quarters of a circle.
With two eyes you see in three dimensions and can judge distances well.

teile.einleitung: Creatinine is a breakdown product of muscle metabolism that is excreted through the kidneys. Its level in the blood is one of the most important laboratory values for estimating kidney function. You do have to know some peculiarities, though.
wichtigste: Creatinine arises fairly evenly from creatine in the muscles.
It is freely filtered in the glomerulus and not reabsorbed.
The creatinine value depends strongly on muscle mass.
Only when filtering performance falls by about half does the blood value rise above the norm.
The eGFR is today mostly estimated with the CKD-EPI formula.
Cystatin C is an alternative value that hardly depends on muscle mass.
After a lot of cooked meat, creatinine can rise temporarily.

abschnitte.text: In the muscles, **creatine** serves as an energy store. A small part of it is constantly and fairly **evenly** converted into **creatinine**. This gets into the blood and is excreted through the **kidneys**. Someone with a lot of muscle makes more creatinine. With very little muscle, a normal value can therefore hide weak kidneys.

Creatinine is freely filtered in the **glomerulus**, the renal corpuscle, and afterwards not taken up again. If its value in the blood rises, the kidney is filtering less. The relationship is not linear, though. The **serum creatinine** rises above the normal range only when filtering performance has already fallen by about half. This range is called the **creatinine-blind range**.

The **creatinine clearance** is calculated like this: urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration. Example: 8000 µmol/l times 1 ml/min divided by 80 µmol/l gives **100 ml/min**. The clearance slightly overestimates the true filtration rate. A small part of the creatinine is namely also given off into the urine by **tubular secretion**.

Today filtering performance is mostly estimated with the **CKD-EPI formula**. It takes account of creatinine, age and sex and gives the estimated glomerular filtration rate, the **eGFR**. An alternative is **cystatin C**. This small protein is made by all cells with a nucleus, freely filtered and hardly depends on muscle mass.

When meat is cooked, some of the creatine in it already turns into creatinine. After a big meal with **cooked meat**, the blood value can therefore **rise temporarily**. For an exact measurement, such influences are taken into account. Very hard physical exertion can also change the value briefly.

gewusst: A normal creatinine value does not rule out the beginning of kidney weakness.
Even the cooking of meat turns part of the creatine into creatinine.

teile.einleitung: Pathogens are tiny living things or particles that can get into the body and make us ill. Most are so small that you can only see them under the microscope. They include viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites, whereas vitamins are not pathogens but important nutrients.
wichtigste: Pathogens include viruses, bacteria, fungi and parasites.
Vitamins are not pathogens, they are vital nutrients.
In coughing and sneezing, pathogens are passed on by droplet infection.
The time between infection and the first signs of illness is called the incubation period.
In Switzerland, ticks can transmit TBE and Lyme disease.
Malaria is caused by single-celled parasites, the plasmodia.
The immune system fights pathogens that have got in.

abschnitte.text: **Viruses** are the smallest pathogens and much smaller than bacteria. They have no metabolism of their own and can multiply only in other cells. To do so, they slip their genetic material into a cell, which then builds new viruses. Viruses cause, for example, colds, flu, measles, chickenpox, Covid-19 and TBE.

**Bacteria** are single-celled living things that occur almost everywhere, in the soil, in water and on our skin. The great majority are harmless or even useful, for example the gut bacteria that help with digestion. A very few make us ill, for example the pathogens of tuberculosis, scarlet fever or Lyme disease. Against bacteria, antibiotics help.

Some **fungi** cause diseases such as athlete’s foot or nail fungus. **Parasites** are living things that live on or in another living thing and harm it. They include single-celled plasmodia, which cause malaria, but also worms such as the tapeworm or lice on the head. Malaria occurs mainly in tropical countries of Africa, Asia and South America.

In **droplet infection**, pathogens fly through the air when coughing, sneezing or speaking. In smear infection, they get into the mouth via hands, door handles or food. Animals can also transmit pathogens: in Switzerland ticks transmit TBE and Lyme disease, in the tropics mosquitoes transmit malaria. Some pathogens also lurk in dirty water.

After infection, the pathogens first multiply in the body without your noticing anything. This time is called the **incubation period**. With a cold it usually lasts only one to three days, with chickenpox about two weeks. Often you can infect others before you yourself seem ill.

Our **immune system** recognises foreign pathogens and fights them with white blood cells and antibodies. Vaccinations prepare the immune system for particular pathogens. Washing your hands regularly with soap, sneezing into the crook of your arm and cooking food well help to keep pathogens away. After a walk in the woods, you should check yourself for ticks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny pathogen that can multiply only in other cells.
A single-celled living thing that can be useful or cause illness.
A living thing that lives at the expense of another and harms it.
The time between infection and the first signs of illness.

gewusst: In and on our body live about as many bacteria as it has cells of its own, most of them harmless.
Viruses are so small that they could be seen only after the invention of the electron microscope in the 1930s.
When sneezing, droplets can fly several metres.

teile.einleitung: Joseph Lister was a British surgeon who made operations much safer in the 19th century. He recognised that germs make wounds inflamed, and he fought them with carbolic acid. He is regarded as the founder of antisepsis.
wichtigste: Joseph Lister lived from 1827 to 1912 and was a surgeon in Great Britain.
Louis Pasteur’s research on germs gave him his idea.
In the 1860s he began treating wounds with carbolic acid in Glasgow.
First he tried the method on an open bone fracture.
With a carbolic acid spray he wanted to kill germs in the air.
His method greatly reduced fatal wound infections after operations.
The genus of bacteria Listeria is named after him.

abschnitte.text: Around 1850, an operation was very dangerous. Many people survived the operation itself but died afterwards of a **wound infection**. The wounds festered, and the fever rose. Nobody knew exactly why this happened. Surgeons often operated in everyday clothes and did not wash their hands thoroughly. Lister wanted to understand where these infections came from.

The French researcher **Louis Pasteur** had shown that tiny living things, that is, **germs**, cause rotting and fermentation. Lister read about this and concluded: if germs get into a wound, it becomes inflamed. So you would have to kill the germs before they do harm. He put this thought into practice in the hospital in **Glasgow** in Scotland.

Lister used **carbolic acid**, which today is called phenol. He first tried it in 1865 on an **open bone fracture**, in which the bone sticks out through the skin. Such fractures at that time became inflamed very often. He soaked dressings in carbolic acid and cleaned instruments and hands with it too. Later he had a **carbolic acid spray** run in the operating theatre, which was meant to kill germs in the air. The number of fatal wound infections fell sharply.

Lister’s method is called **antisepsis**: you kill germs that are already there. Later **asepsis** developed from it: you keep germs away from the start. This includes sterile instruments, gloves, masks and clean operating theatres. Lister himself later gave up the spray. Both ideas are still the basis of every safe operation today.

gewusst: The genus of bacteria **Listeria** was named in honour of Joseph Lister.
The mouthwash Listerine also bears his name.

teile.einleitung: A scratch is a small, long injury to the skin. It arises when something pointed scores across the skin. It is usually harmless, but you should keep it clean.
wichtigste: A scratch is a small, long skin injury.
Cats can scratch with their claws.
Bramble stems with thorns easily scratch the skin open.
You clean a scratch well with water and soap.
Short fingernails stop you scratching until you bleed.
Small scratches usually heal without a scar.

abschnitte.text: In a **scratch**, something pointed scores the skin open. That is why it is usually **narrow and long**. Often only the top layer of skin is injured. Then it hardly bleeds, or only a little. People usually scratch themselves with their **fingernails** when something itches.

**Cats** have sharp claws. When they defend themselves or play wildly, they can scratch. In nature, too, you easily get scratches. **Bramble stems** have many small thorns, which score the skin when you pick berries. Branches, roses or a rough fence can also cause scratches.

Even a small scratch can contain **germs**, especially a cat scratch. So you **clean** the spot well with water and soap. After that you can put a plaster on it. If the spot becomes red, hot or swollen, you should show it to a grown-up or a doctor.

abschnitte.titel: Do not scratch until you bleed
abschnitte.text: When it itches, you want to scratch. But if you scratch too hard, the skin opens and **germs** can get in. Then the spot can become inflamed. **Short fingernails** are less sharp and injure the skin less. Instead of scratching, something cool often helps with itching.

In a small, shallow scratch, only the **upper skin** is injured. First a thin scab often forms. Underneath, new skin grows. After a few days, the scratch has usually healed **without a scar**. Only deep injuries sometimes leave a trace.

gewusst: The top layer of skin can renew itself so well that small scratches vanish without a trace.
A cat’s claws are usually drawn in and come out only when needed.

teile.einleitung: Lactate is the salt of lactic acid and arises in the body when sugar is broken down quickly to obtain energy. For a long time it was seen only as a waste product, but today we know that it is also an important energy carrier.
wichtigste: At rest, the blood contains about 1 mmol of lactate per litre.
Lactate formation regenerates NAD+ so that anaerobic glycolysis can go on.
In the Cori cycle, lactate is built back up into glucose in the liver.
The heart and slow muscle fibres use lactate as an energy source.
Classically, a value of 4 mmol per litre is regarded as the aerobic-anaerobic threshold.
Muscle soreness comes mainly from small injuries in the muscle fibres, not from lactate.

abschnitte.text: Muscles obtain energy from **glucose**, that is, grape sugar. In **glycolysis**, glucose is broken down into pyruvate. In the process, the helper substance **NAD+** is used up. When a lot of energy is needed very quickly, the cell converts pyruvate into **lactate**. This makes NAD+ again, and glycolysis can go on even without enough oxygen. This is called **anaerobic glycolysis**.

At rest, the lactate value in the blood is about **1 mmol per litre**. Lactate is not simply thrown away. The **heart** and the **slow muscle fibres** take it up from the blood and burn it as an energy source. The **liver** builds lactate back up into glucose. This cycle between muscle and liver is called the **Cori cycle**, named after the research couple Carl and Gerty Cori.

In hard exertion, the lactate value rises sharply. The role of anaerobic glycolysis is especially large in runs of **400 m**, which are very fast and yet not quite short. In sports science, a value of **4 mmol per litre** was classically set as the **aerobic-anaerobic threshold**. After hard exertion, lactate is broken down faster if you **jog gently to cool down** instead of standing still at once.

In the past people thought that **muscle soreness** came from lactic acid that stays behind in the muscle. This is now regarded as disproved, because lactate is broken down again after a short time. The main cause is thought to be **small injuries** in the muscle fibres. They arise above all in unaccustomed movements and in braking, for example when running downhill.

gewusst: Carl and Gerty Cori received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1947.
In very hard exertion, the lactate value in the blood can rise to many times the resting value.

teile.einleitung: Keratin is a particularly tough protein substance. Our hair, nails and the outermost layer of the skin are made of it. The hooves, claws and feathers of animals are also made mainly of keratin.
wichtigste: Keratin belongs to the group of substances called proteins.
It is insoluble in water, so hair does not dissolve when washed.
Hooves, claws and feathers are also made mainly of keratin.
Keratin contains sulphur, which is why burnt hair smells so unpleasant.
It is made in the epidermis by the keratinocytes.
The horny layer of the skin consists of dead cells full of keratin.
The outermost layer of the hair is called the cuticle.

abschnitte.text: **Keratin** belongs to the **proteins**. It forms long, fibrous chains that are very resistant to tearing. Keratin is **insoluble in water**. That is why hair and nails do not dissolve when you wash or bathe. The name comes from the Greek word for horn. In fact, **hooves**, **claws**, **feathers**, the horns of cattle and the scales of reptiles are also made mainly of keratin.

Keratin contains a lot of **sulphur**. Between the protein chains, **sulphur bridges** form, which join the chains firmly together. They make hair stable. When hair burns, the sulphur is released, and it smells very unpleasant. In a **perm**, these bridges are broken with a chemical agent. Then the hair is put into curls with rollers and the bridges are tied again in the new shape.

In the **epidermis** there are special cells, the **keratinocytes**. They make the keratin. In time they move outwards, store more and more keratin and die in the process. This process is called **keratinisation**. This is how the **horny layer** arises, the outermost layer of the skin made of dead cells full of keratin. It protects us from loss of water, germs and small injuries and constantly flakes off.

A hair consists almost entirely of keratin. Its outermost layer is called the **cuticle**. It consists of **keratin scales** that lie on top of each other **like roof tiles**. If the scales lie flat, the hair shines. If they are roughened, the hair looks dull. **Fingernails and toenails** are also made of keratin. Because hair and nails consist of dead cells, cutting them does not hurt.

gewusst: The baleen of whales, with which they filter food from the water, is also made of keratin.
The horn of the rhinoceros is not made of bone but of tightly pressed keratin.

teile.einleitung: The periosteum is a thin, firm skin that wraps around the bone on the outside. It contains many nerves and blood vessels. It supplies the bone, lets it grow in thickness and helps in the healing of breaks.
wichtigste: The technical term for the periosteum is periosteum.
The periosteum is rich in nerves, which is why a knock on the shin hurts so much.
It contains blood vessels that supply the bone.
It is important for the growth of the bone in thickness.
Fine collagen fibres, the Sharpey’s fibres, fix it to the bone.
At the joint surfaces the periosteum is missing.
In a break, its cells help to form new bone.

abschnitte.text: Almost every bone is surrounded by a thin, firm skin, the **periosteum**. Its technical term is **periosteum**. It consists of two layers: on the outside of firm connective tissue, on the inside of a layer with many cells. With fine **collagen fibres**, the **Sharpey’s fibres**, it is anchored deep in the bone. Tendons and ligaments also attach to the periosteum.

The periosteum is very rich in **nerves**. That is why it is extremely sensitive to pain. On the **shin**, the bone lies directly under the skin, without protecting muscles. A knock on the edge of the shin therefore hits the periosteum almost directly. This explains why such a knock hurts so much.

In the periosteum run many **blood vessels**. They bring oxygen and nutrients into the bone. The inner layer contains cells that can form new bone tissue. This is how the bone grows outwards in **thickness**. Growth in length, on the other hand, happens at the growth plates near the ends of the bones.

At the **joint surfaces**, the bone is not covered with periosteum. There, smooth **cartilage** lies instead, so that the bones can slide easily in the joint. Cartilage has no nerves, which is why movement does not hurt in a healthy joint. The periosteum ends at the edge of the joint cartilage.

Runners often have pain on the inner edge of the shin. The cause is often an **irritation of the periosteum** from too much or too hard training. Rest and slow build-up usually help. In a **broken bone**, the periosteum plays a big part: its cells help to form **new bone** and to bridge the break.

gewusst: In children the periosteum is thicker and stronger, which is why their breaks heal faster.
Sharpey’s fibres are named after the Scottish anatomist William Sharpey.

teile.einleitung: Whooping cough is an infectious disease of the airways. Typical are violent fits of coughing that can last many weeks. A vaccination protects against it.
wichtigste: Whooping cough is caused by a bacterium.
Typical are strong fits of coughing.
After a fit, you hear a drawn-out breathing in.
The fits of coughing often come especially frequently at night.
Whooping cough often lasts several weeks.
It is passed on by droplets when coughing.
It is especially dangerous for babies, and a vaccination protects.

abschnitte.text: Whooping cough is caused by a **bacterium**. It is called **Bordetella pertussis**, which is why the disease is also called **pertussis**. The bacteria settle in the airways and make toxins. These irritate the mucous membrane strongly. Whooping cough is passed on by **droplets** that get into the air when coughing, sneezing or speaking. It is very infectious.

At the start, whooping cough looks like a cold with a runny nose and a mild cough. After one to two weeks, **strong fits of coughing** come. You cough many times in a row, with hardly any air in between. Afterwards comes a **drawn-out, whistling breathing in** that sounds like a gasp. That is where the disease gets its name. The fits often come especially frequently **at night**.

Whooping cough often lasts **several weeks**, sometimes even months. That is why in some countries it is also called “the hundred-day cough”. Between the fits, many sick people feel quite well. An **antibiotic** can reduce the infection of other people if you take it early. The cough itself, however, often stops only slowly, because the airways need time to recover.

Whooping cough is especially dangerous for **babies**. In them, there is sometimes no cough but **pauses in breathing**. They then often have to be treated in hospital. Babies often catch it from older siblings or adults who are only mildly ill. That is why it is important that the people around them are protected as well.

Against whooping cough there is a **vaccination**. In Switzerland it is recommended already in infancy, together with vaccinations against other diseases. Later come **booster vaccinations**, because protection fades over the years. Adults who have a lot to do with babies should also get vaccinated. Which vaccinations are recommended when is set out in the Swiss vaccination schedule.

gewusst: Even someone who has already had whooping cough can fall ill with it again later, because the protection does not last for life.
In teenagers and adults, whooping cough often shows only as a stubborn cough and is therefore easily overlooked.

teile.einleitung: The lens of the eye sits inside the eye directly behind the pupil. It focuses the light so that a sharp image forms on the retina. Because it can change its shape, we see both near and far things sharply.
wichtigste: The lens of the eye lies directly behind the pupil.
It is a converging lens and focuses the light.
The ciliary muscle changes its shape, and the lens hangs on fine suspensory fibres.
When looking at something close, the lens becomes rounder, which is called accommodation.
From about the age of 45 the lens becomes less elastic, and many people then need reading glasses.
In a cataract the lens becomes cloudy, and it is then usually replaced by an artificial lens.

abschnitte.text: The **lens of the eye** lies directly **behind the pupil** and the iris. It is transparent, elastic and shaped rather like a lentil. All around, it is hung up on fine **suspensory fibres**. These connect it to the ring-shaped **ciliary muscle**. In physics, the lens of the eye is a **converging lens**: it focuses the light so that a sharp image forms on the retina.

So that we can see near and far things sharply, the lens can change its shape. This ability is called **accommodation**. When we look at something **close**, the ciliary muscle tightens, the fibres go slack and the lens becomes **rounder**. This makes it bend the light more strongly. When we look into the distance, the muscle relaxes, the fibres pull tight and the lens becomes flatter.

With age the lens becomes **less elastic**. It can no longer become round enough for close work. That is why many people need **reading glasses** from about the age of **45**. This is called presbyopia. It is quite normal and affects almost everyone at some point.

In a **cataract** the lens of the eye becomes cloudy. You then see as if through a mist, colours look paler and you are easily dazzled. It usually appears in old age. In the operation the cloudy lens is removed and replaced by an **artificial lens**. This is one of the most common operations of all and often takes only a short time.

gewusst: The lens of the eye has no blood vessels, otherwise it would not be transparent.
The image on the retina is upside down, and the brain turns it the right way round again.

teile.einleitung: Tooth decay is a disease of the teeth in which holes form. The culprits are bacteria in the mouth that make acid from sugar. With good dental care, tooth decay can usually be prevented.
wichtigste: Bacteria in the mouth make acid from sugar.
The acid attacks the hard tooth enamel.
The bacteria live in plaque, a sticky layer on the teeth.
At the start, tooth decay often shows as a white or brown spot.
Untreated, the hole gets bigger and hurts.
The dentist fills the hole with a filling.
Milk teeth can also get tooth decay.

abschnitte.text: Many **bacteria** live in the mouth. Some of them feed on **sugar** from food. In doing so they make **acid**. The bacteria sit in **plaque**, a sticky, almost invisible layer on the teeth. The acid attacks the **tooth enamel**, the hardest layer in the body. In time the enamel becomes soft and a hole forms. In everyday language, tooth decay is also called **Zahnfäule**, “tooth rot”.

At the start, tooth decay often shows as a **white or brown spot** on the tooth. It does not hurt yet. If tooth decay is not treated, the hole gets **bigger** and goes deeper into the tooth. If it reaches the tooth nerve, it hurts, especially with cold, hot or sweet things. That is why regular check-ups at the dentist are important, so that tooth decay is found early.

The dentist removes the diseased part of the tooth with a small **drill**. Then he fills the hole with a **filling**. It closes the tooth again and protects it. **Milk teeth** can also get tooth decay. They should be treated as well, because they hold space for the permanent teeth. In Switzerland, many municipalities have a **school dentist** who checks children’s teeth.

Not only the amount of sugar matters but also **how often** you eat. After every snack, the bacteria make acid for a while. Anyone who **constantly** nibbles through the day or drinks sweet drinks gives the teeth **no break**. The **saliva** then cannot neutralise the acid. Better are fixed meals and in between water or unsweetened tea.

It is best to brush your teeth **twice a day** with **fluoride toothpaste**. Fluoride makes tooth enamel more resistant to acid. It is important to brush all surfaces, including at the back and between the teeth. With small children, parents brush afterwards. In Switzerland, many children learn at school, in **school dental care**, how to brush properly.

gewusst: Tooth enamel is the hardest material in the human body, harder than bone.
Tooth enamel cannot grow back, which is why a hole has to be filled by the dentist.

teile.einleitung: In a circulatory collapse, blood pressure suddenly falls sharply. For a moment the brain gets too little blood, you become weak and can collapse. Often a collapse can be avoided with simple means.
wichtigste: In a circulatory collapse, blood pressure suddenly drops.
Standing still for a long time lets a lot of blood pool in the legs.
Getting up too fast can trigger dizziness.
In heat, a heat collapse can occur.
Drinking enough and moving the calves help to prevent it.
The skin is often pale and clammy.
After a collapse you get up slowly.

abschnitte.text: In a **circulatory collapse**, **blood pressure** suddenly falls sharply. As a result the **brain** gets a poorer blood supply. You feel weak, dizzy, and sometimes things go black in front of your eyes. In the worst case, you collapse. The skin often looks **pale** and **clammy** in the process, because the blood vessels of the skin contract.

abschnitte.titel: Standing a long time and getting up fast
abschnitte.text: Because of **gravity**, a lot of blood collects in the **veins of the legs** when you stand still for a long time. Without movement it flows back to the heart only slowly. Someone who **gets up** too fast from lying down can also feel dizzy. The blood then flows into the legs before the circulation has adapted.

In great heat, the **blood vessels of the skin** widen so that the body can give off warmth. In addition you lose a lot of fluid through **sweating**. Both can lower blood pressure so much that a **heat collapse** arises. That is why on hot days it is important to drink **enough water** and to stay in the shade.

Anyone who has to stand for a long time should keep moving their **toes and calves**. Working calf muscles squeeze the veins and push the blood towards the heart. This **muscle pump** keeps the circulation going. Gently rocking on your toes also helps.

Someone who feels weak does best to sit or lie down at once. Raised legs help more blood to flow to the head. After a collapse, the circulation needs time. You should **sit up slowly** and only then stand up. Someone who stands up too fast risks collapsing again. If someone does not recover quickly, you fetch help.

gewusst: The calf muscles are often called the “second heart”, because they pump blood upwards.
Even a few toe movements while standing help the circulation.

teile.einleitung: After a long flight, many people feel tired and muddled. This is called jet lag. It arises when you travel quickly across several time zones and the inner clock no longer matches the time at the destination.
wichtigste: Jet lag arises from fast travel across several time zones.
Typical are tiredness in the day and lying awake at night.
Flights to the east cost most people more effort than flights to the west.
As a rule of thumb, the inner clock adjusts by about an hour per day.
Daylight at the destination helps most to reset the inner clock.
Between Zurich and New York there is normally a time difference of 6 hours.

abschnitte.text: Our body has an **inner clock**. It makes sure that we get tired in the evening and wake up in the morning. Body temperature, hunger and digestion also follow this daily rhythm. The clock is set mainly by **light**. When it gets dark, the body makes the hormone **melatonin**, which makes you tired. If you fly far to the east or west, the inner clock suddenly shows a quite different time from the clock at the destination.

Typical of jet lag are **tiredness in the day** and **lying awake at night**. Some people also have headaches, little appetite or trouble concentrating. The body needs a few days to adjust. As a rule of thumb: about **an hour per day**. With a time difference of six hours, it takes about a week until you are fully in step again.

If you fly **east**, you have to go to sleep earlier than the inner clock wants. Most people find this harder than staying awake longer. That is why jet lag after flying east is usually stronger. An example: **Tokyo** is 8 hours ahead of Swiss time in winter and 7 hours in summer. To **New York** in the west, it is normally 6 hours back.

Jet lag does not depend on the length of the flight but on the **time zones**. Someone who flies from Zurich to **Johannesburg** in South Africa is indeed on the way for about eleven hours. But both cities lie in almost the same time zone, because the flight goes mainly south. So there you have hardly any jet lag, at most tiredness from the long journey.

What helps most is to take in plenty of **daylight** at the destination, best outdoors. This way the inner clock resets faster. It is also good to follow the meal and sleep times of the place at once. A long afternoon nap can make it harder to fall asleep in the evening. Drinking enough and exercise in the fresh air also do you good.

gewusst: The word jet lag comes from English: “jet” is a jet aeroplane, “lag” means delay.
By train or ship there is hardly any jet lag, because you travel so slowly that the body can adjust on the way.
