teile.einleitung: The chin is the lowest part of the face, directly under the mouth. It is formed by the lower jaw. Amazingly, only we humans have a truly projecting chin.
wichtigste: The chin lies at the bottom of the face, under the mouth.
It is formed by the front part of the lower jaw.
Only humans have a projecting chin, not even chimpanzees.
You tuck a violin between your chin and shoulder.
When you nod “yes”, your chin moves up and down.
The male ibex has a beard on its chin.

abschnitte.text: The **chin** is the lowest part of the face, **under the mouth**. Below it the neck begins. The chin is formed by the front part of the **lower jaw**. When you talk or chew, it moves along. If you put your chin on your chest, you look **downwards**. If you nod your head “yes”, your chin moves **up and down**.

We humans have a **projecting chin**. This is something special, because even our closest relatives, the **chimpanzees**, have none. Their lower jaw slopes back at the front. In the Neanderthals, too, the chin was hardly pronounced. Why humans have a chin is still not fully explained. Researchers have various guesses about it.

In many grown men, beard hairs grow on the chin and cheeks. Some let a **beard** grow, while others remove the **stubble** with a razor in the morning. **Samichlaus**, the Swiss St Nicholas, wears a long **white beard** on chin and cheeks. Animals can have beards too: the male **ibex** in the Swiss Alps has a beard on its chin.

The chin helps with many things. A **violin** is tucked between chin and shoulder so that both hands are free. For this, the instrument even has a **chin rest**. Someone sitting thoughtfully at a table often rests their chin **on their hand**. When cycling and skiing, the **chin strap** holds the helmet in place. It should always be fastened.

gewusst: Violas are also held between chin and shoulder, like violins.
Anyone who hits their chin hard, for example in a fall, sometimes needs a few stitches, because the skin there lies directly on the bone.

teile.einleitung: A clinical trial tests whether a new medicine or a new treatment works and is safe. It runs in several phases, from a few volunteers to thousands of patients. Strict rules protect everyone who takes part.
wichtigste: In phase I, an active substance is tested for the first time on a few healthy volunteers.
Phase III, with hundreds to thousands of participants, is the main basis for approval.
Phase IV observes a medicine after approval.
The preparation with the real active substance is called verum, the dummy medicine placebo.
The control group serves for comparison with the treated group.
In Switzerland, a cantonal ethics committee has to approve a trial.
Participants give informed consent.

abschnitte.text: Before an active substance is tested on humans, it is examined in the laboratory. In **phase I**, a small group of mostly **healthy volunteers** receives the substance. It is checked how well it is tolerated and how the body processes it. In **phase II**, the first patients receive the drug in order to find its effect and the right dose. **Phase III** includes hundreds to thousands of participants and provides the most important data for **approval**.

Once a medicine is approved, research does not end. In **phase IV**, you observe how it works in everyday life in very many people. This also reveals **rare side effects** that could not show up in the smaller trials. In Switzerland, **Swissmedic** is the authority that approves and monitors medicines.

To know whether a drug really helps, you need a comparison. One group receives the **verum**, that is, the preparation with the real active substance. The **control group** gets a **placebo**, a dummy medicine, or the treatment that was usual until then. Often **chance** decides who goes into which group. In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the doctors know who gets what.

Research on humans has strict rules. Important principles are set out in the **Declaration of Helsinki** of the World Medical Association of 1964. In Switzerland, the **Human Research Act** governs such trials. Before a trial begins, a **cantonal ethics committee** must approve it. It checks whether benefits and risks stand in a reasonable relation.

Nobody may take part in a trial against their will. Beforehand, participants are told about the **aims**, **risks** and **procedure**. Only then do they freely give their agreement, the **informed consent**. You can drop out at any time without having to give reasons. With children, the parents decide as well, and the child is also asked in a way suited to its age.

gewusst: Of the many active substances tested in phase I, only a small part reaches approval.
Even a placebo can ease complaints, because belief in the effect influences the body.

teile.einleitung: Short-term memory holds information for a short time, for example a phone number until you have typed it in. It has little room and forgets quickly. With a few tricks you can use it better.
wichtigste: Short-term memory stores information only briefly.
According to George Miller, about 7 units fit into it, while newer research speaks of about 4.
Without repeating, a piece of information fades after a few seconds.
Chunking bundles information into bigger units.
Working memory processes information actively, for example in mental arithmetic.
Sensory memory holds sense impressions for only fractions of a second.
The frontal lobe is important for working memory.

abschnitte.text: Everything we see, hear or feel lands first in **sensory memory**. It is also called **ultra-short-term memory**. It holds sense impressions for only fractions of a second. Only what we pay attention to moves on into **short-term memory**. The rest is forgotten at once.

Short-term memory has little room. The psychologist **George Miller** described in 1956 the “magical number seven, plus or minus two”. This means that you can hold about **seven units** at the same time. Newer research even assumes about **four**. Without repeating, a piece of information fades after about 15 to 30 seconds.

A good trick is called **chunking**, from the English word for a “lump”. In it you bundle single parts into sensible packages. A long phone number is easier to remember in **groups of three** than digit by digit. This way more information fits into the limited store.

What helps most is to **repeat a piece of information inwardly**, for example by quietly saying it to yourself. This way it stays active. If someone speaks to you while you are trying to remember, the number is often gone at once. **New stimuli push out** the old ones before they have been firmed up. What you want to keep longer has to pass into **long-term memory**.

When you work actively with information in your head, it is called **working memory**. In **mental arithmetic**, for example, you remember intermediate results and carry on calculating with them. Especially important for this is the **frontal lobe**, the front part of the cerebral cortex, also called the **prefrontal cortex**. It also controls planning and attention.

gewusst: Phone numbers are often written in groups so that they are easier to remember.
The “magical number seven” comes from a famous paper of 1956.

teile.einleitung: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with blood. They lie like a wreath around the heart. If they become narrow or blocked, a heart attack can arise.
wichtigste: The coronary arteries arise just above the aortic valve from the aortic root.
There is a left and a right coronary artery.
The left divides into the anterior interventricular branch and the circumflex branch.
The wall of the left ventricle is supplied with blood mainly in diastole.
Narrowing from arteriosclerosis leads to coronary heart disease.
Coronary arteries are functional end arteries, and a blockage usually leads to a heart attack.
At rest, about 5 % of the cardiac output flows through the coronary arteries.

abschnitte.text: The two **coronary arteries** leave the **aortic root** just above the **aortic valve**. This way they are the first to receive fresh, oxygen-rich blood. The main trunk of the **left coronary artery** divides into the front descending branch, the **anterior interventricular branch** (LAD), and the **circumflex branch**, which runs round the heart. In most people the **right coronary artery** also supplies the **AV node**, an important station of the conduction system.

In **systole**, the heart muscle tenses and squeezes the vessels in its wall. That is why the thick wall of the left ventricle, in particular, is supplied with blood mainly in **diastole**, the relaxation phase. The heart makes up only about half a per cent of body weight, but at rest receives about **5 % of the cardiac output**. Even at rest it uses the oxygen from the blood very strongly.

In **arteriosclerosis**, substances are deposited in the vessel wall and narrow the arteries. If this affects the coronary vessels, it is called **coronary heart disease**. Under exertion, the heart muscle then gets too little oxygen. Typical is a feeling of tightness in the chest, **angina pectoris**, which literally means “tightness of the chest”.

The connections between the branches of the coronary arteries are usually too weak to replace a vessel that is suddenly blocked. They are therefore called **functional end arteries**. If an artery is blocked, the piece of heart muscle it supplies dies. This is a **heart attack**. A blockage of the right coronary artery can also cause disturbances of conduction at the AV node.

With **coronary angiography**, the coronary vessels are made visible. A thin tube, a **cardiac catheter**, is pushed forward to the heart. Through it, **contrast medium** is injected directly into the coronary arteries. On the X-ray you can then see narrowings, which can often be treated straight away.

gewusst: The heart supplies itself first: the coronary arteries branch off right at the start of the aorta.
The heart muscle is supplied with blood mainly in the short pauses between two beats.

teile.einleitung: Everyone knows itching: it tingles on the skin, and you want to scratch at once. Itching is a warning signal from the body. It can have many causes, from mosquito bites to dry skin.
wichtigste: When something itches, you scratch almost by yourself.
In many people, eyes and nose itch in spring because of pollen.
The stinging nettle makes itchy and burning weals.
When a graze heals, the scab often itches.
A bite that has been scratched until it bleeds can become inflamed.
Head lice and chickenpox cause strong itching.
Moisturising helps against dry skin in winter.

abschnitte.text: In the skin there are fine **nerves** that report stimuli to the brain. If the skin is irritated, for example by a sting or a plant, the feeling of **itching** arises. Often the body releases the substance **histamine** in the process. Almost by itself you then begin to **scratch**. Scratching distracts the brain briefly, but afterwards it often itches even more.

The **stinging nettle** has fine stinging hairs. If you touch it, they break off and release an irritating juice into the skin. Itchy, burning **weals** arise, small white or red bumps. In spring, a lot of **pollen** is in the air. In people with hay fever, the **eyes and nose** then itch. Mosquitoes, horseflies or fleas also leave itchy bites.

When a **graze** heals, a crust forms, the **scab**. Underneath, new skin grows, and this often itches. You should not scratch the scab off, or healing takes longer. If you scratch a bite until it **bleeds**, germs can get into the wound. Then the spot can become **inflamed**: it turns red, warm and hurts. Cooling often helps better than scratching.

**Head lice** are tiny insects that live in head hair and cause small bites. They keep turning up in school classes, and this has nothing to do with a lack of cleanliness. You get rid of them again with a special treatment and a fine comb. The childhood illness **chickenpox** causes many itchy blisters all over the body. Here too you should avoid scratching if possible, so that no scars remain.

In winter the air outside is cold and inside it is dry from the heating. The skin then loses moisture and begins to itch. Regular **moisturising** helps against this. Not showering too hot or too long also spares the skin. If itching lasts a long time or comes without a recognisable reason, you should have it checked by a doctor.

gewusst: Even when you only talk about lice or fleas, many people begin to scratch. Itching can seem catching like yawning.
Cold helps against itching, because the nerves then report cold rather than itching.

teile.einleitung: A torn cruciate ligament is a serious injury of the knee joint, usually affecting the anterior cruciate ligament. It often happens in skiing, football or handball. A lot of patience is needed before returning to competitive sport.
wichtigste: The anterior cruciate ligament prevents the lower leg from sliding forwards.
Typical is a twisting of the knee with the foot fixed.
The Lachman test is used to check the anterior cruciate ligament.
An MRI shows a torn cruciate ligament best.
The patellar tendon or the semitendinosus tendon is often used as a replacement.
It usually takes 6 to 12 months before competitive sport.
If the lower leg can be pushed backwards, this points to a tear of the posterior cruciate ligament.

abschnitte.titel: The job of the cruciate ligaments
abschnitte.text: The **anterior cruciate ligament** runs from the shin bone obliquely backwards and upwards to the thigh bone. Above all it prevents the lower leg from sliding forwards in relation to the thigh, the so-called **forward slide**. The **posterior cruciate ligament** prevents the shin bone from slipping backwards. If it is torn, the lower leg can be pushed backwards, which is called a **posterior drawer**.

Typical is a **twisting of the knee with the foot fixed**. The body turns while the foot stays put on the ground or in the ski boot. This often happens in **skiing**, in **football** or **handball**. With a twist and a knock-kneed position, the **medial ligament** and **medial meniscus** can also tear. This combination is called the **unhappy triad**.

In the **Lachman test**, the shin bone is pulled forwards with the knee bent by about 20 to 30 degrees. A soft end point or strong forward sliding points to a tear. Ligaments are soft tissue and hardly visible on an X-ray. That is why **magnetic resonance imaging** (MRI) is used. It shows ligaments, menisci and cartilage exactly.

In **cruciate ligament reconstruction**, the torn ligament is replaced by one of the body’s own tendons. Often a part of the **patellar tendon** or the **semitendinosus tendon** from the back of the thigh is used. The tendon is folded and anchored in the bone. Not every tear has to be operated on, but in active athletes it often is.

The inserted **graft** first has to heal in and be remodelled. That is why athletes usually return to competition only after **6 to 12 months**. In this time they strengthen the muscles around the knee with **physiotherapy** and build-up training. Strong muscles protect the new ligament.

gewusst: A torn cruciate ligament is usually not stitched but replaced by another tendon.
On ordinary X-rays you can hardly see cruciate ligaments.

teile.einleitung: Muscles can work without anything moving. In an isometric contraction, a muscle tenses but stays the same length. This happens, for example, when you hold a heavy bag steady.
wichtigste: Isometric means “same measure”: the muscle length stays the same, the tension rises.
Isotonic means: the muscle shortens at constant tension.
Auxotonic means: length and tension change at the same time, which is the most common in everyday life.
A muscle works eccentrically when it is stretched under tension, for example when walking downhill.
Eccentrically, a muscle can develop the greatest force.
Holding exercises such as the forearm plank train the muscles mainly isometrically.

abschnitte.text: A muscle is made of many fibres that can contract. In an **isometric contraction**, the tension in the muscle rises, but it becomes neither shorter nor longer. The word comes from Greek: “isos” means equal, “metron” means measure. One example is pushing against a wall that does not move. Someone who holds an object steady in their hand is also working isometrically.

If a muscle shortens at constant tension, this is called **isotonic**, that is, “equal tension”. If length and tension change at the same time, it is called **auxotonic**. Most movements in everyday life are auxotonic. If the muscle becomes shorter, it is also called **concentric** work. If, on the other hand, it is stretched under tension, this is **eccentric** work, a kind of braking work.

When walking downhill, the front **thigh muscle** brakes every step while it is being stretched. In this eccentric way of working, a muscle can produce more force than when holding or shortening. This is because the tiny links between the protein filaments in the muscle, the **cross-bridges**, are put under extra load when stretched and can withstand a lot. Anyone who has sore muscles after a mountain hike often feels exactly this braking work.

In physics, **work** is force times distance. If you hold a dumbbell steady, it does not move, so no work is done on the dumbbell: zero joules. Even so, your muscle uses energy and gets tired. This is because with strong tension, the muscle presses on its own **blood vessels**. As a result, less blood with oxygen flows in, and the muscle tires quite quickly in holding work.

Many strength exercises without movement are isometric, for example the **forearm plank**, also called the plank. Here the trunk muscles hold the body straight and still. Such exercises need no equipment and can be done almost anywhere. It is important to keep breathing calmly while holding and not to hold your breath. In sport, different kinds of muscle work are usually combined.

gewusst: A muscle uses energy when holding steady, although physically speaking it does no work on the load.
Even when standing, many muscles work isometrically all the time so that you do not fall over.

teile.einleitung: The larynx sits at the front of the throat and joins the pharynx to the windpipe. It protects the airways and contains the vocal folds, with which we speak and sing. In technical language it is called the larynx.
wichtigste: The larynx is called the larynx in technical language.
It lies between the pharynx and the windpipe.
The thyroid cartilage forms the “Adam’s apple”.
The cricoid cartilage is the only cartilage of the larynx that is a completely closed ring.
The small arytenoid cartilages adjust the vocal folds.
An inflammation of the larynx is called laryngitis and often leads to hoarseness.
In croup, small children have a typical barking cough.

abschnitte.text: The **larynx**, in technical language the **larynx**, lies at the front of the throat **between the pharynx and the windpipe**. It has two important jobs. First, it protects the windpipe so that no food gets in when swallowing. Second, it is the organ of the **voice**. If you put your hand on your throat and hum, you feel it vibrate.

The larynx is made of several **cartilages**. The biggest is the **thyroid cartilage**. At the front of the throat it forms an edge, the **“Adam’s apple”**, which usually stands out more clearly in men. Below it lies the **cricoid cartilage**. It is the only cartilage of the larynx that is a **completely closed ring**. On it sit the two small **arytenoid cartilages**. At the top, the **epiglottis** closes the larynx when swallowing.

Inside the larynx lie two **vocal folds**, often also called vocal cords. The **arytenoid cartilages** can bring them together, pull them apart and tighten them. When breathing, the vocal folds are wide open. When speaking, they lie close together, and the air we breathe out makes them **vibrate**. The tighter they are stretched, the higher the note sounds. Tongue, lips and mouth shape words from it.

An inflammation of the larynx is called **laryngitis**. It often arises with a cold. The vocal folds swell, and you become **hoarse** or briefly lose your voice. Then it helps to rest your voice. In small children, an inflammation below the vocal folds can lead to **croup**. Typical is a **barking cough**, often at night. Cool, moist air can ease the complaints, and with difficulty breathing, medical help is needed.

In **babies**, the larynx still sits **higher** in the throat than in adults. That is why they can **drink and breathe at the same time**. The liquid flows past the side of the larynx. Adults cannot do this, and have to stop breathing briefly when swallowing. In the course of the first years of life, the larynx moves down.

gewusst: The name Adam’s apple comes from an old legend: a piece of the forbidden apple is said to have got stuck in Adam’s throat.
When singing high notes, the vocal folds can vibrate several hundred times a second.

teile.einleitung: Before we swallow food, we chew it. Teeth, tongue, jaw and saliva work together in the process. Good chewing is the first step of digestion.
wichtigste: With the front teeth you bite off a piece.
With the molars you grind the food.
The tongue pushes the food between the teeth.
In chewing, the lower jaw moves up and down.
The strong masseter muscle on the cheek helps with chewing.
From food and saliva, a soft pulp is made.
Anyone who eats slowly and chews well notices sooner when they are full.

abschnitte.text: Our teeth have different jobs. With the flat, sharp **incisors** at the front you bite off a piece, for example from an apple. The pointed **canines** help with holding and tearing. At the back sit the broad **molars**. With them you **grind** the food as in a mill. Children have 20 milk teeth, and adults up to 32 permanent teeth.

In chewing, only the **lower jaw** moves, up and down and a little sideways. The upper jaw is firmly joined to the skull. The strong **masseter muscle** on the cheek pulls the lower jaw powerfully upwards. The **tongue** is very skilful in the process: it keeps pushing the food between the teeth without our biting down on it. The cheeks help too.

While we chew, the **salivary glands** make a lot of **saliva**. It makes the food moist and slippery. From food and saliva, a **soft pulp** is made that is easy to swallow. Saliva also contains a substance that begins to break down starch, for example from bread, already in the mouth. That is why bread tastes slightly sweet when you chew it for a long time.

Anyone who **eats slowly** and chews well notices sooner **when they are full**. The feeling of fullness needs some time to reach the brain. Well chopped-up food is also easier to digest. You should not **talk** with your mouth full. It is impolite, and you can easily choke.

gewusst: The lower jaw is the only bone in the head that can really move.
Cows chew their food twice: after the first eating they bring it up again and chew it once more in peace.

teile.einleitung: A stretcher is a device on which sick or injured people are transported lying down. It is used by the ambulance service, in hospitals and by mountain rescue. This way the injured arrive safely and gently.
wichtigste: On a stretcher, injured people are transported lying down.
Many stretchers have wheels and straps.
With the stretcher, injured people are pushed into the ambulance.
In the ambulance, the stretcher is fastened down.
There are different stretchers for different call-outs.

abschnitte.text: Someone who is injured and cannot walk is laid on a **stretcher**. The stretcher in the ambulance service usually has **wheels**. With them, the paramedics push the person to the **ambulance** and into it. In the vehicle, the stretcher is firmly anchored so that it does not slip during the journey.

On the stretcher, the injured person is secured with **straps**. This way they cannot fall off while being carried or driven. Often the head end can be raised so that the person lies more comfortably or can breathe better. A blanket also keeps them warm.

Not every stretcher looks the same. Simple stretchers consist of two poles with firm cloth in between. In the mountains, **mountain rescue** uses special stretchers that can also be lowered on a rope or fixed to a helicopter. For injuries to the back there are special supports that keep the body still.

gewusst: Rescue stretchers can often be folded up so that they fit well into the vehicle.

teile.einleitung: Lupus erythematosus is an autoimmune disease. In it, the body’s own defence system attacks the body. The disease can affect the skin, the joints and also inner organs.
wichtigste: In lupus, the defence system makes antibodies against parts of the body’s own cells.
A typical sign is the butterfly rash on the face.
Antinuclear antibodies are almost always positive, and anti-dsDNA antibodies are especially specific.
About nine out of ten people affected are women.
UV radiation from the sun can set off rashes and flare-ups.
Hydroxychloroquine, originally developed against malaria, is a basis of treatment.

abschnitte.text: The Latin word **“lupus”** means **wolf**. The changes in the skin probably used to remind people of wolf bites. In **systemic lupus erythematosus**, the defence system attacks the body itself. This is called an **autoimmune disease**. The disease often comes in **flare-ups**: sometimes people affected feel well, and then worse again. About **nine out of ten** people affected are women.

A typical sign is a redness across the cheeks and nose in the shape of a butterfly, the **butterfly rash**. Many people affected have joint pain and fever and are very tired. The **UV radiation** of the sun can set off skin rashes and flare-ups of the disease, so good sun protection is important. If lupus attacks the kidneys, it is called **lupus nephritis**. It is a dangerous involvement of an organ.

In the blood, doctors look for **autoantibodies**, that is, antibodies against the body’s own substances. A screening test is for **antinuclear antibodies** (ANA), which are directed against parts of the cell nucleus. In lupus this test is almost always positive, but it also occurs in other diseases. **Anti-dsDNA antibodies** are especially **specific** for lupus. They are directed against the double-stranded genetic material DNA.

Lupus cannot be cured so far, but it can be treated well. One basis is **hydroxychloroquine**, a drug that was originally developed against **malaria**. In flare-ups, cortisone and other drugs that dampen the defence system are added. There is also **drug-induced lupus**: certain medicines cause a similar illness, which usually fades after they are stopped.

gewusst: Lupus is sometimes called the “disease with a thousand faces”, because it can look very different.
10 May is World Lupus Day.

teile.einleitung: The masseter muscle, called the masseter in technical language, is one of the strongest muscles of the body. It closes the jaw when we bite and chew. Together with other muscles, it forms the chewing muscles.
wichtigste: The masseter muscle closes the jaw.
You can feel it at the side of the cheek in front of the ear when you bite down hard.
It stretches between the cheekbone arch and the lower jaw.
The temporalis muscle also belongs to the chewing muscles.
The chewing muscles are controlled by the trigeminal nerve.
The masseter belongs to the skeletal muscles.
In proportion to its size, it produces a great deal of force.

abschnitte.text: Put your fingers on the side of your cheek, a little **in front of the ear**, and bite your teeth firmly together. You feel a thick muscle bulge: the **masseter muscle**, in Latin **masseter**. It stretches between the **zygomatic arch**, the bone under the eye at the side of the face, and the **lower jaw**. When it contracts, it pulls the lower jaw upwards and **closes the jaw**.

The masseter does not work alone. The **chewing muscles** also include the **temporalis muscle** at the side of the head. You feel it at the temple when you chew. In addition there are two deeper muscles on the inside of the jaw. All the chewing muscles are controlled by the **trigeminal nerve**, the **nervus trigeminus**. This is a cranial nerve that is also responsible for feeling in the face.

The masseter belongs to the **skeletal muscles**, like the muscles on arms and legs. So you can control it deliberately. It is known for producing **a great deal of force in proportion to its size**. Together with the other chewing muscles, it can press the molars together with great force. That way we can also bite through hard nuts or carrots.

Some people press their teeth together or rub them against each other without noticing, often **at night** in their sleep. This is called **teeth grinding**, in technical language bruxism. It is often linked to stress. In the process, the chewing muscles work hard, and the teeth can wear down. In the morning the jaw or head sometimes hurts. The dentist can fit a **bite splint** that protects the teeth at night.

gewusst: Anyone who chews a lot of chewing gum trains their chewing muscles, and they can become somewhat stronger as a result.
The trigeminal nerve is called that, in German “triplet nerve”, because it divides into three large branches.

teile.einleitung: Immunosuppression means that immune reactions are suppressed, either on purpose or unintentionally. Doctors use medicines for this, for example after an organ transplant. However, the risk of infections goes up as a result.
wichtigste: Immunosuppression is the suppression of immune reactions.
After an organ transplant, immunosuppressants prevent the donor organ from being rejected.
The medicine ciclosporin was discovered in the 1970s at Sandoz in Basel.
Ciclosporin and tacrolimus inhibit the enzyme calcineurin in T cells.
Glucocorticoids such as cortisone also suppress inflammation and immune reactions.
With lasting immunosuppression, the risk of infections by opportunistic germs goes up.

abschnitte.text: The immune system protects the body from disease-causing germs. Sometimes, though, it is necessary to slow its reactions. The **suppression of immune reactions** is called **immunosuppression**. Medicines that bring it about are called **immunosuppressants**. Immunosuppression can also arise unintentionally, for example as a side effect of a treatment or through an illness.

In an **organ transplant**, a person receives, for example, a kidney or a heart from another person. The immune system recognises the donor organ as foreign and would attack it. This is called **rejection**. That is why people usually have to take **immunosuppressants** for life after a transplant. This keeps the new organ working.

A particularly important immunosuppressant is **ciclosporin**. It was discovered in the **1970s** at the pharmaceutical company **Sandoz** in **Basel**. It was obtained from a fungus that had been found in a soil sample. Ciclosporin made transplants much more successful. Like the later drug **tacrolimus**, it inhibits the enzyme **calcineurin** in the **T cells**. As a result, these defence cells become less active.

**Glucocorticoids** are often used. These are steroid hormones such as the well-known **cortisone**, which suppress inflammation and immune reactions. **Methotrexate** is a folic acid antagonist, so it slows the action of the vitamin folic acid. In low doses it helps against **rheumatoid arthritis**, a disease in which the immune system attacks the joints. Immunosuppressants are also used in other autoimmune diseases.

Anyone who takes immunosuppressants for a long time is less well protected against germs. In particular, the risk of infections by **opportunistic germs** goes up. These are germs that hardly harm healthy people but make people ill when their defences are weakened. **Chemotherapy** against cancer also often weakens the defences. It damages quickly dividing cells, including in the **bone marrow**, where defence cells arise.

gewusst: The fungus from which ciclosporin was obtained came from a soil sample from Norway.
People with immunosuppression usually should not receive certain vaccinations with live germs.

teile.einleitung: The systemic circulation carries oxygen-rich blood from the heart to all the organs and back again. It is also called the greater circulation.
wichtigste: The systemic circulation is also called the greater circulation.
It begins in the left ventricle.
William Harvey was the first to describe exactly, in 1628, that blood flows in a circle.
After the capillaries, the blood flows into the venules, the smallest veins.
At rest, more than half of the blood is in the veins.
At rest, the kidneys receive about a fifth of the blood that the heart pumps out.

abschnitte.text: The **systemic circulation** begins in the **left ventricle**. From there the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood into the **main artery**, the aorta. It branches into ever smaller **arteries** and finally into tiny **capillaries**. There the blood gives oxygen and nutrients to the cells and takes up carbon dioxide. Afterwards it flows back through the veins into the right atrium of the heart. From there the lesser circulation through the lungs begins.

After the capillaries, the blood collects in the **venules**, the smallest veins. These join to form ever larger veins. Veins have thinner walls than arteries and can stretch well. At rest, **more than half** of all the blood is therefore in the veins. They serve the body as a **blood store**. Venous valves make sure that the blood in the legs does not flow back.

For a long time people believed that blood was constantly newly made in the liver and used up in the body. The English doctor **William Harvey** showed in **1628** that blood flows **in a circle**. He calculated how much blood the heart pumps and realised that the body could not possibly make so much anew. His discovery was a milestone of medicine.

The body distributes the blood according to need. At rest, the **kidneys** receive about **a fifth** of the blood that the heart pumps out, because they clean the blood. During **sport**, the blood vessels in the working **muscles** widen so that they get more oxygen. In **cold**, the small arteries in the skin narrow. This way less warmth is lost. In heat it is the other way round: the skin gets more blood and gives off warmth.

gewusst: All the blood vessels of an adult put together would be many thousands of kilometres long.
For a whole round through the body, the blood needs only about one minute at rest.

teile.einleitung: On almost every food package, it says how many calories are in it. The calorie is a unit of energy. It shows how much energy the body can gain from a food.
wichtigste: A kilocalorie was originally the energy needed to warm 1 kg of water by 1 °C.
1 kcal corresponds to about 4.2 kilojoules.
The legal unit of energy is the joule.
Nutritional information mostly refers to 100 g or 100 ml.
1 gram of alcohol provides about 7 kcal.
If you eat more energy than you use over a longer time, body weight rises.
The energy content is determined in the laboratory with a calorimeter.

abschnitte.text: The **calorie** is an old unit of **energy**. A **kilocalorie**, kcal for short, was originally defined like this: it is the energy needed to warm **1 kilogram of water by 1 degree Celsius**. In everyday life people often say “calories” and really mean kilocalories. The word comes from the Latin “calor”, which means heat.

The legal unit of energy today is the **joule**, named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule. On foods, therefore, both figures are given: kilojoules (kJ) and kilocalories (kcal). **1 kcal corresponds to about 4.2 kJ**. So 500 kcal are roughly 2,100 kJ. Converting is easy: kilocalories times 4.2 gives kilojoules.

Our food contains energy in **carbohydrates**, **fat** and **protein**. One gram of carbohydrate or protein provides about 4 kcal, and one gram of fat about 9 kcal. **Alcohol** also provides energy, namely about **7 kcal per gram**. A comparison: an apple has about 50 kcal, a piece of cake about 350 kcal. It takes **7 apples** to provide as much energy as the piece of cake, but they fill you up much more.

In Switzerland, the **nutritional information** on packages is usually given per **100 g or 100 ml**. This makes it easy to compare different products. Often the amount per portion is given as well. Besides energy, fat, sugar, protein and salt are also stated. Some products also carry the coloured **Nutri-Score**, which is meant to give a quick assessment.

The body needs energy for everything: breathing, thinking, growing and moving. If over a longer time you eat **more energy than you use**, the body stores the rest as fat, and your **weight rises**. If you eat less than you need, it falls. How much energy someone needs depends on age, size and activity. What matters is not only the amount but also that the food is varied.

gewusst: With a **calorimeter**, a food is burned in the laboratory and the heat released is measured.
The body also uses energy while sleeping, because the heart, brain and breathing keep working.

teile.einleitung: The inner clock is a timekeeper in our body. It makes sure that we get tired in the evening and wake up in the morning. Almost all living things, including plants and animals, have such a clock.
wichtigste: The central inner clock of humans sits in the hypothalamus in the brain.
Through the eyes it learns whether it is day or night.
Daylight is the strongest time cue.
The pineal gland makes the sleep hormone melatonin.
In the morning the hormone cortisol rises and helps you wake up.
Without time cues, the day of the inner clock usually lasts a little longer than 24 hours.
In 2017 there was a Nobel Prize for research on the inner clock in the fruit fly.

abschnitte.text: The **central inner clock** of humans sits in the **hypothalamus**, a small area deep in the brain. It controls many processes in the daily rhythm: when we get tired, how high the body temperature is and when certain hormones are made. This rhythm of about one day is called the **circadian rhythm**, from the Latin “circa diem”, about a day.

Through the **eyes**, the inner clock learns whether it is day or night. Special cells in the retina report the brightness to the brain. **Daylight** is the strongest **time cue**, that is, the most important signal that sets the clock. Without such time cues, the inner clock in humans usually runs **a little longer than 24 hours**. Light sets it right again every day.

When it gets dark, the **pineal gland** in the brain makes the sleep hormone **melatonin**. It makes us tired. In the **morning**, on the other hand, the hormone **cortisol** rises strongly and helps us to become awake and active. Bright light from screens late in the evening can slow the making of melatonin. That is why falling asleep is then sometimes harder.

The German researcher **Jürgen Aschoff** had volunteers live for weeks in a **bunker in Andechs in Bavaria** in the 1960s. There was neither daylight nor clocks. The people still slept and ate in a regular rhythm. This was usually a little longer than 24 hours, though. This showed that the clock really sits in the body.

As early as **1729**, the French researcher **Jean-Jacques d’Ortous de Mairan** showed with a **mimosa** that plants have an inner clock. The mimosa opened and closed its leaves in the daily rhythm even in a dark cupboard. In **2017**, three American researchers received the **Nobel Prize** in Medicine. They had discovered in the **fruit fly** the genes that control the inner clock.

gewusst: After a long flight to another time zone, the inner clock needs a few days to adjust, which is called jet lag.
In many teenagers the inner clock shifts later, so they get tired later in the evening.

teile.einleitung: Youth protection means that children and young people are protected from things that can harm them. These include alcohol, tobacco and unsuitable content in films, games and on the internet. In Switzerland there are clear age limits for this.
wichtigste: Beer and wine can generally be bought in Switzerland from the age of 16.
Spirits such as schnapps are sold only from the age of 18.
Alcopops are available only from 18, because they contain spirits.
Since October 2024, the age limit for tobacco products has been 18 across Switzerland.
With test purchases, the authorities check whether shops keep to the age limits.
PEGI marks on video games give age recommendations.
Many social networks allow an account of your own from the age of 13 according to their terms of use.

abschnitte.text: Children and young people are still growing. Their bodies and brains react more sensitively to alcohol and nicotine than those of adults. Certain films, games or websites can also frighten or confuse. **Youth protection** therefore sets **age limits**. It is meant to protect young people, not to punish them. Responsible for the rules being applied are mainly the sellers, but also parents and schools.

In Switzerland, you can generally buy **beer and wine** from the age of **16**. **Spirits**, that is, distilled drinks such as schnapps, whisky or vodka, are available only from **18 years**. This also applies to **alcopops**, sweet mixed drinks that contain spirits. Some cantons have stricter rules. Shops and restaurants have to check age and ask for identification when in doubt.

Since **October 2024**, the following has applied across Switzerland: **tobacco products** and e-cigarettes may be sold only to people aged **18 and over**. Before that, the rules differed from canton to canton. Nicotine quickly makes you dependent, especially in young people. That is why advertising for tobacco is also restricted.

Do shops keep to the rules? The authorities check this with **test purchases**. In them, young people under the legal age try, on commission and under supervision, to buy alcohol or tobacco. If the staff sell anyway, this can lead to a fine. Test purchases show where checks still need to be better.

Video games often carry **PEGI marks** with numbers such as 3, 7, 12, 16 or 18. They give an **age recommendation** and show with symbols whether a game contains, for example, violence or bad language. Films also have age ratings. Many **social networks** allow an account of your own only from **13 years** according to their terms of use. On a mobile phone, tablet and computer, parents can set up **parental controls** that block unsuitable content and limit screen time.

gewusst: PEGI is a European age recommendation and is also used in Switzerland.
In 2022, the Swiss Parliament passed a law on youth protection for films and video games.

teile.einleitung: A ball-and-socket joint is a joint in which a ball-shaped bone head sits in a round hollow. This lets the bone move in almost all directions and even rotate. In humans, the shoulder and the hip are the best-known ball-and-socket joints.
wichtigste: A ball-and-socket joint consists of a round joint head and a matching socket.
It allows movements in almost all directions.
The shoulder joint is a ball-and-socket joint and makes the arm very mobile.
The hip joint is also a ball-and-socket joint.
The shoulder is the most mobile joint of a human, but dislocates more easily for that reason.
Cartilage and joint fluid let the joint glide with little friction.
Worn hip joints can be replaced by an artificial joint.

abschnitte.text: A ball-and-socket joint has two parts: the **joint head**, which is shaped like a ball, and the **socket**, a round hollow. Both surfaces are covered with smooth cartilage. Around the joint lies a joint capsule, which contains a lubricating fluid. Ligaments and muscles hold the head in the socket.

Because the ball can roll all round in the socket, a ball-and-socket joint is very versatile. With it you can raise the arm forwards, backwards and sideways, make it circle and turn it about its own axis. Experts say that the ball-and-socket joint has three **degrees of freedom**. A hinge joint such as the elbow, by contrast, can only bend and stretch.

In the shoulder, the head of the upper arm bone sits in a small, flat socket on the shoulder blade. This socket is much smaller than the head, which is why the shoulder is the **most mobile joint** of the body. It is held mainly by muscles, the so-called rotator cuff. The drawback: the shoulder can dislocate more easily than other joints in a fall.

In the hip, the head of the thigh bone sits deep in a socket in the pelvis. This makes the **hip joint** very stable, but a little less mobile than the shoulder. It has to carry the whole body weight when walking, running and jumping. In older people the cartilage sometimes wears away, and then they get an artificial hip joint.

The principle also exists in technology. Cars have ball joints in the steering and in the wheel suspension. Tripods for cameras, phone holders or movable jointed dolls also use **ball heads**. This way something can be turned in many directions and then screwed tight.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movable connection between two bones.
The round, outwardly curved part of a joint.
The hollow in which the joint head sits.
A smooth, elastic tissue that protects the joint surfaces.

gewusst: With ball-and-socket joints in the shoulder and hip you can swing arms and legs in a circle, but not with the elbow.
The head of the thigh bone in the hip is about as big as a table tennis ball.
Ball joints on cars connect the wheels movably to the steering.

teile.einleitung: The windpipe is the tube through which the air we breathe flows from the throat to the lungs. It lies at the front of the neck and divides into two branches at the bottom. Rings of cartilage keep it open at all times.
wichtigste: The windpipe carries the air we breathe to the lungs.
Rings of cartilage keep it open.
You can feel it at the front of the neck.
When we swallow, the epiglottis closes the windpipe.
In adults it is about 11 centimetres long and divides into two branches at the bottom.
Fine hairs on the inside push dust and mucus out.

abschnitte.text: When you breathe in, air flows through the nose or mouth into the throat and then through the voice box into the **windpipe**. It leads down to the **lungs**. In adults it is about **11 centimetres** long. At the bottom it divides into **two branches**, the **bronchi**, one for the left and one for the right lung. These branch out ever more finely, like an **upside-down tree**.

The windpipe must never collapse, or no more air would get through. That is why it is supported by **rings of cartilage**. These are horseshoe-shaped and open at the back, where the gullet lies. At the front of the neck you can **feel** the windpipe: the rings of cartilage feel like little ridges.

Air and food first take the same path in the throat. To stop anything getting into the windpipe when we eat, there is the **epiglottis**. When we swallow, it folds over the entrance and **closes** the windpipe. The food then slides into the gullet. If something does go down the wrong way, we have to **cough** hard.

On the inside the windpipe is lined with a mucous membrane. On it sit tiny **cilia**. Dust and germs stick in the mucus, and the little hairs **push** everything up and out through the throat. In a **cold** more **mucus** than usual is often made, and you cough it up. Smoking harms these fine hairs.

gewusst: Without rings of cartilage, the windpipe would be pulled shut when we breathe in strongly.
The cilia beat many times a second.

teile.einleitung: A cuddly toy is a soft toy that you like to hold in your arms. Many children have one that goes everywhere with them and comforts them when they fall asleep.
wichtigste: Cuddly toys are mostly made of soft fabric and filled with wadding or fibres.
A cuddly toy made of fluffy fabric is also called a plush toy.
The teddy bear is named after the American president Theodore “Teddy” Roosevelt.
A cuddly toy gives many children comfort and a feeling of safety.
For babies there are comfort blankets, often with a little animal head.
Many cuddly toys can be washed and small holes sewn up.

abschnitte.titel: What a cuddly toy is made of
abschnitte.text: Most cuddly toys are sewn from soft **fabric**. Inside they are filled with **wadding** or soft synthetic fibres, which is why you can squeeze them well. If the fabric is especially fluffy, with short soft hairs, it is called **plush**. That is why cuddly toys are often also called **plush toys**. On toys for small children, the eyes and nose are usually embroidered so that nothing can come loose.

The best-known cuddly toy is the **teddy bear**. Its name comes from the American president **Theodore Roosevelt**, whom many called “Teddy”. For over a hundred years the teddy has been loved all over the world. A famous bear from children’s books is **Winnie the Pooh**. He has adventures with his friends, for example the donkey Eeyore and the tiger Tigger.

A cuddly toy is soft and **familiar**. It smells of home and is always the same, even in a strange place. For many children this gives a **safe feeling** at night. Babies like to hold a **comfort blanket** when falling asleep, a small soft cloth, often with an animal head. Many adults also keep their old cuddly toy as a memento.

If a cuddly toy gets dirty, you can often **wash** it, best in a laundry bag in the washing machine. Beforehand you look at the **label**, because it says how the toy may be washed. Then you let it dry well. If the cuddly toy has a **hole**, you sew it up with needle and thread. This way no stuffing falls out and the toy lasts a long time.

gewusst: The name teddy bear is the nickname of an American president.
Plush is the name for a fabric with short, soft hairs.

teile.einleitung: Influenza, also called true flu, is an infectious disease caused by viruses. In Switzerland there is a wave of flu almost every winter. Flu is usually much more severe than an ordinary cold.
wichtigste: Influenza is caused by flu viruses, in humans mainly type A and type B.
Flu viruses are passed on mainly by droplet infection.
In Switzerland, most flu cases occur in winter.
Sudden high fever is typical.
The Spanish flu began in 1918.
In 2009, swine flu set off a worldwide pandemic.
The FOPH recommends the flu vaccination especially for people aged 65 and over.

abschnitte.text: **Influenza** is caused by **flu viruses**. In humans, mainly **type A** and **type B** cause the yearly waves of flu. Type A viruses are named after two proteins on their surface, for example **H1N1**. The viruses change all the time. That is why you can catch flu several times in your life.

Typical of **true flu** is **sudden high fever**. Often there are also headache, aching limbs, a dry cough and great tiredness. An ordinary **cold**, on the other hand, usually starts slowly, with a runny nose and a scratchy throat, and is milder. Flu is passed on mainly by **droplet infection**, that is, when coughing, sneezing and speaking.

In Switzerland, most flu cases occur in **winter**. Then people spend more time in closed rooms, and the viruses spread more easily. When a flu spreads worldwide, it is called a **pandemic**. The **Spanish flu**, which began in **1918**, was one of the worst pandemics in history, and millions of people died of it. In **2009**, the so-called **swine flu** again set off a worldwide pandemic.

Animals can also fall ill with influenza. **Bird flu** is a form that affects mainly **birds**, such as wild birds and chickens. People rarely catch it, mostly through close contact with sick animals. Experts watch such viruses closely, because flu viruses from animals change and new forms can arise.

The best prevention is the **flu vaccination**. Because the viruses keep changing, the vaccine is put together anew every year. The **Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH)** recommends the vaccination especially for **people aged 65 and over** and for people with certain illnesses who have a higher risk. Against the viruses themselves there are **antiviral medicines**, so-called **virostatics**. Antibiotics do not help, because they work only against bacteria.

gewusst: The word influenza comes from Italian and means influence.
In healthy people, flu can last one to two weeks, and the tiredness often longer.

teile.einleitung: Pneumonia is an inflammation of the lung tissue, usually caused by bacteria or viruses. It is a serious illness but can often be treated well today. Its medical name is pneumonia too, from the Greek word for lung.
wichtigste: Pneumonia is an inflammation of the lung tissue.
Outside hospital, pneumococci are the most common bacterial cause.
Typical signs are fever, coughing and shortness of breath.
Liquid and defence cells collect in the alveoli.
It is often confirmed with an X-ray.
It is especially dangerous for very old people, and the pneumococcal vaccination protects against it.

abschnitte.text: The lungs contain millions of tiny **alveoli**. This is where oxygen gets into the blood. In **pneumonia**, parts of them are inflamed. **Liquid and defence cells** collect in the affected air sacs. As a result less oxygen can get into the blood, and breathing becomes harder.

Pneumonia is usually set off by **bacteria** or **viruses**. Outside hospital, the bacteria called **pneumococci** are the most common cause. Flu viruses or the coronavirus can also cause pneumonia. The germs usually get into the lungs through the air we breathe, for example through other people’s coughs and sneezes.

Typical signs are **fever**, **coughing** and **shortness of breath**. Many people feel very ill and worn out, and some have pain when breathing. With a **stethoscope** the doctor often hears **crackling sounds**, because there is liquid in the lungs. Pneumonia is often confirmed with an **X-ray** of the chest. There, inflamed areas can be seen as pale patches.

Bacterial pneumonia is treated with **antibiotics**. These do not help against viruses, and then rest and relief of the symptoms come first. Pneumonia is especially dangerous for **very old people**, for babies and for people with a weak immune system. The **pneumococcal vaccination** protects against a common form. In Switzerland it is recommended, among others, for small children and older people.

gewusst: The word “pneumonia” comes from the Greek “pneumon”, which means lung.
The flu vaccination can also help to prevent pneumonia.

teile.einleitung: Cognitive behavioural therapy is a form of psychotherapy. It assumes that our thoughts influence how we feel and behave. In therapy you learn to recognise unhelpful thoughts and to find more helpful ones.
wichtigste: The US psychiatrist Aaron T. Beck is regarded as the founder of cognitive therapy.
Albert Ellis developed rational emotive behaviour therapy.
The cognitive triad describes a negative view of oneself, the world and the future.
In the ABC model, the B stands for belief, that is, what you believe about an event.
In cognitive restructuring, unhelpful thoughts are examined and replaced.
Catastrophising and black and white thinking are typical thinking distortions.
Marsha Linehan developed dialectical behaviour therapy.

abschnitte.text: **Cognitive behavioural therapy** combines two approaches. “Cognitive” means that it is about **thoughts** and judgements. **Behavioural therapy** looks at what a person does and how they can learn new behaviour. The basic idea: not only an event itself, but our **interpretation** of it determines how we feel. Someone who changes their thoughts can therefore also influence their feelings.

The US psychiatrist **Aaron T. Beck** is regarded as the founder of **cognitive therapy**. In depression he described the **cognitive triad**: a negative view of **oneself**, of the **world** and of the **future**. Somewhat earlier, **Albert Ellis** had developed **rational emotive behaviour therapy**. His **ABC model** explains: A is a triggering event, **B** is the **belief** about it, that is, what you believe about it, and C is the consequence, that is, feeling and behaviour.

Some thoughts are distorted without your noticing. In **catastrophising**, you derive the worst possible consequence from a small problem: “I got a bad mark, so I will never get through school.” In **black and white thinking**, you see only extremes such as “perfect” or “total failure”. Other traps are overgeneralising or mind reading, in which you believe you know what others are thinking.

In **cognitive restructuring**, you learn to recognise unhelpful thoughts, **check** whether they are correct and replace them with more helpful ones. Often you write thoughts down for this and look for evidence for and against. In depression, **behavioural activation** is used: you deliberately plan in **pleasant activities**, such as a walk or a meeting. Exercises in everyday life are also part of it.

Many new forms have arisen from behavioural therapy. The US psychologist **Marsha Linehan** developed **dialectical behaviour therapy**. It helps people who find it hard to control very strong feelings. Cognitive behavioural therapy is now used for anxiety, depression and many other complaints. In Switzerland it is offered by psychotherapists and specialist doctors.

gewusst: Cognitive behavioural therapy is among the most thoroughly scientifically studied forms of psychotherapy.
In many treatments, patients get “homework” that they practise between sessions.

teile.einleitung: A cantonal hospital is a large hospital that belongs to a canton or is closely tied to it. In Switzerland, the cantons are responsible for hospital care for their population. They plan, help to pay and supervise.
wichtigste: The cantons draw up hospital lists that set which hospitals may treat at the expense of basic insurance.
For inpatient treatment, the canton of residence pays at least 55 per cent of the costs.
Since 2012, people with basic insurance can choose any listed hospital in all of Switzerland for planned treatment.
In 2024 the EFAS reform was accepted at the ballot box.
Many cantonal hospitals, such as Aarau and Baden, are public limited companies owned by the canton.
The ambulance emergency number in Switzerland is 144.

abschnitte.text: A **cantonal hospital** is usually the biggest hospital in a canton. It treats many different illnesses and injuries and often has a large **emergency department**. Examples are the **Cantonal Hospital of Graubünden** in **Chur**, the Cantonal Hospital of St Gallen or the Cantonal Hospital of Aarau. Besides cantonal hospitals there are university hospitals, regional hospitals and private clinics.

Under the Health Insurance Act, the **cantons** are responsible for hospital planning. They draw up **hospital lists**. These state which hospitals may carry out which treatments at the expense of **basic insurance**. Since **2012**, people with basic insurance can choose a **listed hospital in all of Switzerland** for planned treatment. For inpatient treatment, that is, with an overnight stay, the **canton of residence pays at least 55 per cent** of the costs, and the health insurer the rest.

Cantonal hospitals are organised in quite different ways. Some, such as the cantonal hospitals of **Aarau** and **Baden**, are **public limited companies owned by the canton**. Others are public-law institutions. In Ticino, the cantonal hospitals are joined together in the **Ente Ospedaliero Cantonale**, **EOC** for short. The aim of such forms is often that the hospitals can decide more independently.

The cantons have several roles in the hospital system at the same time. They often **own** hospitals themselves, but are at the same time **planners** and **supervisors** of all hospitals. Critics say that cantons could favour their own hospitals as a result. Supporters think that the cantons in this way ensure care for their population. This is discussed again and again in politics.

In **November 2024**, voters accepted the **EFAS** reform. The abbreviation stands for uniform financing of outpatient and inpatient services. In future, treatments with and without an overnight stay are to be paid for by the same formula. If someone urgently needs help, you dial the **ambulance emergency number 144**. Then an ambulance takes the person to the nearest suitable hospital.

gewusst: Many cantonal hospitals train nursing staff and young doctors.
The emergency number 144 is free all over Switzerland, including from a mobile phone.

teile.einleitung: Jogging is easy, relaxed running. You need almost nothing for it except good shoes, and you can do it anywhere: in the forest, in the fields or in town. Jogging strengthens the heart, lungs and muscles.
wichtigste: Jogging means easy running at a calm pace.
For jogging, it is best to put on running shoes.
If you can still talk while running, you are not going too fast.
Soft forest paths are kind to the joints.
A marathon is about 42 kilometres long, a half marathon about 21 kilometres.
At dusk, a high-visibility vest makes you visible.

abschnitte.text: **Jogging** is running at a relaxed, even pace. It is not about being as fast as possible, but about staying out for a long time and relaxed. In the process the **heart**, **lungs** and **leg muscles** are strengthened. Many people also jog because they feel fresh and in a good mood afterwards. The word comes from English and became known here in the 1970s.

Most important are good **running shoes**. They cushion the steps and give the foot support. Comfortable clothes that let sweat through well go with them. When it is dusk or dark, you wear a **high-visibility vest** or clothes with reflectors. This way drivers and cyclists see you in good time. In winter, a hat and gloves help against the cold.

A simple test shows whether you are not going too fast: you can still **talk** while running. Anyone who is only gasping should slow down. Beginners do best to alternate between running and walking. It is worth warming up briefly beforehand. Afterwards, an easy cool-down walk and something to drink do you good. It is better to do a little regularly than a lot rarely.

A soft **forest path** is especially gentle on the joints, because the ground gives way. Asphalt is harder, but stays clean even in the rain. In Switzerland, many municipalities have a **Vita Parcours**. This is a running track in the forest with stations where you do exercises for strength, flexibility and balance. Every exercise is explained on signs.

Anyone who likes running can take part in a **popular race**. The best-known long race is the **marathon** with about 42 kilometres, exactly 42.195 kilometres. The **half marathon** is half as long, so about 21 kilometres. Many races also have short routes for children. In Switzerland, the Grand Prix of Bern or the Zurich Marathon, for example, are well known.

gewusst: The name marathon recalls a legend from ancient Greece: a messenger is said to have run from the town of Marathon to Athens.
The first Vita Parcours came into being in Switzerland at the end of the 1960s, and the idea was later taken up abroad too.

teile.einleitung: Posture describes how we stand, sit and move. Good posture spares the back, and strong muscles help with it.
wichtigste: Seen from the side, a healthy spine has a double S shape.
A sideways curve of the spine is called scoliosis.
An increased round back is called hyperkyphosis, an increased hollow back hyperlordosis.
For the back, it is best to change your sitting posture often.
You lift heavy things from the knees with a straight back.
Training the trunk muscles strengthens the back.

abschnitte.text: The **spine** is not straight. Seen from the side, it has the shape of a **double S**. At the neck and in the lower back it curves forwards, in the chest area backwards. This shape works like a **spring**: it absorbs shocks when walking and jumping. Between the vertebrae lie the intervertebral discs as soft cushions.

Sometimes the spine is curved more than normal. A strongly increased **round back** in the chest area is called **hyperkyphosis**. An increased **hollow back** in the lower back is called **hyperlordosis**. If the spine is curved to the side, it is called **scoliosis**. Many such deviations are slight and harmless. Stronger ones are examined and treated by specialists, for example with physiotherapy.

Many children sit for a long time at school and in front of screens. The best sitting posture is the **next** one: someone who **changes** their sitting posture **often** relieves the back. Standing up now and then and moving also helps. When **looking at a mobile phone**, many tilt the head far forwards. Then the **neck muscles** have to hold much more, and the neck can become tense. It is better to hold the phone a little higher.

You lift a heavy crate **from the knees**: go into a squat, keep the back straight and stand up with the strength of the legs. This spares the spine. The best protection for the back is strong muscles. **Training the trunk muscles**, that is, belly and back, supports the spine like a corset. Climbing, swimming and gymnastics are also good for posture.

gewusst: A person has 24 freely movable vertebrae, plus the sacrum and the coccyx.
The further a head is tilted forwards, the more strongly it loads the neck.

teile.einleitung: Lipases are enzymes that split fats. Without them our body could hardly take in the fats from our food. The most important one is pancreatic lipase from the pancreas.
wichtigste: Lipases are enzymes that split fats, and they belong to the hydrolases.
Pancreatic lipase splits a triglyceride preferably at positions 1 and 3.
This produces 2-monoacylglycerol and two fatty acids.
Pancreatic lipase needs a helper protein called colipase.
Lipases work at the boundary between fat and water.
If pancreatic lipase is missing, fatty stools result.

abschnitte.text: Dietary fats consist mainly of **triglycerides**: three fatty acids are attached to one glycerol. These molecules are too big to get through the wall of the intestine. **Lipases** split them with the help of water. That is why they belong to the enzyme class of the **hydrolases**. Because fat and water do not mix, lipases attack at the **boundary between fat and water**.

The digestion of fat does not begin only in the small intestine. Even in the stomach, **gastric lipase** splits a small part of the fats. Most of the work, however, is done by **pancreatic lipase**. It is made in the pancreas and released into the small intestine. There, the **bile** breaks big drops of fat into many small ones, so that the lipase has more surface to attack.

Pancreatic lipase splits a triglyceride preferably at **positions 1 and 3**, that is, at the outer fatty acids. This produces **2-monoacylglycerol** and **two free fatty acids**. These can be taken up by the cells of the intestine. Bile salts would, however, push the lipase away from the drops of fat. The helper protein **colipase** therefore anchors it at the surface.

abschnitte.titel: When lipase is missing or blocked
abschnitte.text: If too little pancreatic lipase reaches the intestine, for example in a disease of the pancreas, many fats stay undigested. A typical sign is **fatty stools**, which are pale, shiny and foul-smelling. People affected can take enzymes as capsules with their meals. The medicine **orlistat** makes use of lipase in a different way: it **blocks** it in the intestine so that less fat is absorbed. It is meant to help with losing weight.

gewusst: Lipases are also used in washing powders so that they dissolve grease stains.
In the making of some kinds of cheese, lipases help to produce the typical taste.

teile.einleitung: In interval training, strenuous phases and recovery phases alternate according to a fixed plan. In this way you can improve endurance and speed in a targeted way. There are many forms, from classic running training to the short, very hard HIIT.
wichtigste: Interval training is a planned alternation of effort and recovery.
The incomplete rest in between is called the rewarding rest interval.
Intensive interval training has a higher intensity and fewer repetitions than extensive.
In the repetition method, you recover fully between the efforts.
HIIT stands for High Intensity Interval Training.
A Tabata protocol lasts 4 minutes.
Fartlek is a Swedish “speed play” with free changes of pace in open country.

abschnitte.text: In **interval training**, **effort** and **recovery** alternate according to plan. You run, swim or cycle, for example, fast for a minute and then easily for a while. The rest is deliberately **incomplete**: you start again before you have fully recovered. This rest is called the **rewarding rest interval**. In this way the body is strongly challenged and adapts, and the heart and muscles become more capable.

Two kinds are distinguished. In **extensive** interval training, the effort is moderately high, but there are many repetitions. In **intensive** interval training, the **intensity is higher** and there are **fewer repetitions**. Different from these is the **repetition method**: here you recover **fully** between the efforts before the next one begins. In the interval method, on the other hand, the rest stays incomplete.

The interval method became known especially through the trainer **Woldemar Gerschler** and the doctor **Herbert Reindell**. They worked in **Freiburg im Breisgau**, which is why it is also called the **Freiburg interval method**. The Czech runner Emil Zátopek was famous for hard interval training. Even earlier, **fartlek**, in English “speed play”, arose in Sweden. In it you shape the changes of pace freely in open country, for example faster uphill.

**HIIT** stands for **High Intensity Interval Training**, that is, high-intensity interval training. Here the efforts are short but very hard. A well-known form is the **Tabata protocol**, named after the Japanese researcher Izumi Tabata. It consists of 8 rounds with 20 seconds of effort and 10 seconds of rest each. Together that is only **4 minutes**, but they are very strenuous.

In **pyramid interval training**, the intervals become **first longer and then shorter again**, for example 1, 2, 3, 2 and 1 minute. This brings variety to training. Before every interval training you warm up well, and afterwards you jog gently to cool down. Because it is very demanding, you do not do it every day, so that the body can recover.

gewusst: Interval training is common in many sports, from running and swimming to rowing.
Fartlek was developed in Sweden in the 1930s.

teile.einleitung: Clothes protect us from cold, sun and rain. To keep them clean and smelling good, you have to change and wash them regularly. Small pictures on the label show how to care for a garment correctly.
wichtigste: You change socks and underwear every day.
You wash clothes to remove dirt and sweat.
Today you usually wash clothes in the washing machine.
The pictures on the label are called care symbols.
The number in the wash tub shows the highest washing temperature.
Wet clothes do not belong in the cupboard, because they can go mouldy.
You put dirty clothes in the laundry basket.

abschnitte.text: Every day our skin gives off **sweat** and small flakes of skin. These stay in the clothes. That is why you change **socks** and underwear every day. After gym you put on **fresh, dry clothes**, because sweaty clothes soon smell unpleasant and make you cold. You can often wear jumpers or trousers for several days if they are not dirty.

When washing, **dirt**, sweat and smells are removed. The **detergent** dissolves grease and stains, and the water rinses them away. In the past, people washed by hand, with a washboard or at the fountain. Today this is usually done by the **washing machine**. In many Swiss apartment blocks there is a shared laundry room with a plan of who may wash when.

In the garment a small **label** is sewn. On it are **care symbols**. The **wash tub** shows how to wash. If the number **30** is in it, you wash at 30 degrees at most. A triangle stands for bleaching, a square for drying, an iron for ironing. If a sign is crossed out, you must not do that.

After washing, the clothes are wet. You hang them up or put them in the **tumble dryer**. Only when they are completely dry do they go in the **cupboard**. Wet clothes can go **mouldy** there and smell musty. Worn, dirty clothes are not put on the floor but in the **laundry basket**.

Anyone who looks after clothes well can wear them longer. Not every item has to be washed after being worn once. Low temperatures save **energy** and spare the fabric. Clothes that have become too small can be passed on or taken to a **clothes collection**. This way they are used once more.

gewusst: The care symbols are the same in many countries, so you understand them even without language.
A washing machine at 40 degrees uses clearly less electricity than one at 60 degrees.

teile.einleitung: The cruciate ligaments are two strong ligaments inside the knee joint. They cross each other and hold the thigh bone and shin bone together. A tear of the anterior cruciate ligament is a common sports injury.
wichtigste: Each knee has two cruciate ligaments, an anterior and a posterior one.
The anterior cruciate ligament prevents the lower leg from sliding forwards.
The anterior cruciate ligament tears much more often than the posterior one.
In skiing in particular, many cruciate ligaments tear.
The cruciate ligament is tested with the drawer test.
A torn cruciate ligament is often replaced with one of the body’s own tendons.

abschnitte.text: Each knee joint has **two cruciate ligaments**: an **anterior** and a **posterior** one. They lie in the middle of the knee and cross each other, hence the name. The anterior cruciate ligament runs from the shin bone obliquely backwards and upwards to the thigh bone. This way it stops the **shin bone** from sliding forwards. The posterior cruciate ligament prevents it from slipping backwards.

The **anterior cruciate ligament** tears much more often, because it is put under heavy strain by twisting and sudden braking. A tear is one of the commonest serious knee injuries in sport. In Switzerland it happens especially often in **skiing**. There the skis can twist the knee while the body carries on. In **football** too, many cruciate ligaments tear.

Many of those affected hear a **bang** or a “pop” in the knee at the moment of the injury. After that, the knee usually swells quickly and feels unstable. In the **drawer test**, the doctor pulls the lower leg forwards. If it can be pulled out like a drawer, the anterior cruciate ligament has probably torn.

In a strong twist with a blow from the side, three structures can be injured at the same time: the **anterior cruciate ligament**, the **medial ligament** and the **medial meniscus**. This combination is called the **unhappy triad** in English.

Not every cruciate ligament tear has to be operated on. In athletes, though, the ligament is often replaced. For this, a piece of the **body’s own tendon** is taken, for example from the thigh or a part of the kneecap tendon. This is anchored in the knee as a new ligament. After that comes a long period of building up with physiotherapy.

gewusst: The cruciate ligaments get their name because they cross each other in the knee.
Many of those affected hear a bang in the knee when it tears.

teile.einleitung: A collateral circulation is a bypass for the blood. If a blood vessel is narrowed or blocked, blood can keep flowing through side branches and connections. In this way a tissue often stays supplied despite a blockage.
wichtigste: A collateral circulation is a bypass for the blood.
The circle of Willis at the base of the brain makes bypasses possible when vessels are blocked.
In portal hypertension, bypass vessels arise at the gullet, the oesophageal varices.
Widened abdominal skin veins around the navel are called caput medusae.
In coarctation of the aorta, the intercostal arteries form bypasses.
The remodelling of small connecting arteries into collaterals is called arteriogenesis.
A blockage that arises slowly often runs a milder course, because there is time for collaterals.

abschnitte.text: Blood vessels are like a road network. If a main road is closed, cars drive round the closure on side roads. In just the same way, **blood** can keep flowing through **side branches** when a vessel is narrowed or blocked. This bypass is called a **collateral circulation**, and the individual bypass vessels are called **collaterals**. They can protect an organ from severe damage.

abschnitte.titel: The ring of arteries in the brain
abschnitte.text: At the underside of the brain, several large arteries join to form a ring. It is called the **circle of Willis**, named after the English doctor Thomas Willis. If a supplying artery is blocked, blood from the other arteries can step in through this ring. The ring, however, is not fully formed in everyone.

The **portal vein** brings blood from the gut to the liver. If the liver is seriously diseased, blood backs up, and **portal hypertension** arises. The blood looks for detours to the heart. At the gullet, veins widen into **oesophageal varices**, which can bleed dangerously. Around the navel, abdominal skin veins can widen greatly. This picture is called **caput medusae**, after the snake-haired head of Medusa from Greek legend.

In **coarctation of the aorta**, the main artery, the **aorta**, is narrowed at one spot from birth. So that enough blood still reaches the lower half of the body, the **intercostal arteries** form bypasses. They widen greatly over time. On an X-ray you then sometimes see small notches on the ribs, which are made by the widened arteries.

Many collaterals are already present as small **connecting arteries**. If more blood flows through them, they grow and remodel their wall. This process is called **arteriogenesis**. The strongest stimulus is supplied by **increased blood flow** and **shear stress**, that is, the friction of the flowing blood on the vessel wall. That is why a blockage that arises **slowly** often runs a milder course than a sudden one: there is **time for collaterals**. Regular exercise can promote their growth.

gewusst: In some people with narrowed coronary vessels, such good collaterals form that they have hardly any complaints.
In Greek legend, Medusa was a figure with snakes instead of hair.

teile.einleitung: A broken bone arises when a bone breaks under too great a force, for example in a fall. In technical language it is called a fracture. If it is kept still, a broken bone grows together again.
wichtigste: A broken bone is called a fracture in technical language.
Typical signs are strong pain and swelling.
A part of the body that may be broken should not be moved if possible.
If it is kept well still, a bone grows together again.
In children, a simple break usually heals in a few weeks.
In an open fracture, the skin is also injured.
In Switzerland, you reach the ambulance service on the number 144.

abschnitte.text: Bones are very firm, but not unbreakable. In a **fall**, an accident or a hard blow, a bone can break. In technical language this is called a **fracture**. In children, the bones of the **forearm** or the wrist often break, because when falling you support yourself with your hands. Whether a bone is broken is shown by an **X-ray**.

In children, bones are still more flexible and surrounded by a thick periosteum. That is why they sometimes only bend like a fresh twig without breaking right through.
