This is called a **greenstick fracture**. If the skin over the break stays whole, it is a **closed fracture**. If the skin is also injured and a wound has arisen, it is called an **open fracture**. It is more dangerous, because germs can get in.

Often you notice a break from **strong pain** and **swelling**. Sometimes the part of the body is misshapen or can hardly be moved any more. A bruise can also arise. Not every break is clear at once. When in doubt, you always go to the doctor or to hospital.

A part of the body that may be broken should **not be moved if possible**. An injured arm can be held still with a **triangular bandage**, which is tied round the neck like a sling. You calm the injured person and get help. In Switzerland you reach the **ambulance service** on the number **144**. Cooling can ease the pain.

For a bone to grow together well, it has to be **kept still**. For this you get a **cast** or a splint. Sometimes an operation with plates or screws is also needed. In **children**, breaks usually heal faster than in adults, a simple break often in **a few weeks**. After that the bone is firm again at the break.

gewusst: A well-healed bone is often just as strong at the break as before.
The European emergency number 112 also works in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Creatine phosphate is a fast energy store in the muscles. It supplies energy in the first seconds of a maximal effort, for example in a sprint. The store is small, though, and quickly empty.
wichtigste: Creatine phosphate passes its phosphate group to ADP, and this makes ATP.
The enzyme for this is called creatine kinase.
The reaction is called the Lohmann reaction and is reversible.
At maximal effort the store lasts about 6 to 10 seconds.
This way of providing energy is called anaerobic alactacid.
Creatine is made from arginine, glycine and methionine.
The breakdown product is creatinine, a measure of kidney function.

abschnitte.text: Muscles need **ATP**, the energy currency of the cells, for every movement. Only very little of it is in stock, though. Here **creatine phosphate** helps: it passes its phosphate group to **ADP**, and so new ATP arises. The enzyme **creatine kinase** speeds up this reaction. It is called the **Lohmann reaction**, after the biochemist Karl Lohmann, and is reversible.

Creatine phosphate supplies energy in fractions of a second, but the store is small. At maximal effort it lasts only about **6 to 10 seconds**. After that **glycolysis**, the breakdown of sugar, increasingly takes over. That is why creatine phosphate is especially important in the **100 m sprint**, in jumps and throws. For long distances it is nowhere near enough.

In sports physiology, this way of providing energy is called **anaerobic alactacid**. **Anaerobic** means that no oxygen is used up. **Alactacid** means that no **lactate** arises. In the pauses, the store is filled up again with energy from other pathways.

The body makes **creatine** in the kidney and liver from the amino acids **arginine** and **glycine**. **Methionine** supplies a methyl group. Via the blood, creatine gets into the muscles. Creatine and creatine phosphate are constantly converted in small amounts into **creatinine**. The kidney excretes this, and its blood value serves as a measure of kidney function.

**Creatine kinase** sits in the muscle cells. If muscle cells are damaged, it gets into the blood. A strongly raised value therefore usually points to **damage to muscle tissue**. This happens, for example, after a heart attack, after injuries or after very hard physical exertion.

gewusst: Without creatine phosphate, a muscle’s ATP supply would be used up after just a few seconds.
Creatine kinase is an important laboratory value for detecting muscle damage.

teile.einleitung: The scalp is the skin under our head hair. The hair roots sit in it, and it has a very good blood supply. Sometimes dandruff or head lice cause it trouble.
wichtigste: The hair roots sit in the scalp.
The scalp has an especially good blood supply, so small wounds bleed heavily.
A yeast fungus on the scalp can promote dandruff.
Shampoos with an antifungal ingredient often help against dandruff.
Head lice are usually passed on by direct contact from head to head.
Babies often have a harmless crust, cradle cap.

abschnitte.titel: Skin with a good blood supply
abschnitte.text: The scalp is supplied by many **blood vessels**. These feed the **hair roots** so that the hair can grow. That is why even a small **cut** on the head often bleeds very heavily. This looks bad, but is usually less dangerous than it seems. The **hairline** is the line at the forehead where the head hair begins.

On the scalp lives a **yeast fungus** that feeds on **sebum**, the skin’s natural oil. If it multiplies strongly, it irritates the skin, and more greasy **dandruff** forms. Special dandruff shampoos contain ingredients that inhibit the fungus. This calms the skin and it forms less dandruff.

**Head lice** are tiny insects that live in the hair. They can neither jump nor fly. They crawl on to another head mainly when hair touches directly. Several times a day they sting into the scalp and suck blood. Their saliva causes the typical **itching**.
Many babies have a yellowish, scaly crust on the head in the first months of life. It is called **cradle cap**. It is harmless and usually goes away by itself after a few months.

abschnitte.titel: Hair colour and amount of hair
abschnitte.text: How many hairs grow on the scalp also depends on hair colour. **Blonde** people usually have the most hairs, often about 150,000. Their hairs, however, are especially thin. **Redheads** have thicker hairs, but fewer of them.

gewusst: Blonde people usually have more head hair than redheads.
A small wound on the head often bleeds more than one of the same size on the arm.

teile.einleitung: In a cross-allergy, the immune system reacts not only to one substance but also to others that contain similar proteins. So a pollen allergy can, for example, cause trouble when eating fruit or nuts.
wichtigste: A cross-allergy arises from similar proteins in different substances.
Many people with a birch pollen allergy react to raw apples and hazelnuts.
Typical is a tingling and itching in the mouth.
Cooked apple purée is often tolerated, because heat destroys the protein.
People with a latex allergy often react to bananas, avocado or kiwi.
Mugwort pollen and celery can cross-react.
House dust mites and crustaceans share the protein tropomyosin.

abschnitte.text: In an **allergy**, the immune system reacts to a substance that is actually harmless, the **allergen**. In a **cross-allergy**, it also reacts to another substance. The reason: its **proteins** look very similar to the original allergen. The immune system, so to speak, mixes them up.

A protein in the **apple** closely resembles the main allergen of **birch pollen**. Many people with a birch pollen allergy therefore feel a tingling in the mouth when eating raw apples. **Hazel** and birch are closely related, so many also react to **hazelnuts**. This apple protein is **sensitive to heat**, though. In cooking or baking it changes its shape, which is why cooked **apple purée** is often tolerated.

In the so-called **oral allergy syndrome**, there is itching or tingling on the lips, tongue and palate shortly after eating. Sometimes the lining of the mouth swells slightly. Mostly the complaints pass quickly. With strong reactions, such as difficulty breathing, medical help is needed at once.

In the **latex-fruit syndrome**, people with an allergy to latex, for example from rubber gloves, also react to certain fruits. These include **banana**, **avocado** and **kiwi**. Here too, similar proteins are the reason.

**Mugwort** and **celery** have similar proteins. This is called the **celery-mugwort-spice syndrome**, because spices can also be affected. **House dust mites** and **crustaceans** such as prawns are related too: both are arthropods and have a similar muscle protein called **tropomyosin**. So cross-reactions are possible here as well.

gewusst: Some people cannot tolerate a raw apple, but have no trouble with an apple cake.
House dust mites and prawns are both arthropods.

teile.einleitung: Herbal tea is made from dried leaves or flowers of plants. Many herbal teas are old home remedies for tummy ache, sore throat or colds. They taste good and warm you up.
wichtigste: Herbal tea is made from dried parts of plants and hot water.
Camomile tea is often drunk for tummy ache.
Sage tea helps many people with a sore throat.
Peppermint tea tastes fresh and cooling.
Fennel tea is often given to children for wind.
You leave herbal tea to steep for about 5 to 10 minutes.
Freshly made tea can be very hot.

abschnitte.text: For **herbal tea** you take dried **leaves** or **flowers** of plants. You pour hot water over them. Then you leave the tea to **steep for about 5 to 10 minutes**. In this time the herbs give their flavour and active substances to the water. Many herbs also grow in Switzerland, in the garden or in meadows.

abschnitte.titel: Camomile and fennel for the tummy
abschnitte.text: **Camomile tea** is one of the best-known home remedies and is often drunk for tummy ache. It is made from the dried **flowers** of camomile. They are white and have a little yellow head in the middle. **Fennel tea** also calms the tummy and helps against wind. Because it is mild, even small children often get it.

**Sage** has long been used for a **sore throat**. You drink it as a tea or gargle with it. **Peppermint tea** tastes fresh and cooling. This is due to **menthol**, a substance in peppermint. It feels cool in the mouth even when the tea is warm.

**Lime blossom tea** is an old home remedy for **colds** and fever. You drink it warm. The blossoms are gathered in early summer from lime trees. With a cold, warm tea does you good, because the body then needs a lot of fluid.

Tea is made with **boiling water**. Freshly made tea can therefore be **very hot** and scald the mouth. You let it cool down a little before you drink. Herbal tea is no substitute for a visit to the doctor: anyone who is ill for a long time should be examined.

gewusst: Peppermint tea feels cool although it is warm, and menthol is what does this.
Many tea herbs such as peppermint or sage you can grow yourself in the garden or on the balcony.

teile.einleitung: Anyone can hold their breath for a while, for example when diving. But at some point the body forces us to breathe again. Some animals manage it for much longer than we do.
wichtigste: After a while you have to breathe again, because the body needs oxygen.
We often hold our breath when diving.
Diving using only a held breath is called freediving.
With a snorkel you breathe just below the surface of the water.
Scuba divers get air from a cylinder.
The sperm whale can hold its breath for a very long time, and its blowhole is on top of its head.

abschnitte.titel: Why we have to breathe again
abschnitte.text: Our body constantly needs **oxygen** so that the cells can work. At the same time **carbon dioxide** is produced, which we breathe out. If we hold our breath, carbon dioxide builds up in the blood. The brain notices this and triggers an ever stronger **urge to breathe**. That is why after a while you have to breathe again. Afterwards you usually **take a deep breath**.

When **diving** we often hold our breath. With a **snorkel** you can swim just below the surface of the water and still breathe. Diving using only a held breath, without a cylinder, is called **freediving**. **Scuba divers** carry a **cylinder** of breathing air on their backs and can stay under water for a long time with it.

Whales are mammals and breathe air like us. Their **blowhole** is **on top of the head**. This lets them breathe at the surface without lifting their head far out of the water. The **sperm whale** dives very deep and can hold its breath for over an hour. Seals and manatees also stay under water for a long time.

Holding your breath under water can become dangerous if you overdo it. Anyone who dives for too long can pass out without noticing it beforehand. So the rule is: **never dive alone** and never hold breath-holding competitions. In swimming pools and lakes in Switzerland, lifeguards keep watch over safety.

gewusst: Whales do not breathe automatically like us, but decide consciously when to breathe.
Practised freedivers can hold their breath for several minutes.

teile.einleitung: An ambulance takes sick and injured people quickly to hospital. In Switzerland it is often called an Ambulanz or Sanität. In an emergency it drives with blue lights and siren.
wichtigste: In Switzerland, the ambulance is often called Ambulanz or Sanität.
On emergency journeys it switches on blue lights and siren.
In the ambulance work paramedics.
Patients lie on a stretcher.
With blue lights and siren it may drive carefully even through a red light.
Anyone who hears a siren makes way.

abschnitte.text: The **ambulance** is often called **Ambulanz** or **Sanität** in Switzerland. It takes sick and injured people mostly to **hospital**. There they are treated further by doctors. In an emergency, in Switzerland you dial the number **144** to call an ambulance.

In the ambulance work **paramedics**. They look after the injured already at the scene of the accident and during the journey. The patient lies on a **stretcher**, which is fastened in the vehicle. On board there are many devices, for example for oxygen or for monitoring the heart.

On an emergency journey, the ambulance switches on **blue lights** and **siren**. They warn the other road users so that they make way. With blue lights and siren, a rescue vehicle may ignore some traffic rules, for example drive across a crossing at red. It must drive **carefully** while doing so, though.

If you hear a siren as a cyclist, you stop **at the side**. Cars also move aside and form a lane. Rescue vehicles need a clear way, because in an emergency every minute counts. Only when the ambulance has passed do you carry on.

On some ambulances, the word **AMBULANCE** is written on the front in mirror image. There is a clever reason for this: anyone driving in front sees the ambulance in the **rear-view mirror**. There everything appears reversed, and so you can read the word the right way round.

gewusst: You read the mirror writing “AMBULANCE” the right way round in the rear-view mirror.
The emergency number for the ambulance service in Switzerland is 144.

teile.einleitung: Someone who concentrates keeps their attention entirely on one thing. You need this when learning, reading or playing. With a few simple tricks, concentrating becomes much easier.
wichtigste: Concentration means staying attentive to one thing.
Noise, for example a loud television, disturbs concentration.
The mobile phone often distracts when learning.
Enough water and a healthy Znüni, a morning snack, help the head.
Short breaks for movement wake you up again.
Someone who does two tasks at the same time usually makes more mistakes.

abschnitte.text: To **concentrate** means to direct your attention entirely to one task. You block out other things around you in the process. The brain cannot do this for an unlimited time. After a while you get tired and are more easily distracted. That is why breaks are just as important as working.

**Noise** disturbs, because the brain always listens a little. A loud television or loud conversations make it hard to stay with the homework. The **mobile phone** also pulls attention away, because messages and games constantly tempt you. That is why it is better to put it in another room when learning. A quiet, tidy place helps a lot.

The brain needs enough **fluid**, and water is the best drink for it. The right **Znüni**, the morning snack, helps too: an apple and a piece of bread give energy for a long time. Sweets with a lot of sugar, on the other hand, give strength only briefly. Afterwards you often quickly feel limp again.

After sitting for a long time, a short **movement break** helps. Standing up, stretching or a few jumping jacks get the circulation going. Calm, **deep breathing** also calms the body. Afterwards you can settle into the task better.

Many people think they can do two things at once well. The brain, however, is poor at concentrating on two tasks at the same time. Someone who watches music, chats and calculates all at once usually makes **more mistakes**. It is better to finish one task and then start the next.

gewusst: Even a few minutes of exercise can help you be more attentive again afterwards.
The brain listens to sounds even when you do not want to listen at all.

teile.einleitung: Collagen is a protein found in bones, skin, tendons and cartilage. It is the most common protein in the human body. Collagen makes our tissue resistant to tearing and gives bones their elasticity.
wichtigste: Collagen is one of the proteins.
It is the most common protein in the human body.
In bone, it provides elasticity and tensile strength.
Tendons also consist mainly of collagen.
To build collagen, the body needs vitamin C.
Gelatine is made from collagen.
A bone in vinegar becomes flexible like rubber.

abschnitte.text: **Collagen** is one of the **proteins**. It is the **most common protein** in the human body. Collagen forms long, firm **fibres**. These are built like a rope of three strands twisted together. That is why they are very **resistant to tearing**. Collagen is found in the skin, in the bones, in cartilage, in ligaments and above all in **tendons**.

A bone consists of two main parts. The **minerals**, mainly calcium, make it hard. The **collagen** forms a framework and gives it **elasticity and tensile strength**. Only the mixture makes the bone so strong. It is hard and yet can give a little without breaking at once.

If you put a **chicken bone** in **vinegar** for a few days, the acid dissolves the minerals out. What is left is the collagen, and the bone becomes **flexible like rubber**. You can even tie it in a knot. If a bone is strongly **heated** and burned in the fire, on the other hand, the collagen burns away. Only the minerals remain, and the bone becomes **brittle** and crumbles easily.

To build collagen properly, the body needs **vitamin C**. If it is missing for a long time, the collagen fibres become weak. In the past, sailors on long voyages without fresh fruit suffered from **scurvy**. In it, the gums bled and wounds healed badly. Today scurvy is very rare, because vitamin C is found in many fruits and vegetables.

If you boil collagen from animal skin and bones for a long time, **gelatine** arises. It dissolves in warm water and sets when it cools. That is why it is used for **gummy bears**, jelly desserts and some desserts. Gelatine usually comes from pigs or cattle. Anyone who does not want to eat animal products uses substitutes from plants or algae, for example agar-agar.

gewusst: About a quarter to a third of all protein in the body is collagen.
The word “collagen” means “glue producing”, because in the past glue was boiled from bones and skin.

teile.einleitung: Insulin is a hormone, that is, a messenger substance that our body makes itself. It makes sure that sugar from food gets from the blood into the body’s cells. Without insulin, the cells would have no energy, and blood sugar would rise dangerously high.
wichtigste: Insulin is a hormone that lowers the blood sugar level.
It stimulates cells to take up glucose, that is, grape sugar, from the blood.
Insulin is made in the pancreas, more exactly in the islets of Langerhans.
Its opponent is the hormone glucagon, which raises blood sugar.
In the sugar disease diabetes, insulin is missing or does not work properly.
People with type 1 diabetes have to inject insulin for their whole life.
Insulin was discovered in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best.

abschnitte.text: Insulin is a **hormone**, that is, a chemical messenger substance that travels through the body with the blood. Chemically it is a small protein made of 51 building blocks, the amino acids. The name comes from the Latin word “insula” for island. It recalls the islets of Langerhans, the clusters of cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

When we eat bread, pasta or sweet things, **glucose** is made from them in the gut and gets into the blood. The pancreas notices that blood sugar is rising and releases insulin. Insulin works like a key that opens the cells to sugar. Muscles use the sugar as energy, the liver stores it as glycogen, and the blood sugar level falls again.

Blood sugar always has to stay in a certain range. If it is too high, insulin lowers it. If it is too low, for example after sport or long fasting, the pancreas releases **glucagon**. Glucagon brings sugar from the liver’s stores back into the blood, so the two hormones work as opponents.

In **diabetes mellitus**, the sugar disease, this balance is disturbed. In type 1 diabetes, the body’s own immune system destroys the insulin-making cells, often already in childhood. In the much more common type 2 diabetes, insulin no longer works properly, which is often linked to being overweight and little exercise. Untreated, permanently high blood sugar can damage the eyes, kidneys, nerves and blood vessels.

People with type 1 diabetes inject insulin with an **insulin pen** or receive it through a small insulin pump. They measure their blood sugar regularly, today often with a sensor on the skin and a mobile phone. Insulin cannot be swallowed, because like other protein it would be digested in the stomach. Today insulin is usually made by genetic engineering using bacteria or yeast.

In 1921, Frederick Banting and Charles Best in Toronto in Canada managed to obtain insulin from pancreases. In 1922, a seriously ill 14-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson was the first person to receive insulin, and he survived. Before that, type 1 diabetes was a certain death sentence. For this, Banting received the **Nobel Prize** in Medicine in 1923 together with John Macleod.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger substance of the body that sends messages to organs through the blood.
Grape sugar, the most important supplier of energy for our cells.
An organ behind the stomach that makes digestive juice and hormones such as insulin.
A disease in which blood sugar is too high because insulin is missing or works badly.

gewusst: Before insulin was made by genetic engineering, it was obtained from the pancreases of cattle and pigs.
14 November is World Diabetes Day, because Frederick Banting was born on that day.
In 1982, insulin was the first medicine made by genetic engineering to be approved.

teile.einleitung: On a person’s head, a great many hairs grow. They protect the head and keep growing back all through life. Here you find out how head hair grows and why cutting it does not hurt.
wichtigste: A person has about 100,000 to 150,000 hairs on the head.
A head hair grows about one centimetre in a month.
Every day you lose about 60 to 100 hairs, which is normal.
Each hair sits with its root in the scalp.
The visible part of the hair has no nerves.
The hair protects from sun and cold.

abschnitte.text: On a person’s head, about **100,000 to 150,000 hairs** grow. That is so many that you cannot count them. Exactly how many there are also depends on hair colour. The hairs lie like a blanket on the head. They keep off **sunrays** and keep the head **warm**.

The skin under the hair is called the **scalp**. In it, each hair sits with its **hair root**. There the hair gradually grows out. The part we see consists of dead, firm material and has **no nerves**. That is why it does not hurt when you cut hair. If you pull on a hair, though, you feel it at the root.

Head hair grows a little bit every day. In a month, about **one centimetre** adds up. That is much slower than grass in summer, which can grow several centimetres in a week. A hair grows for some years, then falls out. Every day you lose about **60 to 100 hairs** in this way, and new ones grow in their place.

The **parting** is the line where the hair divides to the left and right. You can comb it in the middle or at the side. In many men, hair falls out on top of the head with age. This is called **baldness**. It is quite normal and has nothing to do with a lack of care.

gewusst: Because hair has no nerves, you feel nothing of the cutting at the hairdresser’s.
Dozens of hairs fall out every day without your noticing.

teile.einleitung: Our body consists to a large extent of water. It is in every cell, in the blood and even in the bones. That is why we have to drink enough every day.
wichtigste: The body of an adult consists of about 60 per cent water.
Babies have proportionally even more water in the body than adults.
The brain consists of about three quarters water.
We lose water through sweat, urine and even when breathing out.
Many foods also contain water, for example cucumber.
In Switzerland, tap water is a good and cheap way to quench thirst.

abschnitte.text: About **60 per cent** of an adult’s body is **water**. In a **baby** the share is even higher. With age it slowly falls. Especially much water is in the **brain**: about **three quarters**. Water carries nutrients, helps with digestion and cools the body when we sweat.

Every day the body loses water. Some goes away with the **urine**, some with the **sweat**. We also lose water when **breathing out**, as **water vapour**. You can see this in winter, when the breath becomes visible as a little cloud in the cold air. During sport and in heat we sweat especially much and need to drink more.

It is not only drinks that supply water. Many **foods** also contain a lot of it. The **cucumber** consists almost entirely of water, and so do watermelons, tomatoes and lettuce. Soup, yoghurt and fruit also bring water into the body. Even so, it is important to drink regularly through the day, ideally before you are very thirsty.

In Switzerland, very clean **tap water** comes from the pipes. It is a good and **cheap way to quench thirst**, entirely without sugar. You can do sums well with glasses: if you drink 6 glasses of 2 decilitres each, that makes **1.2 litres** together. If a child loses 1 litre of sweat during sport, it has to drink **5 glasses** of 2 decilitres to replace it.

gewusst: A large part of Swiss drinking water comes from springs and groundwater.
Even a slight lack of water can make you tired and worsen your concentration.

teile.einleitung: In pulmonary fibrosis the lung tissue gradually becomes scarred. The lungs become stiffer and can pass less oxygen into the blood. There are many causes, and in some forms the cause remains unknown.
wichtigste: In pulmonary fibrosis, more connective tissue forms in the lungs.
The diffusion capacity is lowered because the exchange membrane is thickened.
A fine crackling sound when listening to the chest is typical.
Asbestos fibres cause asbestosis, and quartz dust causes silicosis.
On a high-resolution CT scan, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis often shows a honeycomb pattern.
Pirfenidone and nintedanib are the classic antifibrotic drugs.

abschnitte.text: In the walls of the alveoli, more **connective tissue** forms, rather like a scar. The lungs become **stiffer** and do not stretch as well. In addition, the fine **exchange membrane** between the air and the blood becomes thicker. That is why the **diffusion capacity** is lowered: oxygen gets into the blood less well. People affected have shortness of breath, especially when exerting themselves, and often a dry cough.

Some fibroses are caused by substances that are breathed in. Fine **asbestos fibres** cause **asbestosis**. In the past, a lot of asbestos was also used in building in Switzerland, and it has been banned since 1990. **Quartz dust** leads to **silicosis**, a typical occupational disease of miners, for example in tunnel building. Some medicines can also cause fibrosis, and the cancer drug **bleomycin** is known for this. If no cause can be found, it is called **idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis**.

When listening with a stethoscope you often hear a **fine crackling sound** that is reminiscent of opening a Velcro fastening. Lung function tests show how badly breathing is restricted. The **high-resolution CT scan** is important. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis it often shows a **honeycomb pattern**: small hollow spaces with thickened walls that resemble honeycombs.

So far, pulmonary fibrosis usually cannot be cured. The drugs **pirfenidone** and **nintedanib** have been used as **antifibrotic drugs** for over ten years. They can slow down its progress. Breathing exercises, giving up smoking and, if needed, extra oxygen are also important. In severe cases a lung transplant may be considered.

gewusst: In medicine, “idiopathic” means that the cause is unknown.
Because asbestos diseases often appear only decades later, people who worked with asbestos a long time ago still fall ill today.

teile.einleitung: Blinking is the quick closing and opening of the eyelids. It usually happens quite automatically, without us thinking about it. It keeps the eyes moist and clean, and protects them from dangers.
wichtigste: When you blink, the eyelids close and open in a flash.
It makes sure that the eyes stay moist and clean.
A person blinks about 10 to 20 times a minute.
A blink lasts only about a tenth to a third of a second.
The blink reflex protects the eye when something comes near quickly.
When reading and looking at a screen we blink less often.
You can control blinking on purpose, but most of the time it happens without our noticing.

abschnitte.text: In a **blink**, the upper eyelid slides briefly down over the eye and back up again. This happens so fast that we do not even notice the short darkness. Our brain simply blocks it out. A blink lasts about a tenth to a third of a second.

With every blink, the eyelid spreads the **tear film** evenly over the cornea. This thin layer of liquid keeps the eye moist, supplies the cornea with oxygen and washes away dust. The tear liquid comes from the **tear gland** above the eye. It drains away into the nose through tiny channels, which is why your nose runs when you cry.

If something suddenly comes close to the eye, such as a ball or an insect, the eyelids close in a flash. This is called the **blink reflex**. It is also set off when you touch the eyelashes, in very bright light or at a loud bang. This is how the body protects the delicate eyes without our having to think.

An adult blinks on average about 10 to 20 times a minute, which is many thousands of times a day. Newborn babies, on the other hand, blink only very rarely. When reading with concentration, gaming or looking at a **screen**, we blink much less often. Then the eyes can dry out, sting and turn red.

If you sit at a computer or phone for a long time, you should take regular breaks and blink on purpose. A well-known rule says: every 20 minutes, look into the distance for 20 seconds. Drinking enough and getting fresh air also help against **dry eyes**. In the dry air from heating in winter, the eyes are under particular strain.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fold of skin that covers and protects the eye.
A thin layer of liquid that keeps the eye moist.
A quick, automatic reaction of the body without thinking.
The transparent front layer of the eye.

gewusst: Added up, you spend several minutes of every waking day with your eyes closed because of blinking.
Newborn babies blink only a few times a minute, much less often than adults.

teile.einleitung: A toddler is a child of about one to three years old. In this time it learns to walk, talk and much more. Because toddlers do not yet know many dangers, they need good supervision.
wichtigste: A toddler is about 1 to 3 years old.
The order is: baby, toddler, schoolchild.
At about one year, many children take their first steps.
One of the first words is often “Mama”.
At about three years, all the milk teeth are there.
At about three years, most children no longer need a nappy during the day.
In a day nursery, toddlers are looked after while the parents work.

abschnitte.text: In the first year of life, a child is called a **baby** or infant. After that, from about the first to the third birthday, it is a **toddler**. Then comes kindergarten age and later the **schoolchild**. In the toddler years, a child grows fast and learns something new every day. Each child develops at its own pace, however.

Many babies first **crawl** on hands and knees. They pull themselves up on furniture and take their first free **steps** at about **one year**. Soon they walk more steadily, climb on chairs and run around. The hands also become more skilful: toddlers learn to eat with a spoon, build towers and scribble.

At about one year, many children say their first words. Often **“Mama”** or “Papa” is among them, because these syllables are easy to pronounce. At two years, many children already know a few dozen words and form short **sentences** such as “want ball”. Toddlers usually understand much more than they can say themselves.

The first **milk teeth** usually come in the first year of life. At about **three years**, all 20 milk teeth are in the mouth. From the first tooth you should brush them daily. Also at about three years, most children no longer need a **nappy** during the day, because they have learned to use the potty or the toilet.

Toddlers are curious, but do not yet know many **dangers**. They put things in their mouths, climb up and run into the road. That is why you have to watch them especially carefully. Sockets, stairs and cleaning products are made safe. When the parents work, toddlers are often looked after in a **Kita**, a day nursery, or by grandparents and day families.

gewusst: A toddler can grow about ten centimetres in a year.
Toddlers fall over very often when learning to walk, but usually hardly hurt themselves.

teile.einleitung: The incubation period is the time between catching an infection and the first signs of illness. Depending on the disease, it lasts only hours or many weeks. Anyone who knows it understands better how diseases spread.
wichtigste: The incubation period is the time from infection to the first symptoms.
During this time, the germs multiply in the body.
With true flu, it usually lasts about one to two days.
With chickenpox, it lasts about two weeks.
With measles, about 10 days pass before the first signs of illness.
Rabies often has a particularly long incubation period.
The length of a quarantine often depends on the longest usual incubation period.

abschnitte.text: The **incubation period** begins when a disease-causing germ gets into the body. It ends when the first **symptoms** appear, that is, the first signs of illness such as fever or cough. The word comes from the Latin “incubare”, which means roughly “to lie on” or “to hatch”. During this time you usually still feel healthy.

During the incubation period, the **germs multiply** in the body. Viruses get into cells and have themselves copied there, and bacteria divide. Only when enough germs are present and the immune system reacts strongly do you notice anything. Many signs of illness, such as fever, are a result of this defence.

The incubation period is very different depending on the disease. In **food poisoning from bacterial toxins**, the complaints often begin only **a few hours** after eating. With **true flu**, it usually takes **one to two days**. With **measles**, about **10 days** pass before the first signs of illness, and with **chickenpox** about **two weeks**. It can be especially long with **rabies**, often several weeks to months.

With some diseases, you are already **infectious before you feel ill**. In this way germs can be passed on unnoticed. That is why diseases such as flu or chickenpox often spread so fast, for example in schools or families. Good hygiene such as washing hands therefore always helps, not only when someone is already ill.

Someone who has been in contact with an infectious disease sometimes has to go into **quarantine**. This means you stay at home for a time and do not meet other people. How long this lasts often depends on the **longest usual incubation period** of the disease. If this time is over and you have stayed healthy, you probably did not catch it.

gewusst: The word quarantine comes from the Italian word for forty, because in the past ships had to wait 40 days before people were allowed ashore.
With some diseases, the incubation period can vary greatly from person to person.

teile.einleitung: Dandruff consists of small bits of skin that come away from the scalp. It is a nuisance, but mostly harmless and not infectious. With the right care, it often becomes less.
wichtigste: Dandruff is skin cells that have come away from the scalp.
It is usually white or slightly yellowish.
On dark clothes you see it especially well.
Dandruff is not infectious.
Special shampoos can help.
Scratching tends to make dandruff worse.

abschnitte.text: Our skin **renews itself** all the time without our noticing. In the lower skin, new cells constantly arise. On top, old cells come away as tiny flakes. Normally they are so small that you cannot see them. If larger pieces come away on the scalp, they are called **dandruff**.

Dandruff is usually small **white** or slightly yellowish flakes. They look a little like crumbs. You see them especially well on **dark clothes**, for example on a black jumper. On light fabrics they hardly show.

Dandruff can easily be mistaken for **nits**, the eggs of head lice. There is a simple difference, though: dandruff lies loose on the hair and can be **shaken off easily**. Nits, on the other hand, stick firmly to the hair. Dandruff is also **not infectious**, because it comes from your own scalp.

Against dandruff there are **special shampoos** that calm the scalp. It is important not to **scratch** your head hard. Scratching irritates the scalp further, and then it itches and flakes even more. If the dandruff does not get better despite care, a doctor or a pharmacist can help.

gewusst: The skin loses countless tiny flakes of skin every day.
You can tell dandruff from nits by trying to shake them off.

teile.einleitung: The complement system is a group of proteins in the blood that fight disease-causing germs. It belongs mainly to the innate defence. Its proteins activate each other in a chain and can mark bacteria or even destroy them.
wichtigste: The complement system belongs mainly to the innate defence.
It is so called because it complements the action of antibodies.
The classical pathway is triggered by antigen-antibody complexes.
All three pathways of activation come together at factor C3.
In opsonisation, C3b marks germs for the phagocytes.
At the end of the cascade, the membrane attack complex forms pores in the cell wall of germs.
A congenital lack of C1 esterase inhibitor causes hereditary angioedema.

abschnitte.titel: A defence system in the blood
abschnitte.text: In the blood float many different **proteins** that together form the **complement system**. Most are made in the liver. They belong mainly to the **innate defence**, which acts at once against intruders. At the end of the 19th century, the Belgian researcher **Jules Bordet** discovered this defensive power in the blood. The name was coined by **Paul Ehrlich**: complement means “addition”, because the system **complements the action of antibodies**.

The complement factors are at first inactive in the blood. When one factor is activated, it splits and activates the next. This creates a **cascade**, a chain of reactions that quickly amplifies itself. There are **three pathways of activation**. The **classical pathway** is triggered by **antigen-antibody complexes**. The **lectin pathway** recognises certain sugars on bacteria, and the **alternative pathway** starts directly on the surfaces of germs.

All three pathways come together at factor **C3**. C3 is split into two parts. The bigger piece, **C3b**, attaches to the surface of germs. This marking is called **opsonisation**. Phagocytes recognise the marked germs and take them up more easily. Small split products such as **C3a** and **C5a** are called **anaphylatoxins**. They promote inflammation and attract defence cells.

At the end of the cascade, several factors join together. They form the **membrane attack complex**. It bores into the outer coat of a bacterium and forms a **pore**, a small hole. Fluid streams in through this hole, and the cell perishes. The body’s own cells protect themselves from this attack with special proteins.

So that the complement system does not get out of control, there are **regulator proteins** that slow it. One of them is the **C1 esterase inhibitor**. If it is missing from birth or does not work, **hereditary angioedema** arises. “Hereditary” means inherited. Those affected keep having sudden, strong swellings of the skin or mucous membranes. Effective medicines for them now exist.

gewusst: Jules Bordet received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1919 for his research on immunity.
The complement system consists of more than 30 different proteins.

teile.einleitung: An insulin pump is a small device for people with diabetes. It delivers insulin into the body round the clock and so replaces many injections. Modern pumps even work together with a sugar sensor.
wichtigste: The even release of insulin over the day is called the basal rate.
The extra amount for a meal is called a bolus.
The pump holds fast-acting insulin.
The insulin reaches the fatty tissue under the skin.
If the pump fails, ketoacidosis soon threatens.
In automated insulin delivery, the sensor and the pump control the amount together.
CSII stands for continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion.

abschnitte.text: **Insulin** is a hormone from the pancreas. It makes sure that sugar gets from the blood into the body’s cells and supplies energy there. In **type 1 diabetes**, the body no longer makes insulin of its own. Those affected therefore have to supply it from outside, either with injections or pens or with an **insulin pump**. Pump therapy is called **CSII** in technical language, which stands for **continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion**.

The pump is about as big as a small mobile phone and is worn on the body. Through a thin tube and a fine cannula, it delivers **insulin into the fatty tissue under the skin**, that is, the layer of fat directly beneath the skin. There are also **patch pumps** that stick directly on the skin **without a tube**. The pump holds **fast-acting insulin**, which is constantly released in small amounts.

The pump releases small amounts of insulin evenly round the clock. This is called the **basal rate**. It covers the body’s basic need. For a meal, a larger amount is released in addition, the **bolus**. How big the bolus has to be depends on how many carbohydrates the food contains.

Many people with diabetes wear a **glucose sensor** that continuously measures the sugar in the tissue. In modern systems, the sensor and the pump work together. A program calculates how much insulin is needed at the moment and adjusts the delivery **automatically**. Such systems are called **automated insulin delivery** or **closed loop**.

Someone who wears a pump has no store of long-acting insulin in the body. If the supply of insulin is interrupted, for example because the tube is kinked, the insulin is missing after only a few hours. Then **ketoacidosis** soon threatens, a dangerous over-acidification of the blood. That is why those affected check their sugar level regularly and always have a replacement with them, such as an insulin pen.

gewusst: With an insulin pump you can often do sport too, as the basal rate can be lowered for a time.
The pump’s cannula is usually placed in a new spot every few days.

teile.einleitung: Iodine is a chemical element that our body absolutely needs. Without enough iodine, the thyroid gland cannot make its hormones properly. In the past, iodine deficiency was widespread in the Alps.
wichtigste: In German chemistry the element is now officially called Iod, and its symbol is I.
Heated iodine forms a violet vapour.
The thyroid gland needs iodine for the hormone thyroxine, which contains four iodine atoms.
In the Alps, soils and water contain little iodine, so deficiency used to be common.
Iodine deficiency can lead to an underactive thyroid: tiredness, feeling cold, lack of drive.
Switzerland distributes iodine tablets to households near nuclear power stations.

abschnitte.text: Iodine is a chemical **element** with the symbol **I**. In German chemistry it is now officially written **Iod**, but in everyday German “Jod” is still usual. At room temperature it forms dark, shiny crystals. If you heat them, a beautiful **violet vapour** arises. The name comes from the Greek word for violet-coloured. In nature, iodine is found mainly in sea water and in seaweed.

abschnitte.titel: What the body needs iodine for
abschnitte.text: The **thyroid gland** sits at the front of the neck and has the shape of a butterfly. It makes hormones that control the **metabolism**, that is, how fast the body converts energy. The most important thyroid hormone is called **thyroxine** and contains four iodine atoms. If iodine is missing, the thyroid gland can make too few hormones. This is then called an **underactive thyroid**. Typical are tiredness, feeling cold and lack of drive.

In the Alps, **soils and water** contain little iodine. That is why iodine deficiency used to be common there. Many people had a **goitre**, an enlarged thyroid gland. In some children, severe iodine deficiency led to **disturbances of physical and mental development**. Since the 1920s, Switzerland has had iodised table salt. Since then, severe iodine deficiency has become rare here.

In a serious accident at a **nuclear power station**, **radioactive iodine** can get into the air. The thyroid gland would take it up and store it. If you take **iodine tablets** in time, the thyroid gland is already filled with normal iodine and hardly takes up the dangerous kind any more. That is why Switzerland distributes such tablets as a precaution to households near nuclear power stations. You should take them only when the authorities tell you to.

gewusst: Iodine was discovered in France in 1811, in the ash of seaweed.
Tincture of iodine, a brown solution of iodine in alcohol, was often used in the past to disinfect wounds.

teile.einleitung: Cooling is a simple first aid for many small injuries. Cold eases pain and makes sure that an injured spot swells less.
wichtigste: After a sprained foot, cooling and raising it help.
You never put ice directly on the skin, or it can get frostbite.
You wrap an ice pack in a cloth.
Without an ice pack, a wet, cold cloth helps.
Through cooling, a bruise swells less.
A small burn is cooled with running, cool water.

abschnitte.text: In a **bruise** or a **bump**, small blood vessels are injured. Fluid seeps into the tissue, and the spot **swells**. Cold makes the blood vessels narrower. That is why the spot swells less and hurts less. Cooling also helps with a bump on the head, for example after a collision while playing.

Someone who twists their foot should take a **break** at once. Then the foot is **cooled** and **raised**, that is, put higher than the heart. This way less blood flows into the injured spot. If the foot hurts badly or you can no longer put weight on it, you go to a doctor.

A **cold pack** from the freezer is quickly to hand. But you **never** put it directly on the skin, or the skin can get **frostbite**. That is why you wrap the ice pack in a **cloth**. If there is no ice pack, a **wet, cold cloth** also helps. You only cool for a few minutes at a time and then take a pause.

If you have slightly burnt yourself on a hot pan, you hold the spot under **running, cool water**. The water should not be ice cold, but pleasantly cool. With large burns, with blisters on the face or in small children, you call for help, for example the ambulance service on the number **144**.

gewusst: Many cold packs stay soft even in the freezer, because they contain a special liquid.
A bag of frozen peas is a popular replacement for a cold pack, because it moulds well to the body.

teile.einleitung: Cartilage is a firm but flexible tissue in our body. It shapes the ears and the tip of the nose and covers the joint surfaces. Because it has no blood vessels, damage to cartilage heals only very slowly.
wichtigste: Cartilage is firm and flexible at the same time.
A distinction is made between hyaline, elastic and fibrous cartilage.
Elastic cartilage gives the outer ear its shape.
The outer ring of the intervertebral discs consists of fibrous cartilage.
Smooth cartilage on the joint surfaces reduces friction.
Cartilage has no blood vessels, which is why it heals very slowly.
Sharks and rays have a skeleton that is made almost entirely of cartilage.

abschnitte.text: Cartilage is harder than skin or muscles, but softer than bone. You can feel it yourself: your **outer ear** and the **tip of your nose** can be bent and spring back. Both are supported mainly by cartilage. Cartilage consists of few cells that are embedded in a firm, rubbery **ground substance**. In it lie many fine fibres.

Three kinds are distinguished. **Hyaline cartilage** is smooth and bluish white, covers the joint surfaces and joins the ribs to the breastbone. **Elastic cartilage** is especially flexible and shapes the outer ear and the epiglottis. **Fibrous cartilage** is very tough and resistant to tearing. It forms, for example, the outer ring of the **intervertebral discs** and the menisci in the knee.

In the joints, the ends of the bones are covered with a smooth layer of cartilage. This **joint cartilage** reduces **friction**, so that the bones slide easily against each other. It also acts like a shock absorber. With age or after injuries, the joint cartilage can wear away. This disease is called **osteoarthritis**.

Cartilage has **no blood vessels** and no nerves. It is supplied with nutrients through the surrounding fluid. That is why few building materials reach the spot after an injury. **Cartilage damage** therefore heals only very slowly and often not completely. Exercise helps, because it pumps nutrients into the cartilage.

A large part of our skeleton is first laid down as **cartilage**. Only little by little is this cartilage replaced by bone. That is why babies still have a lot of cartilage, for example in the kneecap. At the **growth plates**, children and teenagers grow in length. In some animals the skeleton stays cartilage all through life: **sharks** and **rays** are therefore called cartilaginous fish.

gewusst: Sharks have not a single piece of real bone in their skeleton.
The ears and the nose go on growing a little even in old age.

teile.einleitung: The knee joint joins the thigh bone, shin bone and kneecap. Menisci, ligaments and cartilage make sure that it is stable and moves smoothly. Because it has to withstand a lot, it is often injured in sport.
wichtigste: The menisci in the knee cushion shocks like small pillows.
Each knee has two menisci.
The cruciate ligaments cross in the middle of the joint like an X.
In cycling, the knee joint bends and straightens.
With the knee bent, you can turn the lower leg a little.
In knock knees the knees touch, in bow legs there is a gap between them.
After a jump, the gentlest way to land is with slightly bent knees.

abschnitte.text: In the knee joint, the **thigh bone** and the **shin bone** meet. At the front lies the **kneecap**. The joint surfaces are covered with smooth **cartilage** so that the bones slide easily against each other. A joint capsule encloses the whole thing. Inside it is joint fluid, which acts like a lubricant.

Between the thigh bone and the shin bone lie two crescent-shaped discs of cartilage, the **menisci**. Each knee has **two**: an inner and an outer meniscus. They **cushion shocks** like small pillows and spread the weight. In a fast twist under load, a meniscus can tear. This happens, for example, in football or skiing.

Strong **ligaments** hold the knee joint together. At the sides lie the collateral ligaments. In the middle of the joint, the two **cruciate ligaments** cross like an **X**. They prevent the lower leg and thigh from shifting against each other. A torn cruciate ligament is a common sports injury. Afterwards you often wear a **knee support** or a splint that supports the knee.

The knee joint can mainly **bend and straighten**, for example in cycling or climbing stairs. If the knee is **bent**, you can also **turn** the lower leg a little. If it is straight, it is firm and stable so that we stand securely. When landing after a jump, **slightly bent knees** protect the joint, because the muscles cushion the shock.

The axis of the leg is not the same in all people. In **knock knees**, the knees touch, but the feet stand apart. In **bow legs**, there is a large gap between the knees when the feet are together. In small children, slight bow legs and later slight knock knees are normal. Usually they grow out of it, otherwise a doctor can help.

gewusst: The cruciate ligaments are only about as thick as a little finger, but withstand great forces.
The word “meniscus” comes from Greek and means “little moon”.

teile.einleitung: Almost everyone knows headaches. In everyday speech people usually just say “head pain”. Often something harmless is behind it, and with simple means it goes away again.
wichtigste: Headaches are often called “head pain” in everyday speech.
The brain itself feels no pain.
Drinking too little, tiredness and looking at screens for a long time can cause a headache.
Tense neck muscles from sitting crooked can also trigger a headache.
Migraine is a special form of severe headache.
With a very severe or long headache, you go to the doctor.

abschnitte.text: Amazingly, the **brain** itself has no pain sensors. A headache arises in other places, for example in the **meninges**, in blood vessels or in the muscles of the head and neck. That is why a headache can have quite different causes.

A mild headache often comes from **too little fluid** or from **tiredness**. Staring at **screens** for a long time also strains the eyes and neck. Someone who **sits crooked** for a long time tenses the muscles in the neck, and this can also cause a headache. If you eat very cold ice cream quickly, the blood vessels in the palate react. Then it stabs briefly in the head.

With a mild headache, it often helps to **drink water** and **rest**. Fresh air and a break from the screen also do you good. Many find a **cool cloth** on the forehead soothing. Exercise and a straight posture can also help tense muscles.

**Migraine** is a special form of headache. The pain is strong, comes again and again and often affects only one side of the head. Often bright light or noise are also disturbing. Some of those affected also feel sick. With migraine, a doctor can recommend suitable help.

Most headaches are harmless. But if the headache is **very severe**, comes suddenly or **does not go away for a long time**, a doctor should take a look. This also applies if you feel ill in addition or have knocked your head.

gewusst: The brain feels no pain, although you feel a headache in the head.
The brief pain from eating ice cream fast is often called “brain freeze” in everyday speech.

teile.einleitung: The knee joins the thigh to the lower leg. In the knee lies the biggest joint of the human body. We need it for walking, jumping, sitting and kneeling.
wichtigste: The knee joint is the biggest joint in the human body.
Above the knee lies the thigh, below it the lower leg.
In the knee you can bend the lower leg backwards.
The soft spot at the back of the knee is called the hollow of the knee.
At the front, the kneecap protects the joint.
In inline skating, knee pads protect the knees.
In the horse, a joint on the foreleg is called the “knee”, although it corresponds to our wrist.

abschnitte.text: The knee lies in the middle of the leg. Above it is the **thigh**, below it the **lower leg**. In the knee, the thigh bone and the shin bone meet. At the front lies the **kneecap**, a flat bone that you can feel easily. At the back of the knee is a soft hollow, the **hollow of the knee**.

The **knee joint** is the biggest joint in the body. It works rather like a hinge. You can **bend** the lower leg **backwards** and **straighten** it again. The knee cannot be overstretched forwards, because strong **ligaments** prevent it. With the knee bent, you can also turn the lower leg a little.

Many babies **crawl** on hands and knees before they can walk. Later too we need the knees all the time: climbing stairs, sitting down, jumping and cycling. When landing after a jump, **slightly bent knees** cushion the impact. When you kneel, you support the whole body weight on the knees.

When children fall over in the **playground**, they often land on their knees. Then the skin on the knee is often **grazed**. You clean the wound with water and stick a plaster on it. When inline skating, skateboarding or riding a scooter, you wear **knee pads**. They have hard shells and protect the knees in a fall.

Animals also have joints in their legs. In the **horse**, a joint on the foreleg is called the **“knee”**. In fact, though, this joint corresponds to our **wrist**. The horse’s real knee lies higher up on the hind leg, close to the belly. The name comes from the fact that the joint on the foreleg lies roughly where you would expect the knee in a human.

gewusst: When climbing stairs, the knee joint carries several times the body weight.
Birds have knees too, but they usually lie hidden under the feathers.

teile.einleitung: Climbing is a sport in which you move up rocks or climbing walls with hands and feet. You can climb with a rope on high walls or without a rope on low blocks. Since the Tokyo Games, sport climbing has also been an Olympic sport.
wichtigste: In rope climbing, you wear a climbing harness around your hips and legs.
The rope holds you if you slip.
The person below on the rope belays you.
Bouldering is climbing without a rope on low walls above thick mats.
White powder on the hands stops you from slipping.
Climbing shoes are tight and have a rubber sole.
In Tokyo, sport climbing was Olympic for the first time.

abschnitte.text: On high walls you climb with a **rope**. For this you wear a **climbing harness** around your hips and legs. The rope is fixed to the harness with a knot. Below stands a second person who **belays**: they operate a belay device and hold the rope. If you slip, the rope catches you, and you can lean back against the wall.

In **bouldering**, you climb without a rope on low walls or boulders. You climb only so high that you can jump off safely. Below lie thick **mats** that cushion a fall. Bouldering is often about short, difficult climbing moves that you try again and again. Many climbing halls in Switzerland have boulder areas of their own.

**Climbing shoes** are tight and have a soft **rubber sole**. This way you can stand even on the tiniest footholds. Climbers rub a white powder, **chalk**, on their hands. It takes up sweat so that the fingers do not **slip**. Outdoors on the rock, you wear a **helmet**, which protects against falling stones.

Switzerland, with its **Alps** and the Jura, offers many climbing areas. Besides rocks, there are numerous **climbing halls** with colourful holds. The colour of the holds often shows which ones belong to a route. The **Swiss Alpine Club** (SAC) offers courses and looks after huts in the mountains. Climbing trains strength, flexibility and concentration.

At the Summer Olympic Games in **Tokyo**, sport climbing was included for the first time. The Games were planned for 2020 and took place in 2021. There are three disciplines: **bouldering**, **lead**, that is, climbing at height with a rope, and **speed**, a race on a standardised wall. Speed climbers manage the 15-metre-high wall in a few seconds.

gewusst: The best speed climbers reach the top of a 15-metre-high wall in less than five seconds.
Good climbers climb more with their legs than with their arms, which saves strength.

teile.einleitung: In a pulmonary embolism, a blood clot blocks a blood vessel in the lung. This is a medical emergency. If it is recognised and treated quickly, however, it can usually be survived well.
wichtigste: The clot mostly comes from a deep leg vein.
It reaches the lungs through the right side of the heart and the right ventricle.
Typical signs are sudden shortness of breath and chest pain.
Virchow’s triad describes three factors that make a thrombosis more likely.
The D-dimer test helps to rule it out, and it is usually proved with a CT angiogram.
The basis of treatment is anticoagulants.

abschnitte.text: A **blood clot** is a lump of clotted blood. If it forms in a vein, this is called a **thrombosis**. It usually forms in a **deep leg vein**. If it comes loose, it is carried with the blood to the heart. Through the right atrium and the **right ventricle** it reaches the pulmonary arteries and gets stuck there. This is called a **pulmonary embolism**.

Typical signs are **sudden shortness of breath** and **chest pain**, often when breathing in. A racing heart, coughing or dizziness can be added. Because less blood flows through the lungs, the blood gets less oxygen. A pulmonary embolism is an **emergency**. In Switzerland you then call **144**.

The German doctor Rudolf Virchow described three factors that make a thrombosis more likely, the **Virchow triad**: slowed blood flow, damage to the wall of the vessel, and blood that clots more easily. **Sitting for a long time**, for example on long flights, slows the blood flow in the legs. Bed rest after operations also raises the risk. Moving around, getting up and drinking help to prevent it.

If the suspicion is slight, a blood test, the **D-dimer test**, can rule out a pulmonary embolism. If it is raised, further investigation is needed. Today the embolism is usually proved with a **CT angiogram** of the lungs. In this, the vessels are made visible with a contrast agent. The basis of treatment is **anticoagulants**. They stop the clot from growing, and the body can gradually break it down.

gewusst: The word “embolism” comes from Greek and means roughly “throwing in”.
On long flights it is recommended to get up now and then and move your feet.

teile.einleitung: The carrot is one of the most popular vegetables. In Switzerland it is often called Rüebli. It tastes good raw and cooked and contains a pigment from which the body makes vitamin A.
wichtigste: In many parts of Switzerland the carrot is called Rüebli.
Its orange colour comes from the pigment carotene.
From carotene, the body makes vitamin A, which is important for the eyes.
A little oil or butter helps the body to absorb the vitamin better.
In the past, many carrots were purple or yellow.
Anyone who eats very, very many carrots can get slightly orange skin.

abschnitte.text: The **carrot** is also called Möhre or Mohrrübe in German. In many parts of Switzerland it is called **Rüebli**. We eat its thick **root**, which grows in the ground. Above, it has green, feathery leaves. Carrots can be nibbled raw, grated, cooked or drunk as juice. Well known is the **Aargau Rüeblitorte**, a fine cake with carrots and almonds.

The orange colour comes from the pigment **carotene**. Its name even comes from the carrot. The body turns carotene into **vitamin A**. This vitamin is especially important for the **eyes**, above all for seeing at dusk. It also helps the skin and the defence system. Carotene dissolves in fat. That is why it is best to add **a little oil or butter** to cooked carrots, so the body absorbs it better.

abschnitte.titel: Purple and yellow in the past
abschnitte.text: Today’s orange carrots have not existed for very long. In the past, many carrots were **purple or yellow**. Only a few hundred years ago were orange varieties bred in the **Netherlands**, which then spread everywhere. Today at markets you can again buy old varieties in white, yellow, red and purple.

abschnitte.titel: Too much of a good thing, and the hare
abschnitte.text: Anyone who eats **very, very many** carrots can get slightly **orange skin**, especially on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. This is harmless and goes away again if you eat fewer carrots. In stories and cartoons, the **hare** likes best to nibble carrots. Real hares and rabbits, however, eat mainly grass and herbs, and carrots are more of a treat for them.

gewusst: The word carotene was derived from the carrot, because the substance was first obtained from it.
Carrots are an important winter vegetable, because stored cool they keep for months.

teile.einleitung: Coordination is the good interplay of brain, nerves and muscles. It makes sure that movements succeed smoothly, accurately and safely. In sport, several coordinative abilities are distinguished.
wichtigste: Coordination means matching movements well to each other.
The semicircular canals in the inner ear report turns of the head to the brain.
The coordinative abilities include balance, reaction, rhythm, orientation, coupling and adaptation.
On the balance beam you train balance.
Juggling trains the coordination of eyes and hands.
Between about 7 and 12 years, children learn movements especially easily.

abschnitte.titel: Brain and muscles as a team
abschnitte.text: In every movement, the brain sends orders through the nerves to the muscles. At the same time it receives reports from the eyes, skin, muscles and the **balance organ**. In the inner ear lie the **semicircular canals**. They report turns and the position of the head. From all these reports, the brain controls the movement finely.

The **ability to balance** helps you not to fall over. On the narrow **balance beam** you have to keep making small compensating movements, which trains it well. The **ability to orient** shows where you are in space. In a somersault, you have to know where up and down are despite the turning.

The **ability to react** makes it possible to answer a signal as fast as possible. Sprinters need it at the starting gun, goalkeepers at the shot on goal. The **ability to adapt** helps to adjust a movement in a flash. If the ball bounces off unexpectedly, you have to act differently at once. In ball games this is especially important.

The **ability to keep rhythm** helps to recognise a beat and turn it into movement. You need it when dancing, skipping or hurdling. The **ability to couple** joins movements of arms and legs into a smooth sequence, for example in a jumping jack or a layup. In **juggling**, eyes and hands work closely together.

At the age of about **7 to 12 years**, children learn new sequences of movement especially fast. This is therefore often called the **golden age of learning**. Someone who tries many different sports and games in this time lays a good foundation. Coordination can be improved at any age, though, for example in gym lessons.

gewusst: The balance organ sits in the ear, right next to the organ of hearing.
You can learn to juggle at any age, and the brain adapts as you do.

teile.einleitung: An infusion is a treatment in which fluid flows slowly directly into a vein. It often hangs in a bag on a stand next to the bed. In this way the body gets water, salts or medicines quite directly.
wichtigste: In an infusion, fluid flows slowly into a vein.
The bag often hangs on a stand next to the bed.
A thin tube leads to a small cannula in the vein.
An infusion often contains salt solution, sugar or medicines.
Nursing staff check how fast the fluid drips.

abschnitte.text: In an **infusion**, fluid flows from a bag or a bottle through a thin **tube** into a **vein**. The bag usually hangs on an **infusion stand** next to the bed so that the fluid can flow downwards. In the vein there is a small, soft cannula, also called a venous catheter. It is often placed on the back of the hand or on the forearm. In a small **drip chamber** you can see how the fluid drips.

An infusion helps when someone cannot drink or eat enough, for example with heavy vomiting or after an operation. Often it contains **salt solution**, which gives the body back water and salts. **Medicines** are also given this way, because they work very quickly through the blood. Sometimes an infusion contains sugar or nutrients as food.

How fast an infusion runs is set exactly. For this there is a small wheel on the tube or an electric **infusion pump**. **Nursing staff** check regularly that everything is running correctly and that the place where the needle went in is all right. Someone with an infusion can often still get up and take the stand with them on its wheels.

gewusst: Infusion stands usually have wheels so that you can take them with you in the hospital.
The salt solution in many infusions is about as salty as blood.

teile.einleitung: The cerebellum is a part of the brain at the back of the head. It makes sure that our movements are finely coordinated and that we keep our balance. Although it is small, it contains the most nerve cells of the whole brain.
wichtigste: The cerebellum lies at the back of the head under the cerebrum.
Its technical term is cerebellum.
It coordinates movements and helps with balance.
Practised movements such as cycling run automatically thanks to the cerebellum.
The cerebellum contains more than half of all nerve cells of the brain.
The two halves are joined by the vermis.
If the cerebellum is damaged, walking often becomes unsteady and swaying.

abschnitte.text: The cerebellum lies at the **back of the head**, under the large **cerebrum** and behind the brainstem. In Latin it is called **cerebellum**, which means “little brain”. It consists of two halves. Between them lies a narrow middle part, the **vermis**. The surface is laid in many fine folds, so a lot of tissue has room.

If you cut the cerebellum through lengthways, you see a special pattern. The **white matter** inside branches like a tree with many branches. That is why it is called the **tree of life**, in Latin “arbor vitae”. The grey cortex on the outside contains the nerve cells. Although the cerebellum makes up only a small part of the brain, more than half of all **nerve cells** sit in it.

The cerebellum’s most important job is to coordinate **movements** and **balance**. The cerebrum gives, for example, the order “reach for the glass”. The cerebellum makes sure that the hand reaches just right, not too fast and not too far. For this it constantly receives reports from the muscles, the eyes and the **balance organ** in the ear. This way it can correct movements in a flash.

At the start, **cycling** is difficult, and you have to think of everything at once. With a lot of practice, the cerebellum stores the sequence of movements. At some point it runs **automatically**, without your having to think. This also applies to swimming, skiing or playing an instrument. So the cerebellum is also important in **learning** movements.

If the cerebellum is injured or diseased, it is hard to control movements exactly. Typical is an **unsteady, swaying walk**. Gripping and speaking can also become inexact. Doctors test this with simple tests, for example moving a finger to the nose with the eyes closed. Too much **alcohol** also disturbs the cerebellum temporarily, which is why drunk people sway.

gewusst: The cerebellum makes up only about a tenth of the weight of the brain, but contains the most nerve cells.
Because the cerebellum predicts our own movements, you can hardly tickle yourself.

teile.einleitung: The iris is the coloured ring in the eye that surrounds the pupil. It gives our eyes their colour, for example brown, blue or green. It also controls how much light falls into the eye.
wichtigste: The coloured ring around the pupil is called the iris.
In German it is also called the Regenbogenhaut, “rainbow skin”.
The Greek word “iris” means rainbow.
The iris makes the pupil bigger or smaller.
In front of the iris lies the transparent cornea.
The white of the eye is called the sclera.
With the pattern of the iris, you can recognise a person.

abschnitte.text: The **iris** is the coloured ring around the **pupil**, the black hole in the middle of the eye. In German it is also called the **Regenbogenhaut**, “rainbow skin”. The Greek word “iris” means **rainbow**, because eyes come in many colours. In Greek legend, the messenger of the gods who appeared as a rainbow was also called Iris. A flower, too, the iris, bears this name.

The iris works like the diaphragm of a camera. It **makes the pupil bigger or smaller**. For this it has two tiny muscles. In bright sunlight the pupil becomes small, so that not too much light falls into the eye. In the dark it becomes large, so that as much light as possible gets in. This happens completely by itself, without our having to think about it.

The colour of the iris depends on the pigment **melanin**. A lot of melanin gives **brown** eyes, and little melanin gives **blue** or **grey** eyes. Blue eyes contain no blue pigment: the blue arises from the way light is scattered in the tissue. Many babies have blue eyes in the first months of life, which can become darker later. Rarely, a person has two eyes of different colours.

In front of the iris lies the **cornea**, a transparent layer that protects the eye and focuses the light. Behind the pupil sits the lens. The **white of the eye** is called the **sclera**. It is firm and gives the eyeball its shape. Together these parts make sure that a sharp image forms on the retina.

The pattern of the iris is different in every person, even in identical twins. That is why it can be used **to recognise a person**. In **iris recognition**, a camera photographs the eye, and a computer compares the pattern. Such devices are used, for example, at some airports or at secured doors.

gewusst: The pattern of the iris stays almost the same throughout life.
Even a person’s left and right eye have different iris patterns.

teile.einleitung: Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and microbiologist of the 19th century. He showed that tiny living things cause fermentation and many diseases. His discoveries still save many lives today.
wichtigste: Louis Pasteur came from France and lived from 1822 to 1895.
He recognised that micro-organisms such as yeasts are the cause of fermentation.
Pasteurisation is named after him, the brief heating of, for example, milk.
With swan-neck flasks he disproved that life arises by itself from dead matter.
In 1881 he developed a vaccine against anthrax, and in 1885 he treated Joseph Meister against rabies.
In 1887 he founded the Pasteur Institute in Paris.

abschnitte.text: **Louis Pasteur** was born in France in 1822 and died in 1895. He was first a **chemist** and later turned to the tiny living things that can only be seen under the microscope. This makes him one of the founders of **microbiology**. He did most of his research in Paris and other French cities.

Pasteur found out that **micro-organisms** such as **yeasts** cause fermentation, for example in wine and beer. Other germs make drinks go sour or spoil. He developed a process in which food is heated briefly to kill many germs. It is named after him: **pasteurisation**. Pasteurised milk is found in every shop today, in Switzerland too.

In the past many people believed that life could arise **by itself from dead matter**, for example maggots from meat. Pasteur filled nutrient solution into **glass flasks with a long, curved neck** and boiled it. Dust and germs from the air stayed stuck in the bend. The solution stayed clear. When he broke off the neck, germs soon grew in it. In this way he showed that germs come from the air.

Pasteur developed vaccines using weakened germs. In 1881 he showed on sheep and cattle that his vaccine protects against the animal disease **anthrax**. In 1885 he treated the boy **Joseph Meister**, who had been bitten by a rabid dog, with a vaccine against **rabies**. The boy survived. Two years later, in 1887, the **Pasteur Institute** was founded in Paris, and it is still doing research today.

gewusst: Joseph Meister later worked as a caretaker at the Pasteur Institute.
Pasteur is buried in the Pasteur Institute in Paris.

teile.einleitung: The kiwi is a fruit with a brown, hairy skin and usually green flesh. It comes originally from China and is named after a bird from New Zealand. Kiwis are healthy because they contain a lot of vitamin C.
wichtigste: The green kiwi has a brown, hairy skin.
The flesh is usually green, but there are also yellow varieties.
The kiwi comes originally from China.
It is named after the kiwi, a bird from New Zealand.
A kiwi contains more vitamin C than an orange of the same weight.
The kiwi grows on a climbing plant.
A ripe kiwi gives slightly under light pressure.

abschnitte.text: The ordinary kiwi is about as big as a hen’s egg. Its **skin** is brown and covered with fine hairs, and it feels furry. Inside, the **flesh** is bright green. In the middle lies a pale core, around which many small black **seeds** are arranged in a circle. There are also varieties with yellow flesh and smoother skin.

The plant originally grows wild in **China**. In the past the fruit was therefore also called “Chinese gooseberry”. At the start of the 20th century it was brought to **New Zealand**, where it was grown in large plantations. For sale in other countries, it was later given the name **kiwi**, after New Zealand’s well-known bird. Today the kiwi is grown in many countries, including Italy.

The kiwi does not grow on a tree but on a **climbing plant**. Its long shoots twine up frames or wires, like vines. The plant does not tolerate hard frost. In mild areas you can also grow it in a garden in Switzerland. The fruits are harvested in autumn.

Kiwis contain a lot of **vitamin C**, even more than an orange of the same weight. One kiwi already covers a large part of the daily need. The body needs vitamin C, for example, for the defences and for healthy skin. Kiwis also contain **fibre**, which is good for digestion.

The easiest way is to **halve** the kiwi and spoon out the flesh. You can also peel it and cut it into slices. The skin, by the way, is **edible** if you wash it well. You notice whether a kiwi is **ripe** when it gives slightly under light pressure. Hard kiwis ripen faster next to apples.

gewusst: The kiwi bird and the fruit are both brown and roundish, so the name fits well.
Raw kiwi can make milk in a dessert bitter, because it contains a substance that splits protein.

teile.einleitung: Iodised table salt stands in almost every Swiss kitchen. It contains a small amount of iodine, which the body needs for the thyroid gland. Switzerland was among the first countries to act against iodine deficiency in this way.
wichtigste: Iodised salt was introduced in Switzerland in the 1920s.
It was meant above all to fight goitre, an enlarged thyroid gland.
Soils in the Alpine region are low in iodine, because glaciers and rainfall washed the iodine out.
In Switzerland, iodised table salt contains about 25 milligrams of iodine per kilogram.
The iodine is added as potassium iodide or potassium iodate.
Schweizer Salinen AG makes the table salt and is responsible for the iodisation.

abschnitte.titel: Why the Alps have little iodine
