abschnitte.text: Iodine is a trace element that humans need only in tiny amounts. It reaches our food through soil, plants and animals. In the **Alpine region**, though, the soils are especially low in iodine. During the ice ages, **glaciers** wore away the soil, and rain and snow washed the iodine out over a long time. That is why vegetables, grain and milk from such areas contain little iodine.

In the past, very many people in Switzerland had a **goitre**, a greatly enlarged thyroid gland on the neck. If the thyroid gets too little iodine, it grows in order to take more iodine from the blood. Severe iodine deficiency can also lead in children to **cretinism**, a serious disturbance of physical and mental development. In the **1920s**, Switzerland therefore introduced iodised table salt. After that, goitre and cretinism became much rarer.

abschnitte.titel: How the iodine gets into the salt
abschnitte.text: Iodine is mixed into the salt in the form of **potassium iodide** or **potassium iodate**. In Switzerland, iodised table salt contains about **25 milligrams of iodine per kilogram**. The salt is made by **Schweizer Salinen AG**, which belongs to the cantons. It obtains salt from deposits deep in the ground, for example on the Rhine and in Bex in the canton of Vaud. Many salt packs come with and without iodine, often also with fluoride.

Today people eat a lot of **processed food** such as ready meals, sausage or cheese. These are often made with salt that is not iodised. Even someone who eats less salt, which is good for the heart, takes in less iodine. That is why the iodine supply can run short despite iodised household salt. Experts therefore recommend using iodised salt at home. Bread from the bakery in Switzerland is often baked with iodised salt.

gewusst: A goitre was once so common in some Alpine valleys that it often appears in old pictures and in legends.
The body needs only about 150 micrograms of iodine a day, which are millionths of a gram.

teile.einleitung: The epiglottis is a small, movable lid in the throat. When swallowing, it makes sure that food and drink go into the gullet and not into the windpipe. In technical language it is called the epiglottis.
wichtigste: In technical language the epiglottis is called the epiglottis.
The epiglottis lies behind the root of the tongue.
Its framework is made of elastic cartilage.
If food gets into the larynx, the cough reflex carries it out again.
A dangerous inflammation of the epiglottis is called epiglottitis.
The Hib vaccination has greatly reduced this inflammation in children.

abschnitte.text: In the throat, two paths cross: the air goes into the **windpipe**, the food into the **gullet**. The **epiglottis** lies **behind the root of the tongue**, that is, right at the back and bottom of the tongue, above the entrance to the larynx. When breathing, it stands upright, and the air flows past freely. When **swallowing**, the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds over it. This way the bite slides into the gullet.

In technical language the epiglottis is called the **epiglottis**. Its framework is made of **elastic cartilage**. This cartilage is flexible and springs back into shape after swallowing. The outer ear is also made of such elastic cartilage. The epiglottis is covered with mucous membrane, like the other airways.

Sometimes a crumb or a sip of water still gets past the epiglottis into the **larynx**. Then the **cough reflex** sets in at once. With a strong burst of air, the food is carried out again. This happens mainly when you **laugh or talk with your mouth full**. In that case the larynx is **open**, so that air can flow through. So the rule is: first swallow, then talk.

**Epiglottitis** is a dangerous inflammation of the epiglottis. It swells greatly and can narrow the airways. Those affected have a high fever, pain on swallowing and difficulty breathing. This is an emergency in which you must get help at once. In the past, mainly small children fell ill with it, usually caused by a bacterium. Thanks to the **Hib vaccination**, which protects against this bacterium, the disease is now rare in children.

gewusst: The name epiglottis comes from Greek and means roughly “on the glottis”.
We swallow several hundred times a day, often without noticing, and each time the epiglottis plays its part.

teile.einleitung: Body weight shows how heavy a person is. In children it increases with growth, because bones, muscles and organs become bigger.
wichtigste: Body weight is given in kilograms.
At one year, a child is about three times as heavy as at birth.
The biggest part of body weight is water.
An eight-year-old child weighs about 25 kilograms.
Children become heavier because bones and muscles grow.
Exercise and healthy eating help to have a healthy weight.

abschnitte.text: Body weight is measured with **scales**. It is given in **kilograms**, abbreviated kg. With babies, people often weigh in grams, because they are still very light. You can also calculate with weights: if Tim weighs 30 kg and his father 80 kg, then the father is **50 kg** heavier. Weight varies a little over the course of a day, for example after eating or drinking.

A baby usually weighs about three to four kilograms at birth. In the first year of life it grows very fast. At one year it is about **three times as heavy** as at birth. After that, weight increases more slowly. An **eight-year-old child** weighs about **25 kg**. Every child is different, though, and taller children are usually heavier too.

The biggest part of our weight is **water**. In adults it is about sixty per cent. In addition come **muscles**, **bones**, organs and fat. When children grow, bones become longer and muscles stronger. That is why they become heavier over time. This is quite normal and part of growing up.

A **healthy body weight** fits your height and age. Doctors check this at check-ups using so-called **growth charts**. Plenty of **exercise**, for example playing outdoors, cycling or swimming, keeps the body fit. With it goes **balanced eating** with vegetables, fruit and wholemeal products. Sweets and sugary drinks are better only now and then.

gewusst: A baby roughly triples its weight in the first year of life.
Someone who stands on scales on the Moon shows only about a sixth, because the Moon pulls less strongly. The mass of the body stays the same, though.

teile.einleitung: Some people have straight hair, others wavy or curly hair. A curl is a lock of hair that coils like a spiral. Whether hair grows curly depends mainly on the shape of the hair.
wichtigste: Curls are hairs that coil like a spiral.
Hair that hangs straight down is called straight, and slightly wavy hair is called wavy.
Whether a hair grows straight or curly depends on its shape.
Curls are often inherited.
With curling tongs or curlers you can give straight hair curls for a while.
Sheep also often have curly fleece, which wool is made from.

abschnitte.text: Hair comes in many shapes. **Straight hair** hangs straight down. **Wavy hair** sways gently to and fro but is not strongly curled. **Curls** coil like a spiral. Some curls are big and soft, others very small and tight. All shapes of hair are completely natural.

Every hair grows out of a small hollow in the scalp, the **hair follicle**. If you cut a hair across, you can see its **shape**: straight hairs are rather round, curly ones rather flat or oval. A curved hair follicle also makes the hair grow crooked. What your hair is like is mostly **inherited**. That is why children with curly-haired parents often have curls too.

If you have straight hair, you can give yourself curls for a while. With **curling tongs**, which get hot, you wind locks of hair around them. Without heat you can use **curlers**: you roll up the wet hair and let it dry. After the next wash the curls are usually gone again. You have to be careful with curling tongs, because they are hot.

It is not only people who have curls. Many **sheep** have a thick, curly fleece. **Wool** for jumpers and socks is made from it. Some breeds of dog, such as the poodle, also have curly coats. In Switzerland, sheep are usually sheared in spring.

gewusst: Curly hair often looks shorter than it is, because it coils up.
Damp air can make curls frizz more.

teile.einleitung: Capillaries are the finest blood vessels in the body. They are so thin that you can see them only under the microscope. In them, the important exchange between blood and tissue takes place.
wichtigste: Capillaries are the finest blood vessels in humans.
Their wall consists of a single layer of cells.
Their diameter is about 5 to 10 micrometres.
They lie between the arterioles and the venules.
Their main job is the exchange of substances between blood and tissue.
Blood flows in them much more slowly than in the large arteries.

abschnitte.text: Blood flows from the heart through large **arteries**, which branch more and more. The smallest arteries are called **arterioles**. After them come the **capillaries**, also called hair vessels in German. They are the finest blood vessels of all. After that, the capillaries gather again into small veins, the **venules**, and the blood flows back to the heart.

A typical capillary has a diameter of about **5 to 10 micrometres**. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre. A hair is about ten times thicker. The **red blood cells** are about the same size as the narrowest capillaries. They change shape and push through **one behind another**. The wall of a capillary consists of only **a single layer of cells**.

The main job of the capillaries is the **exchange of substances**. Through their thin wall, **oxygen** and nutrients pass from the blood into the tissue. At the same time, the blood takes up **carbon dioxide** and other waste substances. In a working muscle, the capillaries give off mainly oxygen. So that enough time remains for the exchange, the blood flows **much more slowly** in the capillaries than in the large arteries.

In the lungs, capillaries wrap around the **air sacs** like a fine net. There the wall between air and blood is especially thin. Here the blood takes up **oxygen** from the air we breathe in and gives off **carbon dioxide**, which we breathe out. After that, the oxygen-rich blood flows to the heart and is pumped around the whole body.

gewusst: Almost every cell in the body lies very close to a capillary.
When you blush, many fine blood vessels in the skin widen, and more blood flows through them.

teile.einleitung: With a light microscope you can see things that are far too small for the naked eye, such as cells. It magnifies using glass lenses and light. In many schools it is part of the basic equipment in biology lessons.
wichtigste: The eyepiece is the lens you look through, and the objective lens sits directly above the specimen.
The total magnification is the eyepiece times the objective, for example 10 times 40 equals 400 times.
A light microscope is useful up to about 1000 times magnification.
The condenser focuses the light onto the specimen.
The specimen lies on a thin plate of glass, the slide.
Antoni van Leeuwenhoek discovered tiny living things in the 17th century.

abschnitte.text: At the top you look through the **eyepiece**. At the bottom, directly above the specimen, sits the **objective lens**. There are often several objective lenses on a rotating nosepiece. The specimen lies on a **slide**, a thin plate of glass, which is placed on the stage. Underneath, the **condenser** focuses the light from the lamp onto the specimen. The light has to pass through the object, so specimens must be very thin.

The eyepiece and the objective lens both magnify. You get the **total magnification** by multiplying their values. A 10 times eyepiece with a 40 times objective lens therefore gives a magnification of **400 times**. A light microscope is useful up to about **1000 times**. Beyond that the image gets bigger but not sharper, because light itself sets a limit.

You always start with the smallest objective lens. With the **coarse focus knob** you first bring the image roughly into focus, and then with the **fine focus knob** you make it exact. Only then do you switch to a stronger magnification. This makes it easier to find the spot you are looking for and stops the objective lens touching the glass.

In a school microscope you can clearly see the **nucleus** and the **cell wall**, for example in cells from onion skin. You can also look at tiny living things from a drop of water, hairs or leaves. Much smaller things, such as viruses, can only be seen with an **electron microscope**. The Dutchman **Antoni van Leeuwenhoek** was one of the first to discover tiny living things in the 17th century, using microscopes he built himself.

gewusst: The microscopes of Antoni van Leeuwenhoek had only a single, tiny lens.
Specimens are often stained so that the parts of the cells can be seen better.

teile.einleitung: Bone marrow is a soft tissue inside many bones. In red bone marrow, billions of new blood cells arise every day. Yellow bone marrow consists mainly of fat.
wichtigste: Bone marrow is found inside the bones.
The blood-forming bone marrow is red.
Yellow bone marrow consists mainly of fat.
In babies, almost all the bone marrow is red.
Red marrow can also be found in adults, for example in the breastbone.
White blood cells also arise in the bone marrow.
A donation of blood stem cells can help people with blood cancer.

abschnitte.text: Many bones are not completely solid inside. They look like a **sponge** with many small hollow spaces. In them and in the marrow cavity of long bones sits the **bone marrow**. It is a soft tissue with many blood vessels. A distinction is made between **red** and **yellow** bone marrow.

**Red bone marrow** is the factory of the blood. Here the **red blood cells**, which carry oxygen, arise from **blood stem cells**. The **white blood cells** are also made here, and they fight disease-causing germs. Then there are the **platelets**, which stop bleeding in wounds. Every day, billions of new blood cells arise in this way.

In **babies**, almost all the bone marrow is red. As we get older, in many bones, such as in the arms and legs, red marrow turns into **yellow marrow**. This consists mainly of **fat** and no longer makes blood. In adults, red bone marrow is still found in flat bones such as the **breastbone**, the ribs, the vertebrae and the pelvis. When there is great need, yellow marrow can become blood-forming marrow again.

In some diseases, for example **blood cancer**, the bone marrow no longer works properly. Then a donation of **blood stem cells** can help. Healthy people can have themselves entered in a **register** for this. In Switzerland, Blood Donation SRK Switzerland takes care of it. If someone matches a sick person, they may be able to save a life with their donation.

Animal bones also contain bone marrow. Bones that you put in a **soup** for the marrow are called **marrow bones**. Usually they are beef bones. When cooking, the marrow gives flavour and fat to the broth. In the dish ossobuco, a shin of veal with marrow bones is braised.

gewusst: Red bone marrow makes millions of new red blood cells every second.
Red blood cells live only about 120 days, which is why the bone marrow has to make new ones constantly.

teile.einleitung: Interferons are messenger substances of the immune system. Body cells make them mainly when they have been invaded by viruses, and in this way they warn their neighbouring cells. Today interferons are also used as medicines.
wichtigste: Interferons are so called because they interfere with the multiplication of viruses.
They were discovered in 1957 by Alick Isaacs and the Swiss Jean Lindenmann.
Virus-infected cells make mainly interferon-alpha and interferon-beta.
Interferon-gamma is the only one of type II and strongly activates macrophages.
Type I interferons trigger the making of antiviral proteins in neighbouring cells.
Interferon-beta is used in multiple sclerosis.
A common side effect is flu-like complaints.

abschnitte.text: **Interferons** are proteins that work as **messenger substances** between cells. Their name comes from the word “interference”, that is, disturbance, because they **interfere with the multiplication of viruses**. If a cell is invaded by a virus, it makes interferons and releases them. These reach neighbouring cells and warn them about the intruder.

Interferons were discovered in **1957**. The British researcher **Alick Isaacs** and the **Swiss** researcher **Jean Lindenmann** were working together in London at the time. They observed that after a virus infection, cells release a substance that protects other cells. Jean Lindenmann later became a professor at the University of Zurich.

Interferons are divided into groups. Virus-infected body cells make mainly **interferon-alpha** and **interferon-beta**, which belong to **type I**. In neighbouring cells these trigger the making of **antiviral proteins**, which slow the multiplication of the viruses. **Interferon-gamma** is the only interferon of **type II**. It is made by defence cells and especially strongly activates the **macrophages**, the phagocytes of the immune system.

Today interferons are made in the laboratory and injected as medicines. **Interferon-beta** is used as a long-term therapy in **multiple sclerosis**, a disease of the nervous system. **Interferon-alpha** was for a long time the standard therapy against **hepatitis C**, a virus infection of the liver. Meanwhile there are new medicines for it that act directly against the virus and are better tolerated.

Interferon therapy often has side effects. Especially common are **flu-like complaints** such as fever, shivering, headache and aching limbs. This is no coincidence: in a real flu, too, the body makes interferons, and they contribute to these complaints. Often the side effects become weaker after a few weeks.

gewusst: Part of the complaints that you feel in flu comes from the body’s own interferons.
For a long time it was very difficult to make interferons in large amounts, and only genetic engineering made it easier.

teile.einleitung: When children are ill or need a check-up, they go to the paediatrician. These doctors are specially trained for children and young people. Their field is called paediatrics.
wichtigste: The paediatrician looks after sick children.
The technical word for the medicine of children is paediatrics.
With the stethoscope, he listens to the heart and lungs.
With the otoscope, he looks into the ears.
At check-ups, body height is often measured.
At the paediatrician’s, you get vaccinations against diseases.
If a child suddenly becomes very ill at night, you go to the emergency department at the hospital.

abschnitte.text: Children are not small adults. Their bodies grow and change, and some diseases occur mainly in children. That is why there are **paediatricians**. Their field is called **paediatrics**. This comes from Greek: “pais” means child. Paediatricians look after children from birth to adolescence.

With the **stethoscope**, the paediatrician listens to the **heart and lungs**. He hears whether the heart beats regularly and whether breathing is clear. With the **otoscope**, a small device with a light, he looks into the **ears**. With a wooden spatula and a lamp, he looks into the throat. Often he also feels the belly. None of this hurts.

Healthy children also go regularly to the paediatrician, for a **preventive check-up**. In it, **body height** is often measured and weight determined. This shows whether a child is growing well. The doctor also checks whether the child sees and hears well. In addition, you get **vaccinations** at the paediatrician’s. They protect against diseases such as measles or whooping cough. What you have received is written in the **vaccination record**.

Before going to the paediatrician, you usually **make an appointment**, by phone or online. At the practice you register at reception. Then you wait in the **waiting room** until you are called. There are often books and toys there. If a child is ill with something infectious, it is better to say so on the phone.

abschnitte.titel: When it is urgent at night
abschnitte.text: If a child suddenly becomes **very ill** in the **night**, the practice is usually closed. Then you go to the **emergency department at the hospital**, best to a children’s hospital or a children’s clinic. In many regions there is also a phone number for medical advice. In a life-threatening case, you dial the **ambulance emergency number 144**.

gewusst: The word stethoscope comes from Greek and means roughly “chest viewer”.
Many paediatricians warm the stethoscope in their hand before listening, so that it is not so cold.

teile.einleitung: Blood flows through the body in two circuits. The pulmonary circulation carries the blood from the heart to the lungs and back again. There it takes up fresh oxygen.
wichtigste: The pulmonary circulation is also called the lesser circulation.
It begins in the right ventricle and ends in the left atrium.
From the right ventricle comes the pulmonary trunk, which divides into two pulmonary arteries.
The pulmonary veins bring the blood back, and usually four of them open into the heart.
Blood pressure in the pulmonary circulation is much lower than in the systemic circulation.
Ibn al-Nafis was the first to describe the pulmonary circulation, in the 13th century.

abschnitte.text: The heart is a double pump. The left half pumps blood around the whole body, which is the **systemic circulation** or greater circulation. The right half pumps blood to the lungs, which is the **pulmonary circulation**, also called the **lesser circulation**. The two circuits are connected: the blood passes through them in turn.

Blood low in oxygen from the body comes into the right atrium and then into the **right ventricle**. This is where the pulmonary circulation **begins**. The ventricle pumps the blood into the **pulmonary trunk**, which divides into a left and a right **pulmonary artery**. In the fine capillaries around the alveoli, the blood gives off carbon dioxide and takes up oxygen. The **pulmonary veins** bring it back into the **left atrium**, where the pulmonary circulation **ends**.

In the pulmonary circulation the **blood pressure is much lower** than in the systemic circulation. The lungs lie close to the heart, after all, and their fine vessels are delicate. That is why the wall of the right ventricle is thinner than that of the left. Normally **four pulmonary veins** open into the heart, two from each lung. A special feature is this: here the arteries carry blood low in oxygen and the veins carry blood rich in oxygen.

For a long time people believed that the blood got from right to left through small holes in the wall of the heart. The Arab doctor **Ibn al-Nafis** was the first, in the **13th century**, to describe that the blood flows through the lungs. In Europe this became known only centuries later. In the 17th century the Englishman **William Harvey** described the whole circulation of the blood.

gewusst: The pulmonary arteries are the only arteries in an adult that carry blood low in oxygen.
In one minute about as much blood flows through the lungs as through the whole rest of the body.

teile.einleitung: When it is cold outside, the body has to protect its warmth. It has astonishing tricks for this, for example shivering and goose pimples.
wichtigste: In the cold you get “chicken skin”, as it is called in Switzerland, and elsewhere goose pimples.
When shivering, the muscles move fast and produce heat.
Fingers and toes usually become cold first.
Very great cold can injure the skin, which is called frostbite.
Gloves, a hat and warm clothes protect against the cold.
Metal feels colder than wood because it conducts heat away faster.

abschnitte.text: When we are cold, we begin to **shiver**. The muscles contract very quickly and relax again. This work produces **heat**. In addition, the fine hairs on the skin stand up and small bumps form. In Switzerland this is called **Hühnerhaut**, “chicken skin”, in Germany rather “goose skin”, which in English is goose pimples.

In the cold, the body sends the warm blood mainly to the important **organs** in the belly and chest. The blood vessels in hands and feet become narrower. That is why **fingers and toes** usually become cold first. If you hold an ice cube in your hand for a long time, it even becomes **numb** and you hardly feel anything. In very great cold, the skin on fingers, toes, ears or nose can be damaged. This is called **frostbite**.

Warm clothes help against the cold. **Gloves** protect the hands, a hat the head and warm socks the feet. It is best to put on several layers on top of each other, because warm air stays between the layers. You should change wet clothes quickly, because wetness cools the body strongly. Exercise also helps to stay warm.

In winter, a railing made of **metal** feels much colder than one made of **wood**, although both are equally cold. The reason: metal **conducts heat** away from the hand very quickly. Wood conducts it only slowly. So our skin does not feel the temperature itself but how fast it loses heat.

Cold can also be useful. On a fresh **bump** on the head, you put something cool, wrapped in a cloth. The cold makes the swelling less strong and eases the pain. Ice, however, is never put directly on the skin, or it can be damaged.

gewusst: Goose pimples are a leftover from old times: in animals with thick fur, the fur stands up and so holds more warm air.
Shivering can greatly increase the production of heat in the body.

teile.einleitung: An infectious disease is a disease that arises when tiny disease-causing germs invade the body and multiply there. These include a cold, flu, measles, tuberculosis or malaria. Many of these diseases are infectious and can be passed on from person to person or by animals.
wichtigste: Infectious diseases are caused by germs such as viruses, bacteria, fungi or parasites.
Flu is caused by viruses, so antibiotics do not help against it.
Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium.
The virus HIV can lead to the disease AIDS if untreated.
Malaria is caused by single-celled parasites, the plasmodia.
In Switzerland, a vaccination protects against tick-borne encephalitis (TBE), which is passed on by ticks.
Washing hands, vaccinations and clean water are the most important protective measures.

abschnitte.text: In an **infection**, germs get into the body, for example through the mouth, nose, wounds or an insect bite. There they multiply and damage cells or release toxins. The body defends itself with the **immune system**, which often causes fever, tiredness or inflammation. Not every infection makes you ill: sometimes the body defeats the germs before you notice anything.

**Viruses** cause, for example, flu, colds, measles, chickenpox and Covid-19. **Bacteria** cause, among other things, tuberculosis, scarlet fever, whooping cough and many wound infections. Malaria is passed on by plasmodia, which are single-celled parasites that mosquitoes pass on. Fungi and worms can also cause infectious diseases.

Many germs spread by **droplet infection**, that is, when coughing, sneezing or speaking. Others get into the body through dirty hands, food or water. Some diseases are passed on by animals, for example malaria by the anopheles mosquito or TBE and Lyme disease by ticks. HIV is passed on mainly through blood and through sexual intercourse.

**Antibiotics** work against bacteria, because they attack bacterial cells in a targeted way. Against viruses, antibiotics do not help, so they do nothing for flu or a cold. For some viruses there are special medicines, for example against HIV, so that those affected can now live well for a long time. For many virus infections, what helps most is rest, drinking and patience.

A **vaccination** trains the immune system so that it recognises a germ quickly. In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) recommends vaccinations, for example against measles, whooping cough and, in risk areas, against TBE. Thorough hand washing with soap, sneezing into your elbow and staying at home when you are ill also protect others. In tick areas, long clothes and checking your body for ticks after an outing help.

In the past, very many people died of epidemics such as plague, smallpox or cholera. Thanks to clean drinking water, hygiene, vaccinations and antibiotics, many of these diseases have become rare here. Smallpox has been regarded as eradicated worldwide since 1980. In poorer countries, however, malaria, tuberculosis and diarrhoeal diseases are still a great danger.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny living thing or particle that can cause a disease.
When a disease suddenly spreads strongly in one area.
An epidemic that spreads over many countries and continents.
A medicine that kills bacteria or slows their growth.

gewusst: Smallpox is the first infectious disease of humans to be eradicated worldwide by vaccinations.
The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered by Alexander Fleming by chance in 1928 in a mouldy dish of bacteria.
Because of malaria and other diseases, the mosquito is regarded as the deadliest animal in the world for humans.

teile.einleitung: In a contact allergy, the skin reacts to a substance it has come into contact with. Typical is an itchy, red rash, the allergic contact eczema. Common triggers are nickel, fragrances and substances in hair dyes.
wichtigste: Contact allergy is one of the type IV hypersensitivity reactions.
The eczema usually shows only about one to three days after contact.
Nickel is one of the most common triggers in Europe.
Haptens become an allergen only by binding to the body’s own proteins.
The allergy is detected with the patch test.
Chromate in cement used to cause the “bricklayer’s itch” often.
p-Phenylenediamine in hair dyes and “black henna” is a strong contact allergen.

abschnitte.text: Experts divide allergies into four types. **Contact allergy** belongs to **type IV**, the so-called delayed type. Here it is not antibodies that react but certain defence cells, the **T cells**. That is why the **allergic contact eczema** usually shows only **one to three days** after contact. The skin becomes red, itches, swells and can form small blisters.

Many triggers are very small molecules. They are called **haptens**. On their own they set off no reaction. Only when they get into the skin and bind to **the body’s own proteins** do they become a complete **allergen**. The defence system remembers this substance. At every new contact it then reacts again.

In Europe, **nickel** is one of the most common triggers. It is found in cheap jewellery, watches, belt buckles and the buttons on jeans. **Fragrances** in cosmetics and perfume are also common. The substance **p-phenylenediamine** in hair dyes and in **“black henna”** for painted-on tattoos is a strong contact allergen. In the past, many building workers got the **“bricklayer’s itch”**, caused by **chromate** in cement.

Whether someone has a contact allergy is checked with the **patch test**. In it, small patches with different test substances are stuck on the **back**. After about two days they are removed, and the skin is checked on several days. If it reddens at one spot, you are allergic to that substance. Because fragrances so often cause allergies, several of them are tested together as a **fragrance mix**.

A contact allergy usually stays for life. The most important thing is therefore to **avoid the trigger**. Anyone who is allergic to nickel chooses nickel-free jewellery. Against the rash, ointments that dampen the inflammation help. Laws now limit how much nickel may be released from jewellery or how much chromate cement may contain. Since then the bricklayer’s itch has become much rarer.

gewusst: An ear piercing with a nickel-containing stud can be the start of a lifelong nickel allergy.
Real henna is reddish brown, while black henna often contains the additive p-phenylenediamine.

teile.einleitung: Lyme disease is an illness that is passed on by tick bites. It is caused by bacteria. In Switzerland you can catch it almost anywhere there are ticks.
wichtigste: Lyme disease is caused by bacteria called Borrelia.
It is passed on by ticks, which belong to the arachnids.
Borrelia are usually passed on only after some hours, so remove ticks quickly.
The disease is named after the town of Lyme in the USA.
It is treated with antibiotics.
Untreated, it can lead to inflamed joints, for example.

abschnitte.text: **Ticks** are small animals that suck blood. They belong to the **arachnids**. They sit on grass and in undergrowth and let themselves be brushed off onto passers-by. Some ticks carry bacteria called **Borrelia**. When they suck blood they can pass these on to people. In Switzerland you can catch it **almost anywhere** there are ticks.

The disease is named after the town of **Lyme** in the **USA**. There, many cases of joint inflammation were noticed in the 1970s. The germ was discovered in the early 1980s by the researcher **Willy Burgdorfer**, who was born in Basel. The bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi is named after him.

A typical first sign is the **migrating redness**: a red patch around the bite that slowly spreads. Some people also feel tired or have a fever. Anyone who notices something like this should see a doctor. Lyme disease is treated with **antibiotics**. If it is not treated, it can later cause, for example, **inflamed joints** or problems with the nerves.

Borrelia are usually passed on only **after some hours**. So you should **remove a tick as quickly as possible**, preferably with tick tweezers or a pair of tweezers. After an outing in the woods or meadows, you check your body thoroughly. Long clothes and tick repellents also help. As of 2025 there was **no approved vaccine** against Lyme disease for people in Switzerland. The tick vaccination that you often hear about protects against a different disease, TBE.

gewusst: Not every tick carries Borrelia, and not every tick bite makes you ill.
Ticks do not jump from trees, but are usually brushed off from grass and bushes.

teile.einleitung: An infection is catching disease-causing germs such as viruses or bacteria. They can pass from one person to another in quite different ways. With simple rules you can protect yourself and others well.
wichtigste: In an infection, disease-causing germs get into the body.
An infectious disease can pass on to others.
Catching something through tiny droplets when coughing is called droplet infection.
Catching something through hands and objects is called smear infection.
You sneeze and cough into the crook of your arm.
Germs get into the body through the eyes, nose and mouth.
Not everything is infectious, sunburn for example is not.

abschnitte.text: In an **infection**, tiny **disease-causing germs** get into the body and multiply there. They can be **viruses**, **bacteria**, fungi or small parasites. A disease is **infectious** if it can pass from one person to others. A cold, flu or chickenpox are infectious. **Sunburn**, on the other hand, is not infectious, because it is caused by the sun’s rays and not by germs.

When coughing, sneezing and even when speaking, **tiny droplets** fly out of the mouth and nose. Germs can be in them. If another person breathes them in, they can catch the illness. This is called **droplet infection**. This is how colds and flu spread, for example. A **hygiene mask**, for example on the bus, holds back many of these droplets and so protects others.

Germs can also be passed on through **hands and objects**. This is called **smear infection**. Someone who touches a door handle with germs on it, for example, has them on their fingers afterwards. If you then touch your **eyes, nose or mouth**, the germs get into the body that way. It is also better not to drink from the same bottle as a sick friend, because **germs in saliva** are passed on.

abschnitte.titel: How to protect yourself and others
abschnitte.text: The most important rule is **washing your hands** with soap, especially before eating and after going to the toilet. Wash between the fingers too. If you have to sneeze or cough, do it **into the crook of your arm** or into a tissue and not into your hand. That way fewer germs land on hands and objects. If you are ill, it is best to stay at home and recover.

The body has a defence system of its own, the **immune system**. It recognises many germs and fights them. Fever is often a sign that the body is fighting an infection. Vaccinations train the immune system so that it recognises certain germs faster. Enough sleep, exercise and healthy food also help the defence.

gewusst: Many bacteria in the body are useful, for example in the gut, where they help with digestion.
When you sneeze, droplets often fly further than a metre.

teile.einleitung: The sun feels good, but its UV rays can burn your skin. Sunscreen protects you from this. How strongly it protects is shown by the sun protection factor, or SPF for short.
wichtigste: SPF stands for sun protection factor.
The higher the number, the stronger the protection, and SPF 50 protects the most.
Children need high protection, about SPF 30 or more.
You put cream on before you go out in the sun, and you use enough of it.
After swimming and after a few hours you have to put more cream on.
Ears and neck are often forgotten when putting on sunscreen.

abschnitte.text: The sun gives off **UV rays**. Too much of this leads to **sunburn** and can harm the skin in the long term. The **sun protection factor** shows how strongly a sunscreen protects against sunburn. Roughly speaking, with cream you can stay in the sun about as many times longer as the number says before your skin turns red. The highest level is **SPF 50** or 50+. Children should use at least SPF 30.

It is best to put cream on **before** you go out in the sun. Use **enough** cream so that all bare skin is well covered. Too little cream protects much less than it says on the tube. **Ears**, **neck**, nose, feet and shoulders are often forgotten. The lips also need protection, for example with a lip balm with SPF.

Sunscreen does **not protect all day**. Sweating, towelling dry and swimming rub it off. So after swimming, and also every few hours otherwise, you have to **put more on**. Important: putting more on does not make the protection time longer, it only keeps the protection going. If you are already turning red, you belong in the shade.

The best sunscreen is no substitute for **shade**. The sun is especially strong at midday. A hat, a T-shirt and sunglasses give extra protection. In the mountains the UV radiation is stronger, and snow reflects the light back. That is why sun protection is also important in Switzerland when you go skiing.

gewusst: Even when it is cloudy, a large part of the UV radiation still reaches the Earth.
With every 1000 metres of height, UV radiation becomes about 10 per cent stronger.

teile.einleitung: The kneecap is a flat, hard bone at the front of the knee. It protects the knee joint and helps with straightening the leg. In technical language it is called the patella.
wichtigste: The kneecap lies at the front of the knee.
Its technical term is patella.
It protects the knee joint.
It is embedded in a tendon.
It supports the straightening of the leg.
In newborns it is still made of cartilage.
If you tap below the kneecap, the lower leg shoots forward.

abschnitte.text: The **kneecap** lies at the front of the knee, directly under the skin. In technical language it is called the **patella**. It is roughly triangular and flat. The special thing is that it is embedded in a **tendon**. This tendon joins the big muscle at the front of the thigh to the shin bone. Bones that lie in a tendon like this are called **sesamoid bones**, and the kneecap is the biggest of them.

When you **straighten** the leg, the thigh muscle pulls on the shin bone through the tendon. The kneecap acts like a small **lever** in the process. It holds the tendon a little away from the joint, so the muscle can pull with more force. Without a kneecap, straightening the leg would be much more strenuous. When bending, it slides up and down in a groove on the thigh bone.

The kneecap **protects** the knee joint from the front like a small shield. If you fall on your knee, it absorbs part of the shock. With a loose, straight leg you can feel it easily. It feels **hard** and can be **moved easily**. If you tense the thigh, however, it sits firm.

In a **newborn baby**, the kneecap is still made of **cartilage**. Cartilage is firm, but softer and more flexible than bone. Only in toddler age does it slowly begin to **turn to bone**. It takes many years until the kneecap is made entirely of bone.

At the doctor’s, the doctor sometimes taps just below the kneecap with a small **reflex hammer**. Then the **lower leg shoots forward** without your wanting it. This is a **reflex**. The blow stretches the tendon, and the spinal cord at once sends a signal back to the muscle. This is how you check whether the nerves are working properly.

gewusst: The kneecap is the biggest bone in the body that lies in a tendon.
In the knee-jerk reflex, the leg reacts before the brain even notices what has happened.

teile.einleitung: Tickling is a light touch on the skin that sets off a tingling. Many people have to laugh when it happens, even if it is not always pleasant. Researchers are still amazed today at why you can hardly tickle yourself.
wichtigste: Tickling arises from light touches on the skin.
Most people laugh when they are tickled.
Especially ticklish are often the soles of the feet, the armpits and the belly.
You can hardly tickle yourself, because the brain expects the touch.
Chimpanzees and other great apes also make laughter-like sounds when tickled.
When someone says “stop”, you stop at once.

abschnitte.text: Experts distinguish two kinds. A very light stroking, for example with a **feather**, sets off a fine tingling. A stronger tickling on the belly, sides or **soles of the feet** makes most people laugh. Both are felt through fine **nerves** in the skin. Even when an ant crawls over your arm, its little legs move the hairs on the skin, and you feel a tingling.

When you touch yourself, your **brain** plans the movement beforehand. So it knows exactly where and when the touch comes. That is why the **surprise** is missing, and the tickling feels much weaker. Important for this is, among other things, the **cerebellum**, which coordinates movements. If someone else tickles you, the brain cannot predict the touch so exactly.

Not only humans are ticklish. Young **chimpanzees**, gorillas and orangutans pant when tickled, which sounds like laughing. They often tickle each other when playing. In **rats**, too, researchers have observed that they make very high sounds when tickled, which humans cannot hear. In many animals tickling is part of play and strengthens the bond.

It can also tickle in the nose. Often **dust** is to blame, sometimes also pollen or pepper. These particles irritate the **mucous membrane** in the nose. The body reacts with a **sneeze** and throws the particles out with a lot of air. In this way it protects the airways.

Tickling can be fun, but also unpleasant or even too much. Someone who is tickled sometimes laughs although they do not like it at all. That is why a clear rule applies: when someone says **“stop”**, you stop **at once**. This way tickling stays a game that everyone enjoys.

gewusst: Even people who are very ticklish feel almost nothing when it is their own hand.
Rats laugh when tickled in such high notes that you need a special device to hear them.

teile.einleitung: Someone who is short-sighted sees near things sharply, but distant things blurred. Short-sightedness is very common and can be corrected well with glasses or contact lenses. A lot of time outdoors can prevent it in children.
wichtigste: In short-sightedness, the sharp image forms in front of the retina.
Usually the eyeball is a little too long.
The technical term is myopia.
It is corrected with a diverging lens.
The refractive power of a lens is measured in dioptres.
A lot of time outdoors in daylight protects children.

abschnitte.text: In a healthy eye, the cornea and lens focus the light exactly on the **retina**. In **short-sightedness**, the light rays meet already **in front of the retina**. Only a blurred image arrives on the retina itself. Usually this is because the **eyeball** has grown a little too long. Even one millimetre makes a clear difference.

In technical language, short-sightedness is called **myopia**, a word from Greek. Short-sighted people see well close up, for example when reading. The blackboard or street signs they see blurred, though. Many **screw up their eyes** when they look into the distance. An eye doctor or an optician can measure the eyes exactly.

Short-sightedness is corrected with a **diverging lens**. It is thinner in the middle than at the edge. It spreads the light rays out a little so that they meet only on the retina. Such lenses come as **glasses** or as **contact lenses**.

The **dioptre** gives the **refractive power** of a lens. It is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres. A lens with a focal length of 0.5 metres therefore has 1 divided by 0.5 = **2 dioptres**. The more strongly a lens bends light, the bigger the number. For glasses against short-sightedness, there is a minus before the number.

Studies show: children who spend a lot of time **outdoors** every day become short-sighted less often. **Daylight** and looking into the **distance** have a protective effect. Anyone who reads a lot or works at a screen does best to take regular breaks and look out of the window into the distance.

gewusst: Even one millimetre too much length of the eyeball makes the image in the distance clearly blurred.
Glasses lenses against short-sightedness are thinner in the middle than at the edge.

teile.einleitung: Bones are the hard, firm parts of our body that give it support and shape. All the bones together form the skeleton, which in an adult has about 206. But bones are not dead and rigid: they are living tissue that grows and can repair itself.
wichtigste: An adult human has about 206 bones.
All the bones together are called the skeleton.
The skull protects the brain.
The longest bone is the thigh bone.
Bones consist mainly of calcium and collagen and are therefore hard and yet slightly elastic.
Blood cells are made in the bone marrow.
A broken bone grows together again, often with the help of a cast.

abschnitte.text: All the bones together form the **skeleton**, the framework of our body. It gives the body its shape, carries its weight and protects the organs. The skull protects the brain, the ribs protect the heart and lungs, and the spine encloses the spinal cord. Without a skeleton we would collapse inside ourselves like a pudding.

An adult has about 206 bones, a newborn on the other hand about 300 bone parts. As we grow, many of these fuse together, for example in the skull and in the pelvis. In both hands alone there are 54 bones. The longest bone is the **thigh bone**, and the smallest is the stirrup in the ear, which measures only about 3 millimetres.

On the outside, a bone is surrounded by a thin skin, the periosteum, with nerves and blood vessels. Beneath it lies a hard, firm layer. Inside, many bones are built like a sponge, which makes them light and stable at the same time. In their hollow spaces is the **bone marrow**, in which billions of new blood cells arise every day.

Bones are joined to each other by **joints**, for example at the knee, at the shoulder or in the fingers. Muscles are fixed to the bones with tendons and pull on them, and this is how we move. Cartilage on the joint surfaces makes sure that the bones slide smoothly against each other. Ligaments hold the joints together.

In a fall, a bone can break, which is called a **fracture**. The doctor takes an X-ray to see the break. So that the bone parts grow together properly, they are often held still with a cast or a splint. In children, a break usually heals in a few weeks, and in older people it takes longer.

Bones need **calcium**, which is found, for example, in milk, cheese, yoghurt and some vegetables. Vitamin D helps the body to take up the calcium and is made in the skin by sunlight. Exercise such as running, jumping and climbing makes the bones stronger. Until about the age of 30, the body builds up bone mass, and after that it slowly decreases.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the bones of the body together, the framework of the body.
Soft tissue inside the bones that makes blood cells.
The technical word for a broken bone.
A picture made with invisible rays in which you can see bones in the body.

gewusst: In proportion to its weight, bone is more stable than some kinds of steel.
Babies have about 300 bone parts, which grow together as they grow into about 206 bones.
The smallest bone of a human, the stirrup in the ear, is smaller than a grain of rice.

teile.einleitung: A hospital bed is a special bed for sick or injured people. It has many practical parts that help patients and nursing staff. It can be adjusted, pushed and braked.
wichtigste: A hospital bed has wheels underneath so that you can push it.
The wheels have brakes so that the bed does not roll away.
Height and backrest can be adjusted with buttons.
With the call button you call the nursing staff.
Side rails protect from a fall out of bed.
Next to the bed stands a bedside table.

abschnitte.text: A hospital bed has **wheels** underneath. This way sick people can be taken in their bed to examinations or to another room without having to get up. When the bed is in the room, the **brakes** are put on. Then it does not roll away when someone gets in or out.

A **motor** raises and lowers the bed. The **head end** can also be raised so that you can sit comfortably, read or eat. The **height** is important for the nursing staff too. At the right height they do not have to bend so low, which spares their back.

Beside the bed lies a **call button**. When you press it, the nursing staff know that you need help. Many hospital beds have **rails** at the side. They protect from a fall out of bed, for example after an anaesthetic or in the night.

Next to the bed stands a **bedside table**. On it you have a drinking bottle, a book, glasses or a mobile phone within reach. Often a **tray** can be folded out from it so that you can eat in bed. This way the space around the bed becomes almost like a little home for a while.

gewusst: With a hospital bed you can take sick people through the whole hospital without their having to get up.
The adjustable height protects above all the backs of the nursing staff.

teile.einleitung: A broken bone can repair itself. The healing runs in several steps, from the bruise through the callus to firm bone. So that everything grows together properly, the break has to be held still.
wichtigste: In the first hours, a bruise forms at the break.
New tissue, the callus, first bridges the broken ends.
Early callus consists mainly of connective tissue and cartilage.
Osteoblasts build new bone tissue.
A cast or a splint makes sure the broken ends grow together properly.
A simple forearm break in adults can bear load after about 6 weeks.
Children heal faster than adults.

abschnitte.text: In a break, small **blood vessels** also tear. In the first hours, a **bruise**, also called a haematoma, therefore forms at the break. An **inflammation** follows: the spot swells and hurts. This is important, because it attracts defence cells and building cells. They clear away destroyed tissue and begin the build-up.

After a few days, new tissue grows between the broken ends, the **callus**. At first it consists mainly of **connective tissue** and **cartilage**. It is still soft and joins the fragments like a bridge. After that minerals are stored in it, and the callus turns into firm bone. On an X-ray you see it as a thickening around the break.

Special cells build the new **bone tissue**. They are called **osteoblasts**. Other cells, the **osteoclasts**, break down unnecessary bone again. In this way the thickened callus is smoothed over time. This **remodelling** can take months to years. In the end the bone often has almost its original shape again.

So that the broken ends **grow together properly**, they must not move against each other. That is why the bone is held still with a **cast** or a **splint**. If the break is complicated, a surgeon joins the fragments in an operation with **plates, screws or nails** made of metal. A simple break of a forearm bone can bear load again in adults after about **6 weeks**.

**Children** normally heal broken bones faster than adults, because their bodies are still growing and the periosteum is very active. An **open fracture** is especially dangerous. In it the skin is injured, and **germs** can get into the wound and the bone. Such a bone infection heals badly. **Smoking** and poor nutrition can also slow healing.

gewusst: Bones are among the few tissues that can heal without a scar after an injury.
The word “callus” comes from Latin and means “hard skin”.

teile.einleitung: The little finger is the smallest finger on the hand. It lies right at the outside, on the other side from the thumb. Although it is small, it helps with gripping, with typing and even with promises.
wichtigste: The little finger is the smallest of the five fingers.
It lies right at the outside, opposite the thumb.
A person normally has two little fingers, one on each hand.
In touch typing, the right little finger presses the enter key.
Many children make a promise by hooking their little fingers together.
In German, “Kleiner Finger” is its name, and in English it is “little finger”.

abschnitte.text: Each hand has five fingers: thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger and **little finger**. The little finger is the shortest. It lies right at the **outside**, on the opposite side from the thumb. Like most fingers, it has **three finger bones** with small joints. A person normally has two little fingers, one on each hand.

The little finger is more important than you think. In firm **gripping**, for example on a bar or a hammer, it gives a lot of hold. On the ball of the hand below the little finger lie **muscles** of their own that move it. Anyone who injures their little finger quickly notices how much it is missed when holding things.

abschnitte.titel: The little finger at the computer
abschnitte.text: In **touch typing**, each finger has its own keys. The little fingers are responsible for the keys at the edge. The right little finger presses, for example, the **enter key** and the right shift key. The left little finger operates, among others, the left shift key. This way you hardly need to look at the keyboard when typing.

Many children make an especially firm **promise** by **hooking** their little fingers together. The little finger is also known from a **proverb**: “Give him the little finger and he takes the whole hand.” This means: if you give someone a little, they at once want much more. In English the little finger is called **“little finger”**.

gewusst: In technical language the little finger is called “digitus minimus”, which means “smallest finger”.
On the foot, too, there is a little toe, and it also lies right at the outside.

teile.einleitung: Leucocytes are the white blood cells. They belong to the immune system and are the body’s defence force against germs. They track down bacteria, viruses and other invaders and make them harmless.
wichtigste: Leucocytes are the white blood cells.
They are responsible for defending the body against germs.
Leucocytes are made in the bone marrow.
There are different kinds, for example granulocytes, lymphocytes and monocytes.
Some leucocytes simply eat germs up.
Lymphocytes make antibodies and remember germs.
During an infection the number of leucocytes in the blood often rises.

abschnitte.text: **Leucocytes** are called white blood cells in everyday English, and the word comes from the Greek “leukos”, meaning white. They are colourless and much rarer than red blood cells. One microlitre of blood, a tiny droplet, contains about 4000 to 10000 leucocytes, but around 5 million red blood cells. Unlike red blood cells, leucocytes have a cell nucleus.

Leucocytes are made in the **bone marrow** from stem cells. From there they enter the blood and travel all around the body. Many leave the blood vessels and move into the tissue, to the places where germs have got in. Some kinds live only a few days, others many years.

The most common leucocytes are the **granulocytes**, which rush quickly to an inflammation and eat bacteria. In the tissue, monocytes turn into macrophages, the eating cells that swallow germs and cell debris. **Lymphocytes** work in a more targeted way: B lymphocytes make antibodies, while T lymphocytes recognise and kill infected cells. Some lymphocytes become memory cells, which remember a germ for years.

If bacteria get into your finger through a cut, for example, leucocytes hurry to the spot. The area turns red and warm and swells up. This is inflammation. The yellowish **pus** consists mostly of dead leucocytes and bacteria. A fever also helps the defence, because many germs cope badly with heat.

In a blood test the laboratory counts the leucocytes. Too many white blood cells often point to an infection or inflammation. In **leukaemia**, a cancer of the blood, the bone marrow makes large numbers of diseased leucocytes. Too few leucocytes can make the body prone to infections.

begriffe.erklaerung: The body’s defence system against germs.
Proteins that recognise germs and mark them.
A defence cell that wraps itself around germs and digests them.
A white blood cell that fights particular germs in a targeted way.

gewusst: Leucocytes can move on their own and squeeze their way through the walls of blood vessels.
Thanks to memory cells, you usually get many illnesses, such as chickenpox, only once.
A single granulocyte can eat many bacteria before it dies itself.

teile.einleitung: The immune system is the body’s own defence against disease-causing germs such as bacteria, viruses and fungi. It consists of protective barriers, many different defence cells and protein substances that work together like a well-organised army. The special thing is that it can remember germs and fight them faster next time.
wichtigste: The first protective barrier against disease-causing germs is the skin and the mucous membranes.
Phagocytes such as macrophages take in germs and digest them.
Antibodies are protein substances that mark certain germs in a targeted way.
Cytotoxic T cells kill virus-infected body cells in a targeted way.
In humans, B lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow.
Memory cells recognise germs again, which is why many people get chickenpox only once.
A fever can be useful because it makes it harder for many germs to multiply.
An allergy is an excessive immune reaction to substances that are really harmless, such as pollen.

abschnitte.text: Before germs get into the body at all, they have to get past obstacles. The **skin** is a dense protective layer. The **mucous membranes** in the nose, mouth and gut catch germs with mucus. Tears and saliva contain substances that destroy bacteria. Stomach acid kills many germs that we swallow with our food.

If germs make it into the body, the **innate defence** attacks at once. White blood cells such as the **phagocytes**, for example macrophages, enclose germs and dissolve them. The place often turns red, warm and swollen, which is an inflammation. **Fever** is also part of the defence, because many germs multiply less well at a higher temperature. The innate defence is fast, but not specialised for a particular germ.

The **acquired defence** is slower, but very targeted. The **B lymphocytes**, which mature in the bone marrow, make antibodies. These protein substances fit exactly one particular germ and mark it so that phagocytes can find it. **Cytotoxic T cells**, also called killer cells, recognise body cells that have been invaded by viruses and kill them. T helper cells coordinate the whole defence like conductors.

After an infection, **memory cells** stay behind. If the same germ comes back, they recognise it and the defence starts very fast. Often you do not even notice that you were infected. That is why many people get chickenpox only once. Vaccinations, in which you receive weakened germs or parts of germs, are based on the same principle.

Sometimes the immune system reacts wrongly. In an **allergy**, it fights substances that are really harmless, such as pollen, cat hair or peanuts. In Switzerland, about one person in five suffers from hay fever. In an **autoimmune disease**, the immune system attacks the body itself. In type 1 diabetes mellitus, for example, it destroys the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protein substance that recognises and marks a particular germ.
A large phagocyte that takes in and digests germs.
White blood cells of the targeted defence, for example B and T cells.
An overreaction of the immune system to harmless substances.
A disease in which the defence attacks the body itself.

gewusst: The T in T cells stands for thymus, where these cells mature.
A large part of the immune cells is found in the gut.
Macrophage means, translated, large eater.

teile.einleitung: Karl Landsteiner was an Austrian doctor and researcher. He discovered the blood groups and so made blood transfusions safe. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1930.
wichtigste: Karl Landsteiner came from Austria and was a doctor.
Around 1900 he discovered the human blood groups.
He originally called today’s blood group O group C.
In 1908, with Erwin Popper, he demonstrated the polio virus.
In 1930 he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.
In 1940, with Alexander Wiener, he described the rhesus factor.
On his birthday, 14 June, it is World Blood Donor Day.

abschnitte.text: Karl Landsteiner was born on **14 June 1868** in Baden near Vienna in **Austria**. He studied **medicine** in Vienna and became a **doctor**. Soon he was interested mainly in research. He studied how the blood and the body’s defence system work. For many years he worked in Vienna as a researcher.

abschnitte.titel: The discovery of the blood groups
abschnitte.text: In the past, **blood transfusions** were very dangerous. Sometimes the foreign blood helped, sometimes it clumped and the patient died. Around 1900, Landsteiner mixed blood from different people and observed which samples clumped. In this way he discovered the **blood groups**. He called them A, B and **C**, and group C is now called **O**. A little later, colleagues also found group AB. Now suitable blood could be chosen.

Landsteiner also researched diseases. In **1908**, together with **Erwin Popper**, he showed that polio is caused by a germ, the **polio virus**. This finding was an important step. Decades later, a vaccine against polio could be developed. Today, thanks to vaccinations, the disease has disappeared in many countries.

After the First World War, Landsteiner left Vienna. In his later years he worked in **New York** at a well-known research institute. In **1930**, he received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine** for the discovery of the blood groups. In **1940**, together with **Alexander Wiener**, he described a further blood characteristic, the **rhesus factor**. Landsteiner died in New York in 1943.

gewusst: On **14 June**, Landsteiner’s birthday, **World Blood Donor Day** takes place every year.
The rhesus factor is named after rhesus monkeys, whose blood the researchers worked with.

teile.einleitung: A vaccination trains the immune system to recognise a germ before you become ill. That way the body can react at once in a real infection. Vaccinations are among the most important inventions in medicine and have even wiped out smallpox completely.
wichtigste: A vaccination trains the immune system to recognise a germ before you become ill.
In an active vaccination, the immune system makes antibodies and memory cells.
In a passive vaccination, you receive ready-made antibodies.
In 1796, Edward Jenner vaccinated a boy with cowpox to protect him from smallpox.
Smallpox was declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in 1980.
A booster vaccination lengthens the protection.
In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Public Health publishes the official vaccination schedule.

abschnitte.text: In an **active vaccination**, you receive weakened or killed germs or only parts of them. The body does not become properly ill from this, but the immune system recognises the parts as foreign. It makes **antibodies** and **memory cells**. If you later meet the real germ, the defence recognises it at once. The disease then does not break out at all, or only weakly.

In a **passive vaccination**, you receive ready-made antibodies, for example after a bite from a possibly rabid animal or after an injury when there is no protection against tetanus. It works at once, but protects only for a few weeks. An active vaccination needs some time before the protection is built up, but lasts much longer. With some vaccinations, a **booster vaccination** is needed after some years. It reminds the immune system and lengthens the protection.

**Smallpox** was one of the most dangerous diseases for centuries. The English country doctor **Edward Jenner** noticed that milkmaids who had caught the harmless cowpox did not get smallpox. In 1796 he vaccinated a boy named James Phipps with cowpox and showed that he was protected from smallpox afterwards. The word vaccine comes from the Latin word vacca for cow. Later, Louis Pasteur developed vaccines against rabies and other diseases.

Thanks to a worldwide vaccination campaign, smallpox was declared eradicated by the **World Health Organization** WHO in 1980. Polio, too, has now disappeared from almost all countries. When very many people are vaccinated, a germ can hardly spread any more. This also protects people who cannot be vaccinated themselves, for example babies or sick people. This is called **herd immunity**.

The **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH) publishes the Swiss vaccination schedule every year, together with the Federal Commission for Vaccination. It recommends, for example, vaccinations against measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus and whooping cough. When to vaccinate is written in the **vaccination record**, which should be kept safe. Vaccinations in Switzerland are voluntary. Many children are vaccinated at the paediatrician’s or by the school medical service.

begriffe.erklaerung: A preparation with weakened germs or parts of germs that trains the defence.
Defence cells that remember a germ for a long time.
A further vaccination that lengthens the protection.
Protection of a whole group when very many are vaccinated.

gewusst: Smallpox is so far the only human disease that has been completely eradicated.
Even before Jenner, people in China and in the Ottoman Empire tried to protect themselves with material from mild cases of smallpox.
In the Covid-19 pandemic, mRNA vaccines came into wide use for the first time from the end of 2020.

teile.einleitung: Carbohydrates are, alongside fats and proteins, the most important nutrients. They give the body mainly energy. They include sugars, starch and fibre.
wichtigste: Glucose is the most important source of energy of the cells and is carried in the blood.
Plants such as the potato store carbohydrates as starch.
Lactose is the sugar of milk, fructose the sugar in fruit and honey.
Maltose arises when grain germinates and is important for malt.
1 gram of carbohydrate provides about 4 kcal.
About half of daily energy should come from carbohydrates.
In Aarberg and Frauenfeld, sugar is made from sugar beet.

abschnitte.text: The smallest building blocks of carbohydrates are the **simple sugars**. The most important is **glucose**, also called **grape sugar**. It is carried in the blood to all cells and is their most important **source of energy**. The brain needs especially a lot of it. Another simple sugar is **fructose**, fruit sugar, which is found mainly in fruit and in honey.

If two simple sugars join, a **double sugar** arises. Our **household sugar** consists of glucose and fructose. **Lactose** is milk sugar, and it occurs naturally in milk. **Maltose**, malt sugar, consists of two glucose building blocks. It arises when grain germinates and is important for making **malt**, for example for Ovomaltine.

The **multiple sugars** consist of many glucose building blocks. Plants such as potatoes, rice and grain store their energy as **starch**. In digestion, starch is slowly broken down into glucose. That is why it keeps you full for a long time. **Fibre** is carbohydrate that the body can hardly digest. It is still important, because it supports digestion.

1 gram of carbohydrate provides about **4 kcal** of energy, which is about 17 kilojoules. According to nutrition recommendations, about **half** of daily energy should come from carbohydrates, best from wholemeal products, potatoes, vegetables and fruit. **Grape sugar** makes **blood sugar** rise especially fast, because it does not first have to be broken down. Wholemeal bread, on the other hand, makes it rise more slowly.

In Switzerland, household sugar is obtained from the **sugar beet**. The beets grow on fields in the Central Plateau. In autumn they are harvested and taken to the two sugar factories in **Aarberg** in the canton of Bern and in **Frauenfeld** in the canton of Thurgau. There they are sliced, the sugar juice is leached out, thickened and processed into crystals. In other countries, sugar is also obtained from sugar cane.

gewusst: If you chew bread for a long time, it tastes sweet, because saliva breaks starch down into sugar.
Plants build up carbohydrates from water and carbon dioxide with the help of sunlight.

teile.einleitung: Bone density shows how much mineral is in a bone. The higher it is, the firmer and more break-proof the bone. Sport, good nutrition and a healthy lifestyle help to keep bones strong.
wichtigste: Bone density is usually measured with a special X-ray measurement.
People reach their highest bone density at around age 30.
About 99 per cent of the calcium in the body is in bones and teeth.
Sport with jumping and running strengthens bones especially.
Smoking harms bone density.
In osteoporosis, bone density falls sharply.
Osteoclasts are cells that break down bone tissue.

abschnitte.text: Bones consist of a framework of **collagen** in which minerals are stored. The most important of these is **calcium**. About **99 per cent** of the calcium in the body is in bones and teeth. **Bone density** shows how much mineral is in a piece of bone. It is a measure of how firm the bone is.

Bones are alive. **Osteoblasts** constantly build new bone tissue, and **osteoclasts** break down old. In children and teenagers, building predominates. At around **30 years**, people reach their highest bone density. After that, slowly more is broken down than built up. Someone who builds strong bones when young therefore has a reserve later.

Bones become stronger when they are put under load. **Sport with jumping and running** works especially well, for example skipping, ball games or dancing. Also important are **calcium** from dairy products or green vegetables and **vitamin D**, which the body makes with the help of sunlight. **Smoking** and a lot of alcohol, on the other hand, demonstrably harm bone density.

In **weightlessness**, the bones do not have to carry any weight. That is why they break down quickly. Astronauts lose about **1 per cent** of bone density **per month**. On the space station they therefore train every day on special equipment. Someone who has to lie in bed for a long time also loses bone mass.

Bone density is usually measured with a **special X-ray measurement**, often at the hip and the spine. If bone density falls sharply, it is called **osteoporosis**. The bones become porous and break more easily. In older people, the **fractured neck of the thigh bone** is especially feared, a break close to the hip joint. Osteoporosis affects mainly older women, but also men.

gewusst: In the body of an adult there is about 1 kilogram of calcium, almost all of it in the bones.
The word “osteoporosis” means “porous bone”.

teile.einleitung: Our body consists of many parts, which all have a job of their own: head, neck, trunk, arms and legs. Each of these body parts has a name, and many of them are divided into smaller parts. Anyone who knows the body parts can, for example, say exactly where it hurts at the doctor’s.
wichtigste: The human body is divided into head, neck, trunk, arms and legs.
The neck joins the head to the trunk.
On each hand you have five fingers, the thickest of which is the thumb.
The joint in the middle of the arm is called the elbow.
The joint in the middle of the leg is called the knee.
Arms and legs together are called limbs.
Inside the trunk lie important organs such as the heart, lungs and stomach.

abschnitte.text: On the **head** are important sense organs: eyes, ears, nose and mouth with the tongue. The face consists of forehead, eyebrows, cheeks, chin, lips and nose. In the skull the brain is well protected. The hair on the head protects from sun and cold.

The **neck** joins the head to the trunk, and in it run the windpipe, the gullet and important blood vessels. The **trunk** is the main part of the body and consists of chest, belly, back and pelvis. In the chest lie the heart and lungs, in the belly the stomach, intestines, liver and kidneys. Along the back runs the spine, which holds the whole body upright.

The arm begins at the shoulder and consists of upper arm, forearm and hand. In the middle lies the **elbow**, a joint with which we bend and stretch the arm. Between forearm and hand lies the wrist. We need arms and hands for grasping, carrying, writing and throwing.

Each hand has five fingers: thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger and little finger. The **thumb** is the thickest finger and can be placed opposite the other fingers, which is why we can grasp so well. The middle finger is usually the longest. The inside of the hand is called the palm, the outside the back of the hand.

The leg begins at the hip and consists of thigh, lower leg and foot. In the middle lies the **knee**, protected at the front by the kneecap. Between lower leg and foot lies the ankle joint with the ankle bone. At the back of the lower leg is the calf, and the foot has a heel, a sole and five toes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The middle main part of the body without head, arms and legs.
The arms and legs of a person or animal.
A movable connection between two bones, such as the knee or elbow.
A part of the body with a particular job, for example the heart or lungs.

gewusst: If you knock your elbow, it tingles strongly because a nerve lies close under the skin there, which is why people speak of the “funny bone”.
For most people, the span of their outstretched arms is about as great as their height.
Without a thumb, it would be very hard to hold many things, such as a pen or a spoon.

teile.einleitung: Alveoli, also called air sacs, are tiny bubbles at the ends of the finest airways in the lungs. This is where the most important part of breathing happens: oxygen enters the blood, and carbon dioxide is given off. A person has hundreds of millions of them.
wichtigste: A large part of the lungs consists of tiny air sacs, the alveoli.
Gas exchange takes place in the alveoli.
Oxygen passes into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes out into the air we breathe.
An adult has about 300 million alveoli.
Each air sac is surrounded by a fine network of blood vessels.
Together they have a huge surface of about 100 square metres.
Smoking can destroy the alveoli permanently.

abschnitte.text: **Alveoli** are tiny sacs filled with air. Each is only about 0.2 millimetres across, as small as a grain of sand. They hang like grapes at the ends of the smallest airways, the **bronchioles**. The technical word alveolus comes from the Latin word for a little hollow.

Around each alveolus lies a dense network of the finest blood vessels, the **capillaries**. Between the air and the blood there is only an extremely thin wall, much thinner than a sheet of paper. Oxygen passes through this wall into the blood, and carbon dioxide goes the other way. This process is called **diffusion**: substances move from where there is a lot of them to where there is little.

An adult has about 300 million alveoli. If you cut them all open and spread them out flat, they would cover about 100 square metres. That is more than half of a volleyball court. This large surface is needed so that enough oxygen gets into the blood.

abschnitte.titel: So that they don’t stick together
abschnitte.text: Inside, the alveoli are covered by a thin, soap-like layer, the **surfactant**. It makes sure that the damp air sacs do not collapse and stick together when we breathe out. In babies born very early this substance is often still missing. They are then given it as a medicine so that they can breathe.

In **pneumonia**, alveoli fill with liquid and gas exchange becomes harder. In emphysema, which is often caused by smoking, the walls between the air sacs burst. Large bubbles form with much less surface. People affected then find it hard to breathe even with small efforts.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for an air sac in the lungs.
The finest blood vessel, thinner than a hair.
When substances spread out by themselves from where there is a lot to where there is little.
A soap-like substance that keeps the alveoli open.

gewusst: Every red blood cell flows past an alveolus in less than a second and loads up with oxygen as it does so.
A newborn baby has only a small part of its alveoli, and most of them form in the first years of life.

teile.einleitung: The Inter-Association for Rescue Services, IVR for short, is the umbrella organisation of the rescue services in Switzerland. It sets quality guidelines for rescue services and emergency call centres. In this way, quick and good help in an emergency is meant to be assured all over Switzerland.
wichtigste: The IVR is the umbrella organisation of the rescue services in Switzerland.
In French it is called Interassociation de sauvetage.
Rescue services that meet its guidelines receive recognition.
Ambulance emergency call centres 144 are also recognised according to IVR guidelines.
Paramedics are trained at a higher vocational college.
One aim: in 90 per cent of call-outs, the rescuers are on the spot within 15 minutes.

abschnitte.text: The **Inter-Association for Rescue Services (IVR)** is the **umbrella organisation** of the rescue services in Switzerland. An umbrella organisation unites many organisations of one field under a shared roof. Because Switzerland is multilingual, the association has several names. In French it is called **Interassociation de sauvetage**. The IVR draws up guidelines for how rescue services and emergency call centres should work.

Rescue services that meet the **quality guidelines** of the IVR receive **recognition**. In the process, it is checked, for example, whether enough trained staff and suitable vehicles are available. The **ambulance emergency call centres 144** are also recognised according to IVR guidelines. There, specialists take the calls and send the right help. For the rescue services, the guidelines name a goal for the **response time**: in **90 per cent of call-outs**, the rescuers are to be on the spot **within 15 minutes**.

Various professions work in the rescue services. **Paramedics** are trained in Switzerland at a **higher vocational college**. They treat injured and sick people at the scene and on the way to the hospital. **Ambulance transport staff** earn a **federal certificate of proficiency**. They accompany mainly patients who have to be transported, and support the rescue team.

gewusst: The emergency number 144 for the rescue service applies all over Switzerland.
The response time counts the time from the alarm until the rescuers arrive at the scene.
